**Runtime verification via `/proc/maps` — arm A is genuinely running the pinned library:**

## But not on these runs

The Makefile's own comment is explicit: the nsys target *"DEFAULTS to the profiling config, which is 3 steps with grad_accum 4 instead of 1000 steps with grad_accum 64… **Do not read throughput off it**"*. And profiling adds overhead that would contaminate the tok/s we're measuring right now.

So the clean split is:

- **Three short nsys runs afterwards** → kernel-name verification only. ~10 steps at grad_accum 4, so a few minutes each rather than 19.

Symbol counts prove the library is different; `/proc/maps` proves the right library loaded; only nsys proves the dispatcher **routed to the kernel we think it did**.

That matters here more than usual, because the whole experiment hinges on one dispatch row. If the enum change didn't take effect at runtime for some reason, all three arms would look identical and we'd wrongly conclude "V2c does nothing".

## The mechanism, exactly

**Ours:**
```cpp
const uint64_t a_desc_stage = ...;                        // loop-invariant, 64-bit
a_desc = a_desc_stage + (a_walk_off >> 4);                // NEW 64-bit value, every wgmma
wgmma_...(desc_a, ...)   →   asm : "l"(desc_a)            // 64-bit operand
```

A 64-bit add compiles to `UIADD3` + `UIADD3.X` (add-with-carry) = **2 instructions per wgmma**. Measured: 27 M UIADD3 against ~9.1 M HGMMA on line 5566, 16 M on 5622.

**cuBLAS:**
```
UMOV UR16, 0x2000040        ← 32-bit immediate: UR16 holds ONLY the varying low word
UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2      ← 1 instruction, in place, high word never touched
```

**The gap is the carry.** Their high word lives in a separate register that never changes, so there's nothing to propagate into. Ours is one 64-bit value, so ptxas must emit the carry add — it cannot prove the carry is zero.

And it *is* provably zero: the encoded address occupies bits 0–13 (`desc_encode(x) = (x & 0x3FFFF) >> 4`), so no offset we add can carry into bit 32. **We know it, the compiler doesn't.**

That also explains §H40 cleanly: forcing a low-word add *reconstructs* the 64-bit value for the `"l"` constraint, and ptxas charges exactly one `UMOV` per add for the merge. It wasn't a failed idea, it was the right idea defeated by the operand type.

## What the fix would be

Keep the descriptor as a mutable low word accumulated in place with 32-bit adds, with the invariant high word held separately, and get them to the `wgmma` as an adjacent register pair without a merge — either via a `.reg .b64` written as halves, or by restructuring the asm constraint.

**Best case saves ~21 M of 43 M descriptor adds — about 30% of the 70 M excess.**

## But here is the honest expected value, before we spend a day

Three measurements say this won't convert:

| evidence | result |
|---|---|
| §H50 — these kernels at locked clock | **cycle parity** (1.010× / 0.996×), tensor pipe 92–99% full |
| §H53 — `cs` cut 7.8 M / 10.8 M instructions | **+0.00%**, D = −0.075 ± 0.231 |
| §H27b4 — cut **76%** of k-loop vector ops | recovered **2.1%** of the power gap |

Instructions here cost *power*, not cycles. Scaling from §H27b4: a ~12% instruction cut plausibly recovers well under 1% of the power gap. Against a 223 tok/s deficit, that is single-digit tok/s — the same place the V2c pin landed today.

And today gave us the cleanest calibration yet: **our best crossover-verified GEMM win, t = 11.39, bought +7 tok/s.**

## What I'd actually recommend

Not "don't do it" — but **don't do it first, and don't do it blind.**

There's a cheap decisive test before any restructuring: the mechanism predicts ~2 UIADD3 per wgmma. If we can confirm in SASS that ptxas emits the carry add, and then confirm on a single tile that removing it is even *possible* without ptxas clawing it back the way §H40 saw — that's an afternoon, not a week. If ptxas claws it back again, we stop, and we've lost nothing.

Meanwhile the hybrid work has a genuinely different profile: **Kota's library is reportedly ahead of cuBLAS by 100–200 tok/s, and we are 223 behind.** That's a ~400 tok/s swing available from routing, versus single-digits from instruction cuts on kernels already at cycle parity.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-01 14:53 IST]

Good question, and the answer is the opposite of what you'd expect from the name.

**ZeRO-1 *is* the data-parallel mechanism — it replaces DDP, it doesn't sit on top of it.** The script's own header says it:

> *"each rank holds the full model params but only 1/world_size of the optimizer state; per step, grads reduce-scatter (avg) across ranks, the fused Adam update runs on each rank's FP32 shard, and updated params all-gather back — **no separate DDP grad all-reduce**"*

So `NP` isn't "turn on DDP" — `NP` is just **how many ranks ZeRO-1 shards across**. And with `NP=1`, `world_size = 1`, which means **it shards nothing** — each rank holds the whole optimizer state, and you get no memory benefit at all.

Rough memory per rank for 4B:

| | NP=1 | NP=2 |
|---|---|---|
| params bf16 | 8 GB | 8 GB |
| grads bf16 | 8 GB | 8 GB |
| optimizer state (fp32 master + Adam m,v) | **48 GB** | **24 GB** |
| subtotal | **64 GB** | **40 GB** |
| + activations | ? | ? |

The 1.7B run used **128 GB** of the 143 GB card at `mini_batch=4`. 4B has ~2.3× the parameters and a wider model, so activations will be larger too. At NP=1 that's 64 GB of state before activations — likely OOM. At NP=2 it's 40 GB, which leaves real headroom.

**So `NP=2` is correct**, and it's not DDP — it's ZeRO-1 across GPU 2 and 3.

One thing worth verifying before we run: the script sets `overlap_param_refresh = (world_size > 1) && ...`, which tells me it expects `world_size > 1` as the normal case. Let me confirm it doesn't hard-fail at `world_size == 1` — that would settle it definitively rather than by my arithmetic.

Want me to check that, then set `max_steps` to ~15 and run on GPU 2+3?

## Your checkpoint question — yes, and it's worse than you think

**If you ran 7 steps with cuBLAS and then ran BluBLAS, it would resume from the cuBLAS checkpoint at step 7.** The `CheckpointManager` auto-loads the newest file in `checkpoints_bluscript/` by prefix — it has no idea which BLAS wrote it, because the checkpoint holds model weights and optimizer state, not a backend identity.

So the BluBLAS arm would start at step 7 with cuBLAS-trained weights, run only the remaining steps, and report a tok/s from a different warmup state. **Both arms would produce plausible numbers and the comparison would be meaningless** — and nothing in the output would say so. That's precisely the failure we just hit, only harder to spot because it wouldn't skip *all* the steps, just some.

Good catch. It's disabled now (`bef21f2`), which removes it at the source.

> tool `Bash`: Confirm checkpoint behaviour and delete the 30GB

### What's actually wrong — three things, all dispatch

**1. We don't cluster.** cuBLAS clusters *every single GEMM* — 1x2 or 2x1, no exceptions. We run `1x1` on 6 of 12 call sites, and **all six of our worst ratios are exactly those six**.

The cleanest proof is `nt 8192,3072,1024` at **2.01x**: we pick the *same tile* cuBLAS does (128x192). The only difference is cluster 2x1 + raster v versus our 1x1 + rs0. Same tile, no cluster, double the time. That's already a controlled experiment.

**2. We never set a raster.** Every one of our kernels is `rs0`. cuBLAS sets `h` or `v` on all of them. Per §H48 that knob alone measured +6.80 points.

**3. Wrong tile in two places.** We never pick 192x192 (cuBLAS uses it for the biggest forward GEMM and for wQ/wO dgrad) and never 320x128 (down wgrad).

### The good news

**Every config cuBLAS uses for 4B is already compiled in our library:**

```
256x128 cl1x2  ✓ 19    320x128 cl1x2  ✓  3
128x256 cl2x1  ✓ 33    128x192 cl2x1  ✓  2
192x192 cl1x2  ✓ 30    192x192 cl2x1  ✓102
```

Nothing needs writing. No new kernels, no new tuning. This is purely populating level-1 with 12 rows. And on top of matching cuBLAS's geometry we can stack the knobs cuBLAS doesn't have (`ubd`, `rs`, `skew`, `dh`), which were worth 6–7 points each on 1.7B.

Ranked by what it buys: **gate+up wgrad (29% of the loss), down fwd (14%), wQ/wO dgrad (10%), wK/wV dgrad (9%), wQ/wO wgrad (8.5%), wQ/wO fwd (8%)** — top six are 79% of the gap.

### How do you want to pin them?

**Option A — match cuBLAS's geometry directly and A/B the trainer.** Fastest path to a number. Build the 12 rows from the table above, run the trainer, measure. One 2-GPU run.

**Option B — short standalone sweep on the 12 shapes first, one GPU.** For each shape, race cuBLAS's geometry against our knobbed variants of it and pin the measured winner. Removes all guessing, and it's the right order given `tile and raster are COUPLED` — but it costs a couple of hours on one card before we touch the trainer.

I'd lean **B**, because the gaps are so large that guessing which knob stack rides on top of the new geometry is exactly the kind of thing that has burned us before, and B only needs GPU 3. But A gets you a trainer number today.

## I had TNT/NTN mapped backwards

The harness defines layouts at [test_bgemm_sm90_matrix.cu:777-778](examples/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix.cu#L777-L778): `opA=T` for `tn`, `opB=T` for `nt` — standard, and the same convention the trainer TSV uses. So the shapes were right.

But when I read cuBLAS's kernel names out of the trainer, I inferred `TNT = tn (wgrad)` and `NTN = nt (dgrad)`. The standalone run proves that's **inverted**: ask for `nt` and cuBLAS runs a **TNT** kernel; ask for `tn` and it runs **NTN**. I derived that mapping from instance counts and FLOPs — but every shape in a fwd/dgrad/wgrad triple has *identical* FLOPs, so FLOPs could never have distinguished them. That inference was unsound.

**Consequence: for the 10 nt/tn rows I pinned the variant cuBLAS uses for the *other* pass.** Those numbers measured the wrong thing. The 5 `nn` rows are unaffected and valid.

Re-derived with the correct attribution, the cross-check you asked for actually passes **15/15 — standalone cuBLAS picks the identical variant to trainer cuBLAS on every shape.** And the standalone run is direct measurement, so I no longer need the trainer inference at all.

## EOD

i measured our 4B against cuBLAS end to end and found we were 11.2% behind, 30,299 against 27,247 tok/s, and 97% of that whole gap sat in the GEMM alone — 190.4 seconds against 153.5. reading the template parameters straight out of the profile, every one of our ten 4B kernels was running unrastered with no descriptor hoist and half of them unclustered, while cuBLAS clusters and rasters every single gemm it issues. the tier-2 decision tree had simply never seen these shapes

i pinned thirteen of the fifteen 4B shapes to the geometry cuBLAS itself chooses, after measuring each one standalone at locked clock, one config per process, with the verdict taken from nsys kernel time and every pin confirmed by reading the kernel name back out of its own profile. that took the trainer to 28,703 tok/s and 94.7% of cuBLAS, with gemm going from 80.6% to 89.1%. two shapes i deliberately left out of the table because matching cuBLAS there is worse than what the tree already picks — one of them, tn 3072x1024x8192, runs at 47.4% on the identical tile, cluster and raster as cuBLAS, so that one is the kernel itself and no dispatch entry can reach it. i have parked it as a follow-up

then i relinked kota's blas into our own trainer, identical runner and libtensor with only libblublas swapped and both workers verified through proc maps. he gets 30,078 tok/s and sits at 98.4% of cuBLAS on gemm where we sit at 89.1%. non-gemm time comes out identical to within 0.2% across all three arms, which is the control that proves only the gemm differs. his 32.4k figure does not reproduce in absolute terms here, but neither does his 32.2k cuBLAS baseline — both his arms sit about 7% above both of ours including cuBLAS itself, which is the same library in both places, so that is his environment and not his blas. his ratio does reproduce

i then vendored the production trainer with the latest head of every repo and ran 4B on it with his blas. it does 37,875 tok/s at 55.57% mfu, up 25.9% on the same blas. i checked the work is genuinely the same rather than trusting the number — gemm launches per step come out 83,371 against 85,064, 98% — and the gain is not in the gemm at all. gemm time per step actually rose 5.6% while non-gemm fell 35%. that puts gemm at 56.5% of gpu time on production against 44.3% on the old tree, so our side of the work matters more there, not less, and every per-shape conclusion i drew today was measured on a trainer carrying a 35% heavier non-gemm load

what is still open is the cuBLAS arm on production, which is what 37,875 needs to be measured against before any of it means anything directionally. both arms are built and snapshotted, the runner is compiled for each and the 4B config is committed, so it is a launch when the cards are free. after that the other three model sizes on production, and then the hybrid on top of kota's tree

## Why — the power trace answers it

| arm | clock | power | temp | % of samples ≥690 W |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **cuBLAS** | **1635 MHz** | 691.8 W | 79°C | 93% |
| BluBLAS (Kota) | **1566 MHz** | 693.0 W | 79°C | 90% |

**cuBLAS runs 69 MHz faster (+4.4%) while drawing slightly *less* power.** Both arms sit pinned against the 700 W cap for ~90% of the run.

Work it through:

| | tok/s per MHz |
|---|---|
| cuBLAS | 22.50 |
| Kota | **23.05** |

**Per clock cycle Kota's BLAS is actually 2.4% more efficient than cuBLAS.** But it draws more power per unit of work, so on a power-capped card it loses 4.4% of clock — and that costs more than the per-cycle efficiency wins back. Net: −1.9%.

That also explains the thing that puzzled me earlier: BluTrain's *own attention kernels*, identical code in both arms, ran 3.7% slower under Kota's BLAS. They weren't slower — the whole card was clocked lower.

**So his deficit is a power-efficiency problem, not a throughput-per-cycle problem.** That's a completely different thing to fix, and worth telling him.

## 120M is attention-bound, not GEMM-bound

| model | head_dim | attention kernels | **GEMM share** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **120M** | **64** | `gqa_v2`, `gqa_backward_dKdV`, `gqa_backward_dQ` — **generic** | **1.6%** |
| 600M | 128 | `gqa_v62_sm90`, `gqa_bwd_vj1d` — **fused sm90** | 46.8% |
| 1.7B | 128 | same fused sm90 | 54.0% |

**At head_dim 64 BluTrain falls back to a completely different, much slower attention path.** The fast fused sm90 kernels only exist for head_dim 128. That's why 120M does 16.5K tok/s while 600M does 80K — the smaller model is spending **916 of its 950 seconds inside attention**.

## Box setup (once)
```bash
apt-get install -y libyaml-cpp-dev          # YAML trainer needs it, not preinstalled
mkdir -p ~/gautam_k/blublas/data            # scp 3 train + 1 val flux shard in
```

## Build the two production arms — CPU only
```bash
cd /root/gautam_k/blublas/blutrain_prod
export PATH=/usr/local/cuda/bin:$PATH

make all MODE=production WITH_BLUBLAS=0 -j$(nproc)     # cuBLAS
cp Tensor-Implementations/lib/libtensor.so Profiler/lib/libprofiler.so \
   dist/lib/libdist.so /root/arms_prod/cublas/

make all MODE=production WITH_BLUBLAS=1 -j$(nproc)     # Kota's BLAS
cp Tensor-Implementations/lib/libtensor.so Tensor-Implementations/lib/libblublas.so \
   Profiler/lib/libprofiler.so dist/lib/libdist.so /root/arms_prod/blublas/
```
**The check that catches a silent no-op:**
```bash
nm -D /root/arms_prod/cublas/libtensor.so  | grep -c blublas   # expect 0
nm -D /root/arms_prod/blublas/libtensor.so | grep -c blublas   # expect 12
```

## Our BLAS as a third arm
```bash
cd /root/gautam_k/blublas && make all -j$(nproc)        # -> build/libmyblas.so
cp /root/arms_prod/blublas/{_train_runner,libtensor.so,libprofiler.so,libdist.so} \
   /root/arms_prod/ours/
cp build/libmyblas.so /root/arms_prod/ours/libblublas.so
```

## Compile the trainer binary
`make run-train` compiles then **deletes** `_train_runner`, so extract the command:
```bash
make -n run-train MODE=production WITH_BLUBLAS=1 CONFIG=<cfg> \
  | grep -E '^\s*(mpic|/usr/bin/mpic)' | head -1 > /tmp/compile.sh
bash /tmp/compile.sh && cp ./_train_runner /root/arms_prod/<arm>/
```

## Run one arm
```bash
D=/root/arms_prod/<arm>
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$D:/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu:$PWD/Profiler/lib:$PWD/dist/lib

( while true; do echo "$(date +%s) $(nvidia-smi -i 0 \
    --query-gpu=clocks.sm,power.draw,temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu \
    --format=csv,noheader,nounits)"; sleep 2; done ) > $OUT/gpu_samples.csv &

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 nsys profile --stats=false --force-overwrite=true --trace=cuda \
  -o $OUT/nsys_<name> $D/_train_runner --config=<cfg> > $OUT/train.log 2>&1 &
# then auto-stop once 31 step lines exist
```
4B adds `mpirun --allow-run-as-root -np 2 -x LD_LIBRARY_PATH` with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,3` — and profile **one rank only**, two nsys writers hung the export.

## Keep the profile small
```bash
sleep 20    # let nsys finalise, or the CSVs come out EMPTY
for r in cuda_gpu_kern_sum cuda_api_sum; do
  nsys stats --report $r --format csv $OUT/nsys_<name>.nsys-rep > $OUT/nsys_reports/$r.csv
done
```
350–460 MB stays on the box, **20 KB copied**.

## Prove which BLAS actually ran
```bash
for P in $(pgrep -f _train_runner); do
  grep -o '/[^ ]*libblublas\.so' /proc/$P/maps | sort -u; done
```

## Are the two scripts different beyond configs?

**The ZeRO machinery is identical** — both pull in the same `owt::zero::ShardedOptimizer`, `SymmetricShardedOptimizer`, `ZeroConfig`, `ZeroOptimizerBase`, `AdamVariant`, `ReduceDtype`. Same optimizer code.

What differs is how they're driven:

| | `bluscript_zero.cpp` (his) | `train/production/bluscript.cpp` (ours) |
|---|---|---|
| lines | 1338 | 1438 |
| config | **hardcoded** + env vars | **YAML** via `ConfigParser`/`TrainingConfig` |
| knobs | `BLU_ZERO_V2`, `BLU_SYMMETRIC`, `BLU_MAX_STEPS`, `BLU_NO_OVERLAP`, `BLU_FP` | `parallelism.zero_variant: v1\|v2`, `zero_symmetric`, … |
| parallelism | ZeRO only | **ZeRO or DDP** |

So his `BLU_ZERO_V2=1 BLU_SYMMETRIC=1` has an exact YAML equivalent (`zero_variant: "v2"`, `zero_symmetric: true`) — both scripts can do the same thing.

**But here's the real difference in what we ran:** our 1.7B config has `parallelism.enabled: false` — I turned it off because ZeRO across one rank shards nothing. **He runs ZeRO v2 + symmetric at NP=1.** At NP=1 the sharding is a no-op but the code still goes through the ZeRO optimizer path, which handles fp32 master weights and Adam moments differently from the plain path. That can absolutely move throughput.

That's the most important question in the whole plan, and the answer is **yes with one condition** — I'll come to it after explaining his dispatcher.

## How Kota's dispatcher works

### Step 1 — Entry and legality (`blublasBgemmSM90_dispatch_nn`)

```c
if (M <= 0 || N <= 0 || K <= 0) return true;
int N_padded = (N % 8 == 0) ? N : ((N + 63) / 64 * 64);
int K_padded = (K % 16 == 0 && N % 128 == 0) ? K : ((K + 63) / 64 * 64);
```

It first asks: **can my kernels handle these dimensions as-is?** If N isn't a multiple of 8, it rounds N up to a 64-multiple and copies the matrix into a padded scratch buffer. Same for K. Padding costs a copy, so he avoids it whenever alignment allows.

He also handles **non-packed leading dimensions** in two regimes: if the row stride is 16-byte aligned, TMA descriptors carry the stride directly and there's zero copy; if it's misaligned, `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` *cannot express it at any tile size*, so it's forced down the padding path.

### Step 2 — The wave-utilisation model (the heart of it)

```c
waves       = ceil(total_tiles / 132)          // 132 = H200 SM count
utilization = total_tiles / (waves * 132)
```

The idea: **a wide tile does more work per CTA but produces fewer CTAs.** If you end up with fewer tiles than SMs, some SMs sit idle for the *entire* kernel.

His own example: `N=768`, `BM=128` gives `grid_m=32`. With `BN=256` that's `grid_n=3` → only **96 tiles on 132 SMs**, so 27% of the GPU never gets work. He measured those shapes at **42–54% of the reference** before this fix.

So `sm90_pick_bn` picks **the widest BN that still reaches full SM occupancy**, narrowing only when the wider tile would leave SMs idle.

### Step 3 — Hardware-measured thresholds, not guesses

- **BN=192 gets priority** — measured to beat 256, 128 *and* the cluster kernel (N=1536: 192→302T vs 256→227T vs 128→295T)
- Its occupancy bar is **3/4 of SM count (99), not the full 132** — deliberately interpolated between a confirmed win at 97% occupancy and a confirmed loss at 3%
- **WIDE-N EXCLUSION:** the BN=192 gate is skipped when `N % 256 == 0 && N >= 3072`, because at wide N it fires anyway and costs 3–5% (4B-o 745.6T vs 774.7T, 4B-ffn2 777.7T vs 813.7T)

There's also an honest note in his comments that these thresholds were once **silently relaxed without measurement** and he reverted them.

### Step 4 — The routing (`do_nn`), in order

```
1. narrow-K special case      -> 128x128x32_sw64 or 128x128x16_sw32
2. bn_choice = sm90_pick_bn(M, N, batch)
3. bm192_ok        guard      -> 192x128x64_regsplit
4. bm256_narrow_ok guard      -> 256x128x64_2WG_regsplit
5. bn_choice == 192           -> 128x192x64
6. depth4_retest_ok guard     -> 192x128x64_regsplit
7. fallback switch on bn_choice:
     256 -> 128x256x64_regsplit      64 -> 128x64x64_regsplit
     160 -> 128x160x64_regsplit      32 -> 128x32x64
     128 -> 128x128x64_regsplit      16 -> 128x16x64
                                    else -> 128x8x64
```

**Every path ends in a real kernel.** That's why it's generic — any (M,N,K) lands somewhere, versus our table which returns `0xFFFF` on a miss and falls to a weak fitted tree.

## Now your question — will performance stay the same?

**Yes, *if* we templatise by addition with behaviour-preserving defaults.** Not automatically.

The dispatcher picks an entry point *by name*. If we keep those names and the code behind them generates the same instructions, nothing changes. But "same name" does not mean "same kernel" — if we swap his implementation for ours, the register allocation, instruction schedule and defaults could all shift, and performance could move either way.

```c

// Sm90Config_* alias keeps its meaning unchanged. 0 = today's behaviour
// byte-for-byte.
```

**Every new knob goes last in the parameter list with a default that reproduces today's behaviour exactly.** Then existing configs compile to identical code, and new capability is strictly opt-in.

And it's checkable without guessing — three levels:
1. **symbol diff** — same entry points present (we just used this on coopB)
2. **SASS/instruction diff** — same generated code for unchanged configs
3. **kernel-name check in nsys + 30-step A/B** — same variants selected, same throughput

So: keep his dispatcher untouched, add knobs with inert defaults, and verify at the SASS level that the dispatched configs didn't change. If the SASS is identical, the performance *cannot* differ.

```
Call 1:  ld = NON-PACKED (K+32, N+32, N+32)
         -> builds a descriptor with row_stride = K+32, caches it

Call 2:  SAME pointers A,B,C.  SAME M,N,K,batch.  ld = PACKED (K, N, N)
```

The cache-hit test is now:
```c
s_tc.valid && s_tc.a==A && s_tc.b==B && s_tc.c==C
           && s_tc.m==M && s_tc.n==N && s_tc.k==K && s_tc.batch==batchCount
           && s_tc.lda==lda && s_tc.ldb==ldb && s_tc.ldc==ldc;   // <- H66
```

- **Without** the ld terms: every other field matches → **cache HIT** → the padded descriptor gets reused → reads rows at stride `K+32` when they're actually at `K` → **wrong answer, no error**
- **With** them: `s_tc.lda (K+32) != lda (K)` → **cache MISS** → descriptor rebuilt correctly

So Check 3 is a genuine regression test for exactly that bug.

## But being in the cache key does NOT alone guarantee correctness

I want to be precise here. The key only guarantees **the cache cannot serve a descriptor built for different leading dimensions.** It says nothing about whether the descriptor was built *right* in the first place. That's what the other two checks do:

| check | what it proves |
|---|---|
| 1. PACKED | the change is **inert** — existing behaviour unchanged |
| 2. NON-PACKED + **poison in every gap** | the descriptor uses the **right stride** — a wrong one reads poison and diverges loudly instead of quietly |
| 3. CACHE | a stale descriptor **cannot** be served |

Together those three cover it. Individually none would.

## And a real gap in my own test I should flag

**My test only covers NN.** TN and NT go through *different* descriptor functions — `init_3d_tma_MN_sm90` for MN-major operands and `init_4d_tma_B_NK_sm90` for K-major B. I patched all four, but I'm only exercising two of them. Let me fix both that and the compile:

All three pass bit-exact. But a test that passes is only meaningful if it **would have failed** without the fix. Let me prove it has teeth — temporarily remove the ld terms from the cache key and confirm Check 3 breaks:
> tool `Bash`: Negative control: prove the test detects the cache-key bug

Let me clear up the confusion — the negative control proved the **opposite** of a problem.

## What the negative control showed

```
WITHOUT ld in the cache key:   Check 3 FAIL   maxRelErr=36.18536   bad=65472 / 65536
WITH    ld in the cache key:   Check 3 PASS   maxRelErr=0.00000    bad=0
```

**Nearly every element wrong.** So the cache-key addition isn't optional — without it, a non-packed call after a packed one on the same buffers returns garbage.

## Does it cause cache misses? No.

The key only misses when the leading dimensions **actually change**. In steady-state training the same GEMM is called with the same shapes *and* the same strides, so `lda==lda` every time → **cache hits exactly as before**. A miss happens only when the ld genuinely differs — and in that case reusing the descriptor would be *wrong*, so the miss is the correct behaviour.

Cost: three `int` comparisons per launch. Against a kernel that runs for microseconds, that's nothing.

## "We never had these — do we need them?"

You're right that we never had them, and our template worked fine — **because our entry points never pass non-packed strides.** Our path is always packed.

But **his dispatcher says the model does produce them:**
> *"TMA-encodable (ld % 8 == 0): the descriptors carry the stride directly and the non-padded fast path runs with zero copies. This is the case the model actually produces."*

So in the production tree those calls exist. Without `lda`, each one falls to `cudaMemcpy2DAsync` into a scratch buffer — **a copy of the whole matrix before every GEMM.** That's the loss we'd be taking.

| | benefit | cost |
|---|---|---|
| **with lda** | skips a full-matrix copy on non-packed calls | 3 int compares per launch |
| **without** | — | a `cudaMemcpy2DAsync` per non-packed GEMM |

This settles it, and it changes the answer. Let me address each of your questions directly.

## "Is his warpspecialized_template a knob in our case?"

**No — both trees have one, and in both it IS the kernel, not a knob.** The difference is what it absorbs:

- **his:** 18 knobs, clustering lives in separate `cluster_nn*` files
- **ours:** ~40 knobs *including* clustering

So porting our template is not a step *after* the tile union — the tiles are just typedefs on our template, so they'd come with it.

## "Do we cover his whole thing plus our extras?"

**Not yet — three of his 18 knobs have zero counterpart in ours:**

```
SUPER_M              our refs: 0
K_LOOP_TWO_LEVEL     our refs: 0
MIN_BLOCKS_PER_SM    our refs: 0
```

And `SUPER_M` is not a minor one. His own comment:

> *"Tile visit order. Sweeps SUPER_M rows of tiles across all N before advancing, so consecutive tiles share operand data in L2 instead of streaming past it."*

**His dispatcher actively uses it** — that measured comparison in his code reads "dispatcher (BN=192+SUPER_M=32)". He ships `superM16/32/64` config variants. Our `RASTER_SWIZZLE` is a related idea (CUTLASS-style swizzle rasterisation) but it is *not* the same mechanism.

`MIN_BLOCKS_PER_SM` also load-bears — it's inside a smem budget assert: `SMEM_BYTES * MIN_BLOCKS_PER_SM <= SMEM_BUDGET`.

## So: wholesale is not possible right now

If we swapped his template for ours today, **every config using those three knobs would break**, and his dispatcher routes to some of them. We wouldn't be adding capability — we'd be losing three of his.

**Incremental isn't just safer, it's forced.** And the order has to be:

```
8a. add SUPER_M, K_LOOP_TWO_LEVEL, MIN_BLOCKS_PER_SM to our template   <- must come first
8b. port our template into his tree, alongside his (not replacing yet)
8c. re-express his 54 config typedefs in our knob vocabulary
8d. move entry points over family by family, verifying each against the floor
8e. delete his template once nothing references it
```

His tree has **54 config typedefs**, not the 27 I said earlier (that was distinct tile/variant pairs from entry points — the typedef count is higher). Each has to land on our knobs.

## Correcting my own framing

I'd been describing "tile union" and "port the template" as separate steps of similar size. That was loose. The tile union I did was **in our tree** — adding his seven *shapes* to our registry. The port is the big one, and it can't start until 8a is done.

Also worth flagging: one of his typedefs is literally `Sm90Config_320x128x64_FAILED_DO_NOT_USE` — so his config list carries known-dead entries too, which we should not carry across.

**To be straight about your question:** my "3 missing, 15 present" was a **name and grep comparison** — exactly the method you're telling me not to trust, and exactly what got coopB wrong. I should not have presented it as a finding. Treat it as unverified until this comes back.

## What's running

**13 agents in three passes** over both templates:

**Pass 1 — analyse (6 agents, one per knob group).** Each reads *his* code at every site that reads the knob, describes what the code actually does differently when it's on vs off — which branches, which instructions, what changes in execution order or memory traffic — then hunts *our* template for **that mechanism by behaviour**, trying at least three search terms drawn from the mechanism itself, never the name.

Groups: epilogue (4 knobs) · split-K (2) · registers/occupancy (3) · k-loop/descriptor (3) · rasterisation/swizzle (2) · pipeline depth (1).

**Pass 2 — adversarial verify (one agent per knob).** Each is told to *refute* the verdict: if it says PRESENT, prove the two mechanisms differ in a way that matters; if ABSENT, prove the mechanism exists in ours under another name. Verdicts that survive a hostile reading are the ones worth acting on.

**Pass 3 — completeness critic.** Enumerates his full template parameter list to catch knobs the sweep missed entirely, looks for structural differences that aren't exposed as knobs at all, and names the single verdict most likely to still be wrong.

Every verdict must carry file:line and a quote of the deciding code from **both** sides, and any ABSENT must list the searches that came back empty.

## Meanwhile

I'm deliberately *not* running a parallel shallow check — a fast name-based second opinion would only risk contradicting the careful one and muddying the conclusion.

**GPU: 0 MiB, 0%, nobody on it — free for your colleagues.** This audit is pure source reading, no GPU.

# Where we are

## The knob audit — the name-level answer was wrong

I re-ran the comparison the way you insisted: **22 agents, one per knob, each finding the *mechanism* in his code (which instructions, which smem, which barriers change) then hunting ours *by behaviour*, never by name** — then a second agent trying to refute each verdict, then a critic looking for knobs the sweep missed. 0 errors, 408 tool calls.

It was worth doing. The refute pass **overturned a verdict**, and the critic found **4 knobs the sweep never enumerated**.

| | count |
|---|---|
| PRESENT in ours | **11** |
| PARTIAL | **3** |
| ABSENT | **7** |

Not "3 missing of 18". But **2 of the 7 absent are dead in his own tree** — `SPLITK_FP32_STORE` (its only reader is smem sizing; its one config was reverted 2026-07-31) and `K_STEP_UNROLL` (105 instantiations parsed, every one passes 0; his own comment says *"NOT YET VALIDATED"*). Those cost nothing to skip.

## The four things that actually gate step 8

**1. `NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS` is hardcoded `2` in our template (line 375).** His derives it (`BM/64`) or takes an override, and ships it ON at `256x128x64_2WG`. This is the one absent knob that blocks expressing his configs in our template. Our own file already admits it at :2610 — *"Matching cuBLAS properly needs NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS to become a knob"* — and :2623 says *"must not be started"*. That warning was written when it was a side quest; in the hybrid it's first in line. It also dissolves the `K_LOOP_TWO_LEVEL` problem below.

**2. His template silently drops the K tail.** `k_iters = (K / BK) / gridDim.y` — integer truncation, **no ceil, no assert anywhere**. Ours ceils and lets the TMA zero-fill. **Routing any `K % BK != 0` shape to his kernel body returns a wrong answer with no error.** That's a hard correctness gate, not a perf note — our residue handling has to travel *with* the template.

**3. `EPI_DIRECT_STG` — ours is a strict subset of his.** His knob deletes two 128-thread `BAR.SYNC` per tile; in ours those barriers sit as *ungated siblings* of the `if constexpr`, so they're still emitted. §H27z.98 measured barrier-count changes at 3.4 pts of barrier stall.

**4. `K_LOOP_TWO_LEVEL` — ours is welded to `WGMMA_SKEW`, which forces BM ≥ 256.** **51 of his 53 aliases are BM ≤ 192**, so our version can't be instantiated on almost any of his tiles. Fixes itself once (1) lands.

## Split-K — decided, and one honest correction

Your call was *"if ours is best na we will use ours only"*. It is — but **not on the axis I'd have guessed.**

On the path that actually fires in production, **precision is a tie.** His has both an atomicAdd path and a deterministic-workspace path; the live 600M/1.7B profiles show **only Path B** (deterministic, `{128,2}` → `128x128x64_regsplit_ws`). His atomicAdd finisher appears **zero** times. Both designs: fp32 partials, fp32 ascending sum, one bf16 rounding.

Ours still wins, on five other counts read off code:

1. His atomicAdd path is **still reachable** at `bn64, K≥16384` — 4B/7B dW shapes can hit it, and it's not bit-reproducible run-to-run
2. His scratch is `static`, **not `thread_local`, no mutex** — and one cache *per template instantiation*, which is **the exact bug we already fixed in §H27z.27** (61 FAILs at maxRelErr exactly 1.00000)
3. His split-K epilogue **ignores `ldc`** (hardcodes `N`) while his other epilogues use `c_ld`
4. His factor **silently downgrades**: `while (sk>1 && k_units%sk) --sk` vs our exact `splitk_begin/end`
5. **Two of his six plan rows are `sk=1`** — not split-K at all, just the plain kernel with a `_ws` config

Cost in production: **1.449%** of GPU kernel time at 600M, **1.081%** at 1.7B.

**Ours ships whole; his atomicAdd path is dropped, not ported.**

## Three latent bugs the dive found in *our* split-K

One is real and live:

- **PDL fires before the partials are written.** `griddepcontrol.launch_dependents` sits at :6091 — *inside* the tile loop, *before* the epilogue's workspace `STG` at :6457. The reduce's `wait` therefore doesn't order those writes. The comment at :6086 claims the wait side alone is sufficient; that's true for a dependent reading *inputs*, **false for one reading this kernel's own output**. `..._sk2_dh_rot2_pdl_d6_shfl` sets both `SPLIT_K=2` and `PDL=true` and is dispatched for TN 2048x512x16384. It probably never fires because a GEMM CTA owns a whole SM — but that's an occupancy accident, not a guarantee.
- Odd-N `float2` misalignment in the partial store — unreachable today (all split-K entries have even N)
- `WGMMA_SKEW` + empty slice would hang — unreachable today (all `sk*` configs set SKEW=false)
- `Splitk_gating.cuh` is **dead code** — zero callers, included by nothing

## Two features, not knobs

**`grep -ic bias` over our 8,427 lines returns 0.** He has a TMA'd bias tile, four bias shapes, and a whole `launch_bgemm_sm90_addmm`. He also has a host-built Hilbert / tall-ratio tile-order map (0 hits in ours). Both are additive and break nothing — deferred past the perf gate.

Verified against the code. Three corrections, and one finding that outranks the whole knob audit.

## Correction: our split-K stopped firing this morning

Our only pinned split-K row is `2048×512×**16384**`. Commit **`7ebfc65` — today** — is *"B=2, global_batch 524288"*, which drops B×T from 16384 to **8192**.

I checked the table directly:

```
{ 2048, 512,   128, TN_64x128x64 },   //  58.6 TF
{ 2048, 512,  1024, TN_64x128x64 },   // 279.5 TF
{ 2048, 512,  4096, TN_64x128x64 },   // 444.0 TF
{ 2048, 512, 16384, TN_128x128x64_2x1_v_sk2_... },   // 607.6 TF   <- our only split-K pin
```
**No K=8192 row. And `grep -c "1536, *512"` returns 0** — 600M's shape was never in the table at all.

So under the config we've been measuring, both shapes miss the lookup, fall to tier 2, and land on `TN_64x128x64` — which our own comment calls **"our WORST site … 455.5 TF (70.3% of cuBLAS)"**.

**His `sm90_tn_splitk_plan` fires on both.** That's the whole of it:

| | worth |
|---|---|
| reduce-algorithm choice (his atomics vs our deterministic) | **~1.0–1.4%** of GPU time |
| dispatch-rule choice | **70.3% → 93–98%**, two GEMMs per layer |

I had the priority backwards. **His selection front-end is the valuable half, not his back-end.**

## Two claims of mine that were wrong

**`ldc` is not a discriminator.** I gave it to us. His split-K epilogue does hardcode `N` — but **ours makes the same flat assumption** in the reduce (`Splitk_reduce.cuh:135` writes `C[idx]` over `batchCount*M*N`). Neither enforces it. Struck.

**Our own alpha comment is mathematically wrong.** Our template:6440 claims applying alpha per-slice "would raise it to the S-th power". It wouldn't — `Σ α·pₛ = α·Σ pₛ`. His alpha-per-split is correct, and costs nothing when `alpha == 1` (the training case). What we *actually* gain is **beta**: his split-K structurally can't do it (`if (beta != 0.0f) { …plain launcher…; return; }`).

## The one same-shape number points against us

Same shape, same tile, same split factor: **his 98.5% of cuBLAS, ours 93.6%.** Different harnesses, different dates, no verified clock lock, code comments not a paired run — so per your own apples-to-apples rule I'm **not** calling that a 5-point gap. But it's the only same-shape data that exists and it doesn't favour us, and the 12-round ABBA that would settle it has never been run by either side.

Also worth flagging: our pinned row is internally inconsistent. The comment says *"the no-cluster form beats 2x1_v by 6.1% (607.6 vs 572.6), so the cluster is a liability at this shape"* — yet the pin **is** the clustered `2x1_v`, and the no-cluster enum `TN_128x128x64_sk2 = 24` exists with a live case at :758 and is dispatched by nothing. Either the comment is stale or the pin is wrong. That decides which of our configs is the fair contender.

## What survives unchanged

Our back-end still wins the tiebreakers — exact ceil partition vs his floor-twice plus silent `--sk` downgrade; beta; one budgeted process-wide arena vs his per-instantiation unbudgeted `static` (the §H27z.27 bug we already paid 61 failures to find); dtype-generic for SM103. And our determinism **is** measured, in code: *"60/60 bit-exact, 5/5 runs identical"*. None of that is a performance claim.

**Revised: our back-end + his front-end, retire his atomicAdd path.**

The PDL ordering hazard is still blocking and it's ours alone — his reduce launches with plain `<<<>>>`, no PDL attribute, so he can't have it.

---

Everything is in **§H69** with a corrections block. My "want me to start blocker 1" question stands, but the evidence has changed what I'd recommend: **`NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS` is still the right first move for the template port** — but the split-K dispatch gap is a bigger, cheaper win sitting in front of it, and it's a table edit, not a refactor. Which do you want first?

## The PDL bug, fixed

**What was wrong:** our GEMM told the reduce kernel "I'm done, you can start" *before* it wrote the numbers the reduce reads. And it said it on the very first tile, so almost nothing was written yet.

The old comment in our code said this was safe — "the wait side alone guarantees correctness". That's only true when the next kernel reads our *inputs*. The reduce reads our *output*. So it wasn't safe.

It probably never gave a wrong answer, because one of our GEMM blocks fills a whole SM, so the reduce can't actually start early. But that's luck, not a guarantee — it breaks the moment the tile gets smaller.

**What I changed:**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| normal (no split-K) | signal after last wgmma | **same, unchanged** |
| split-K | signal after last wgmma — too early | signal after the whole tile loop, once every partial is written |

I also added `__threadfence()` before the split-K signal. That's needed: the partials are plain stores, and the thing that normally makes them visible to the next kernel is grid completion — which is exactly what PDL skips. It costs one fence per thread per kernel, not per tile, so it's nothing.

**Non-split-K is provably untouched.** `USE_SPLIT_K` is `_SPLIT_K > 1`, so for every normal config the old line reads `USE_PDL && !false` = `USE_PDL` — identical — and the new block is `USE_PDL && false` = deleted at compile time.

**Scope:** 14 configs combine split-K with PDL, **5 of them are live in the dispatch table**.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-03 15:17 IST]

Let me clear that up properly — my wording was bad, and it made two statements that are actually the same thing sound like a contradiction.

## What a TMA store is, and why anyone waits

When a tile finishes:
1. the math warps write the results into **shared memory** (`c_buf`)
2. they tell the copy engine "send this block to global memory"
3. the copy engine does it **in the background**
4. the warps must not touch `c_buf` again until the engine has finished reading it

`tma_store_wait<0>()` means *"wait until my copies are done."*

## The old way vs the deferred way

A persistent block does many tiles in a loop.

**Old way — wait at the end of each tile:**
```
for each tile:
    compute
    write c_buf
    start copy
    WAIT            <-- stall right here, doing nothing
```

**Deferred way — wait at the START of the next tile:**
```
for each tile:
    WAIT for the PREVIOUS tile's copy    <-- moved up here
    compute
    write c_buf
    start copy
    (no wait)
```

Now a whole tile of maths sits between starting the copy and waiting for it. The copy finishes for free. **Both of us do this. Identical.**

## Where the gap is — count the copies

Say the block does 5 tiles:

| step | what happens | which copy gets waited for |
|---|---|---|
| tile 1 | wait (nothing pending), compute, **start copy 1** | — |
| tile 2 | **wait for copy 1**, compute, start copy 2 | 1 ✓ |
| tile 3 | **wait for copy 2**, compute, start copy 3 | 2 ✓ |
| tile 4 | **wait for copy 3**, compute, start copy 4 | 3 ✓ |
| tile 5 | **wait for copy 4**, compute, start copy 5 | 4 ✓ |
| loop ends | | **copy 5 — never waited for** |

Every copy gets picked up by the *next* tile. **The last one has no next tile.** So exactly **one** copy is always left hanging, no matter how many tiles there are.

His code adds **one** wait after the loop to catch that last copy. Ours doesn't.

**So the two things I said are the same thing:**
- "he waits once more after the last tile" → that one extra wait
- "costs one wait per block per kernel" → the same one wait

**The risk:** the copy engine is still reading shared memory. Our kernel exits. Shared memory gets handed to whatever runs next. If the engine hasn't finished, the write either lands wrong or never lands.

**Why we've probably never been bitten:**
- one of our GEMM blocks fills a whole SM, so nothing else can move in until our block is completely gone
- the hardware may well drain outstanding copies at block exit anyway

No — you've got it slightly off, and it's my fault for saying "start" and "end". Let me fix that.

## Both of us wait at the start. That part is identical.

The difference is **not** where the wait is. It's that **he has one extra wait, and we don't.**

Say the block does 3 tiles:

| | **OURS** | **HIS** |
|---|---|---|
| tile 1 | wait (nothing pending) → compute → **start copy 1** | wait (nothing pending) → compute → **start copy 1** |
| tile 2 | **wait for copy 1** ✓ → compute → start copy 2 | **wait for copy 1** ✓ → compute → start copy 2 |
| tile 3 | **wait for copy 2** ✓ → compute → start copy 3 | **wait for copy 2** ✓ → compute → start copy 3 |
| loop ends | — | **wait for copy 3** ✓ ← *his one extra line* |
| kernel exits | **copy 3 was never waited for** | everything waited for |

Read the two columns. Rows 1–3 are **word for word the same**. He only differs on the row after the loop.

## So the wait-at-the-start is not the problem

The wait-at-the-start is the good idea, and we both have it. It works perfectly — for every copy *except one*.

Why? Because each tile waits for the **previous** tile's copy. So:
- copy 1 gets waited for by tile 2 ✓
- copy 2 gets waited for by tile 3 ✓
- copy 3 would get waited for by tile 4 — **but there is no tile 4**

The last copy always falls off the end. That's not a bug in the idea, it's just what the idea leaves behind. **He sweeps it up. We don't.**

## Think of it like posting letters

You post a letter, then go do other work. Before you post the *next* letter you check the previous one arrived. Good system — the checking happens while you're busy anyway, so it's free.

But the **last** letter: you post it and walk out the door. You never check it arrived.

He checks the last one before leaving. We don't.

## So do we have a problem?

**Maybe. I can't prove it either way, and that's exactly the issue.**

The copy engine is still reading our shared memory when we exit. If the hardware finishes it off automatically, we're fine and always have been. If it doesn't, that last tile's output could be wrong.

Two reasons we've probably never seen it:
- one of our blocks fills an entire SM, so nothing else can move into that shared memory until we're completely gone
- the hardware may well clean it up on its own

But **nothing in the docs promises it.** CUTLASS puts a wait in exactly that spot, and they don't add instructions for fun.

So the honest label is: **not a proven bug — an open door.** We rely on something nobody guaranteed us.

His fix is one instruction, once per block, at the very end of the kernel where there's nothing to slow down anyway. There's no reason to keep the door open. **Take his.**

# Answering your multicast question — and I have to correct myself twice

## 1. coopA/coopB — we settled it, and we did **not** copy the mistake

Our research (§H17) **proved** it, not guessed:

> `1x2_h_bz_coopB` is cuBLAS's most common kernel — **23,325 shapes**. A 1x2 cluster multicasts **A**. If `coopB` meant "B-multicast", that kernel could not exist.

That came from our own capture of **60,733 real cuBLAS kernel names**. It also explicitly retracted an earlier note of ours that had claimed coopA/coopB = multicast.

**What it actually is: tile shape.**

| tag | tiles | pattern |
|---|---|---|
| coopA | 128x256, 256x128 | both dims *even* multiples of 64 |
| coopB | 192x192, 320x128, 192x128, 128x192 | one dim is an *odd* multiple of 64 |
| no tag | 112x128, 128x128, 176x128 | small / odd M |

Cooperative vs Pingpong are two CUTLASS **schedules** (separate files, not a flag). Multicast is a **separate axis**, decided only by cluster shape. §H12.5's decision — *don't implement a coopA/coopB axis* — still stands.

## 2. Our multicast is real and honest

```
_MULTICAST_A, _MULTICAST_B                       (template slots 7, 8)
NEEDS_A_MULTICAST = MULTICAST_A && CLUSTER_N > 1   A is shared across the N-peers
NEEDS_B_MULTICAST = MULTICAST_B && CLUSTER_M > 1   B is shared across the M-peers
```

Any cluster shape, both operands independent, all three layouts, validated. Nothing named coopA or coopB anywhere in our code. **The `coopB` name was Kota's**, on a template file — and we deleted that file in §H65.

## 3. Correction — I told you "his tree has zero clusters." That was wrong.

I grepped only his *warpspecialized template*. He **does** have cluster and TMA multicast, in two separate files, and **both are compiled and dispatched**:

| file | included by |
|---|---|
| `Bgemm_sm90_cluster_nn_template.cuh` | nn/nt/tn variants, the dispatcher, the swiglu template |
| `Bgemm_sm90_cluster_nn_v2_template.cuh` | the three variants, `Bgemm_sm90_bf16.cuh` |

Its own header: *"EXPERIMENTAL: 2-CTA thread block cluster + TMA multicast for NN's A operand."* Real mechanics inside — remote barrier arming through `mapa.shared::cluster`.

So the accurate statement is: **his warpspecialized template can't cluster; his tree can, through two older experimental templates that do 2-CTA only, A operand only, NN-oriented.** Ours is general.

**This adds work I hadn't listed.** Those files are live dispatch targets — replacing them with our knobs is a dispatch change, not just a template change.

Not one of these changes an add, a multiply, a rounding, or an accumulation order. There is no path from any of them to a different number coming out.

|---|---|

The one thing worth naming: the cache uses `cuTensorMapReplaceAddress` instead of re-encoding. If that produced a subtly different descriptor, results *could* differ. It's the documented API for exactly this, and we fall back to a full rebuild if it fails — but it's the only change with any theoretical path to a different result, so it goes on the validation list.

## Performance: four are ~zero, one has a real cost

| change | cost | how sure |
|---|---|---|
| register asserts | **exactly zero** | compile-time only, no runtime code |
| raster cap 4→6 | **exactly zero** | SASS-proven — no config passes >4, nothing changed |
| tail drain | **near zero** | +1 instruction per *kernel*, not per tile, at the very end where there's nothing left to overlap. And the copy it waits on has already had a full epilogue to finish. |
| TMA cache | **should be faster** | replaces 3 driver encode calls with 3 pointer patches per GEMM call. Host-side. Costs a ≤4-iteration lookup loop and ~3.3 MB of thread-local memory. |
| **PDL fix** | **real, unmeasured** | see below |

## The PDL fix is the one I can't wave away

I moved the trigger from early in the tile loop to after the loop. That's the price of correctness — but it **is** a price.

Our own measurement (§H27zu) found the GEMM→reduce handoff costs us **+2,336 ns** where cuBLAS's equivalent is **−192 ns**, and called that single transition "V1's entire remaining gap." PDL on the reduce was there to attack exactly that.

By firing later, the reduce gets less head start. Some overlap survives — the dependent launches once *all* blocks have signalled, and blocks finish at staggered times, so it still overlaps the grid's tail — but less than before.

**Two things keep this contained:**
- it only affects **split-K** configs — 5 dispatched entries, and split-K is 1.0–1.4% of GPU time
- the alternative (his approach: no PDL on the reduce at all) gives up *all* of the overlap. Mine keeps some. So of the two safe options, this is the better one.

**I have not measured it.** That's a GPU run and I haven't asked for the card yet.

## What still needs the GPU to close out

1. **PDL fix** — measure the split-K pin with the fix vs without, and confirm bit-identical output
2. **TMA cache** — confirm the address-replace path gives bit-identical results to a full rebuild, and see if the host-side saving shows up
3. **Tail drain** — confirm no regression (expect none)

All three are the same run, on one pinned shape, and I'll ask before touching the card.

## Item 5 couldn't be first — his cluster templates are live code

Deleting them before our template is in his tree would just break the build. So this is really the main port (step 8c), and item 5 falls out of it.

## The seam is the entry points

His dispatcher is 127 KB of routing logic — the part we're keeping. It calls leaf functions by name:

```
blublasBgemmSM90_bf16_tn_128x256x64_template(...)
```

Those are `extern "C"` and defined in his variants files. **So if I redefine those functions to call our launcher with our configs, his dispatcher needs zero changes.** That's the clean cut.

## But both templates collide on every name

```
Sm90WarpspecConfig    ours 515 refs   his 54
Sm90Layout            ours  16        his 17
bgemm_sm90_kernel     ours   2        his 11
launch_bgemm_sm90     ours   4        his  3
Sm90SmemLayout        ours   8        his  5
make_gmma_desc_k_major, tma_store_wait, ...
```

Neither is namespaced. And "they're in different `.cu` files" is **not** a fix — two headers defining the same type differently is an ODR violation across translation units too. It usually links and is still undefined behaviour.

## So I namespaced ours — in a way that changes nothing here

```cpp
namespace blublas_ws {
    ... all 8,500 lines ...
}

#ifndef BLUBLAS_SM90_NO_GLOBAL_USING
using namespace blublas_ws;      // our tree: everything keeps working untouched
#endif
```

- **Our tree:** the `using` re-exports everything. Not one existing reference changes.
- **The hybrid:** defines `BLUBLAS_SM90_NO_GLOBAL_USING`, so our names stay scoped and can't touch his.

One flag, reversible, no churn across 8,500 lines.

I deliberately left the split-K headers **outside** the namespace — their names (`splitk_reduce_kernel`, `launch_splitk_reduce`) don't collide with his (`sm90_splitk_reduce_kernel_v4t`), and keeping them global means the workspace arena stays one process-wide instance instead of one per namespace.

## Verifying this is a no-op is slightly awkward

Namespacing changes every mangled symbol name, so my usual name-keyed SASS diff will show 481 "renamed" kernels. I'll compare the **instruction streams as a set** instead — if the same 481 streams come out, nothing changed but the labels.

# What 2WG actually is — and it's the opposite of what the name suggests

## The two designs

**His:** every consumer warpgroup owns a horizontal slice of M. **Always** an M-split. So the warpgroup count grows with the tile.

**Ours:** fixed at 2 warpgroups, but the **split axis is chosen** — M when the atom count is even, N when it's odd.

| tile | HIS default | OURS |
|---|---|---|
| BM=64 | 1 WG · **1 atom/WG** · 256 threads | 2 WG · 1 atom/WG · 384 threads |
| BM=128 | 2 WG · **1 atom/WG** · 384 threads | 2 WG · 1 atom/WG · 384 threads |
| BM=192 | 3 WG · **1 atom/WG** · 512 threads | 2 WG · **3 atoms/WG** · 384 threads |
| BM=256 | 4 WG · **1 atom/WG** · 640 threads | 2 WG · **2 atoms/WG** · 384 threads |
| BM=320 | 5 WG · **1 atom/WG** · 768 threads | 2 WG · **5 atoms/WG** · 384 threads |

**His atoms-per-warpgroup is always 1.** On every single tile.

## Two things that matters for

**1. wgmma per drain.** One atom = 4 wgmma. Our own §H27zo finding says cuBLAS runs 2 warpgroups × 2 atoms = **8 wgmma per drain**, and more is better for keeping the tensor pipeline fed. His is stuck at 4 everywhere. Ours reaches 8, 12, 20 on the bigger tiles.

**2. Registers.** His thread count explodes with BM:

| tile | his regs/thread | ours |
|---|---|---|
| BM=128 | 170 | 170 |
| BM=192 | 128 | **170** |
| BM=256 | 102 | **170** |
| BM=320 | **85** | **170** |

That's why his `CONSUMER_REGS` values shrink — 240 at NCW=2, 160 at NCW=3, **96** at NCW=5. He's register-starved on big tiles and hand-tuning around it.

## So what is `_2WG`?

On 256x128 his default is 4 warpgroups. `_2WG` forces it to 2 → 2 atoms/WG, 384 threads.

**That's exactly our default.** His override exists to climb back to where we already are.

## Verdict on the missing feature

**We don't need it as a capability.** We're not missing anything he can do — we already do the good case by default, and his default is the weaker one.

**But the knob is still worth having as a tuning axis**, for one specific value I hadn't considered: **NCW = 1**.

```
BM=128, NCW=1  ->  1 consumer warpgroup, 2 atoms/WG, 256 threads, 256 regs/thread
```

That would give BM=128 tiles two atoms per warpgroup — which is what `WGMMA_SKEW` needs and currently can't have on 128-tiles. **41 of his 53 configs are BM=128**, and 128x128/128x256 are our biggest production shapes.

So: take the knob, but not for his reason. His reason is "get back to 2." Ours would be "go down to 1 and unlock skew on the 128 tiles."

Found the real structural difference — and it's not what counting suggested.

## His MN-major load is **one** TMA instruction. Ours is a **loop**.

**His** (producer, MN-major A):
```cpp
tma_4d_gmem2smem(A_smem, &A_tmap, 0, kp_g * BK, A_x / SWIZZLE_W, batch, mbar);
```
One instruction. His descriptor is built 4-D — `init_4d_tma_A_KM_mn_major_sm90(&A_tmap, A, K, M, BK, BM, …)` — so the swizzle atoms are a **dimension inside the box**. The TMA engine walks them.

**Ours** (`issue_operand_3d_mn`):
```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < ATOMS; ++i)
    tma_3d_gmem2smem(dst + i*ATOM_BYTES, tmap, mn0 + AW*i, k0, batch, mbar);
```
Our descriptor is 3-D — `init_3d_tma_MN_sm90(&A_tmap, A, K, M, A_BK_BOX, …)` — with the box only one swizzle atom wide, so **we issue one TMA per atom** and the loop is unrolled.

For 128x256 TN that's A=2 atoms + B=4 atoms = 6 TMA per k-step where he issues 2.

**That is a genuine design difference, found by reading the code — the opcode histogram could never have told me this.** It just said "42 vs 14".

## Honest gap

6 static TMAs doesn't multiply to 42 on its own — there's another factor of ~7 I haven't accounted for. I'm not going to guess at it. That's the next thing to chase.

## Second difference found

Our **consumer** has four k-loop bodies — align, the unrolled ring, residue, and a plain fallback (lines 5994–6014). His has one. That's the price of our K-residue support: he truncates K and needs no tail, we round up and handle it. Correctness we have and he doesn't, paid for in code size.

## Where the investigation stands

| finding | how found |
|---|---|
| beta epilogue emitted but never run | opcode histogram → then reading the code |

His kernel body is now fully read. Here's the definitive answer to the question you pushed on, then the state of everything.

## Is he buggy? **No.** And I was wrong about *how* he's safe.

The two "gate" functions I cited earlier — `sm90_tile_aligned`, `sm90_m_aligned` — are **dead code. Never called.** Citing them was my error.

**His real mechanism is host-side padding**, at all three entry points:

```
N_padded = (N % 8 == 0) ? N : round_up_64(N)
K_padded = (K % 16 == 0 && N % 128 == 0) ? K : round_up_64(K)
M_padded (TN only) = aligned ? M : round_up_128(M)
if nothing changed -> run kernel on (M,N,K) directly
else               -> dispatch_padded_helper: malloc + memset + copy in, run, copy out, free
```

Every route either passes an aligned shape through or pads first. **The truncating descriptors never see a ragged dimension.** Complete. Not a bug. He even says why in his own comment: *"TN's BM=128 kernels were never validated for ragged M … letting ragged M reach that path would be a real, unvalidated risk."*

## Does padding ever fire in production? **Never.**

| model | GEMM shapes | would pad |
|---|---|---|
| 1.7B (real profile) | 15 | **0** |
| 600M (from yaml) | 18 | **0** |
| 4B (from yaml) | 17 | **0** |

Every M, N, K in all three is a multiple of 64. The 35 "hits" I found first were all from `t2_isolation_cases.tsv` — the deliberately ragged *test* set. Zero from any real shape.

## So which design is better? It's a trade, and you called it right

| | **his: pad at entry, lean kernel** | **ours: residue in kernel** |
|---|---|---|
| aligned shapes — every trainer GEMM | zero extra work | 4 k-loop bodies + 6 TMA/step vs his 2, paid every call |
| ragged shapes — general BLAS | 3 sync `cudaMalloc` + 3 sync `cudaFree` + 3–4 copies **per call** | TMA zero-fill, ~free |
| correctness rests on | the entry-point padding | nothing outside the kernel |

**For the trainer, his is strictly better.** You were right: gate once on the host, never pay in the hot loop.
**For a general BLAS, ours is strictly better.** His padding cost when it fires is brutal.

## My proposal — take both, same trick as the beta fix

Add a `RESIDUE_FREE` kernel template parameter. Launcher compiles both, picks residue-free when `M % BM == 0 && N % BN == 0 && K % BK == 0`. Aligned shapes get his leanness with no padding copies; ragged shapes get our in-kernel handling. Zero host cost either way. **Not implemented, not measured** — your call.

One honest note: the 6-vs-2 TMA issue is the 3-D descriptor (§H74), *not* residue — `RESIDUE_FREE` wouldn't remove it. Separate question.

## The last two pieces of his body, now read

- **Hilbert tile map**: fires when the output grid is square or taller than 4:1; standard curve, 16-slot host cache. A feature we don't have.
- **Bias epilogue**: 4 compile-time modes (Scalar / PerCol / PerRow / Full), Full mode TMA-prefetches the bias tile into the C staging buffer. His comment: specialising took the epilogue from 11,080 to ~2,600 instructions — the same lesson as A1B0.

# Found it. And it's the exact opposite of what static counting said.

## The answer: we execute **3.3× more instructions at runtime**

| metric | HIS | OURS | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **executed instructions** | 32.1 M | **104.8 M** | **+227%** |
| duration | 216 µs | 312 µs | +44% |
| tensor pipe active | **91.1%** | 62.6% | **−31%** |
| L1 throughput | 69.1% | **98.3%** | **+42%** |
| DRAM bytes | 131 MB | 141 MB | +8% |
| waves / SM | 1 | 1 | same |

Same on 192x192: **+62% executed instructions**, tensor pipe 93.9% → 80.5%.

## Why static counting lied

I was counting instructions **in the binary**. What matters is instructions **executed**.

```
static  (what I measured all morning) : ours FEWER on 13/13 tiles
executed (what actually runs)         : ours 3.3× MORE
```

A small loop body that runs many times beats a large one that runs few. Our kernel is *smaller* and runs *far more often*.

## Where it goes — L1 is the smoking gun

**Our L1 throughput is 98.3% — saturated.** His is 69%. Our tensor pipe sits idle at 62.6% while his runs at 91.1%.

**We are not compute-bound. We are shared-memory-bound.** The tensor cores are waiting on L1/SMEM.

And this fits hypothesis 1 exactly: our **per-atom TMA loop** issues 6 TMA requests per k-step where his 4-D descriptor issues 2 (§H74). Three times the requests, three times the mbarrier and address traffic, hammering L1 — and the extra executed instructions are that loop running every iteration.

## The stall numbers prove it's not a stall problem

Every stall metric is **lower** for us — barrier −68%, long-scoreboard −67%, wait −64%. Our warps stall *less*. They're just doing far more work per unit of output. That rules out synchronisation and rules in raw instruction volume.

## What this means

The "3× TMA" difference I dismissed as **"uniform instructions, so cheap"** is the main cost. I was wrong twice about it — first calling it a candidate to adopt from him, then dismissing it as harmless.

**But adopting his 4-D descriptor is still not the answer**: it truncates MN to multiples of 64 (§H74/§H76) and is the form we deliberately retired. The right fix is a *third* option — keep our rank-3 correctness but stop issuing one TMA per atom, e.g. a wider box or a 4-D descriptor gated on `MN % 64 == 0` at launch, the same trick as A1B0.

**Card released, artefacts pulled.** That's the real answer to "where did we lose": **L1 saturation from per-atom TMA issue, starving the tensor pipe by ~30%.**

# Definitive: the box **cannot** be wider than one swizzle atom

The driver rejects it on every swizzle mode:

```
SW128  atom 64   box 64  -> OK        box 128 -> FAIL invalid argument
SW64   atom 32   box 32  -> OK        box  64 -> FAIL invalid argument
SW32   atom 16   box 16  -> OK        box  32 -> FAIL invalid argument
```

So our per-atom loop **is not a design choice we can simply widen.** With a rank-3 MN-major descriptor, hardware forces one TMA per swizzle atom. That's why we issue 7 where he issues 2.

## Which means his 4-D descriptor isn't a style difference — it's the only way to get one TMA

His `{swizzle_w, K, MN/swizzle_w, batch}` makes the atom a **gmem dimension**, so the TMA engine walks the atoms itself instead of us issuing one call each. That's the whole 3× — and it's why he's faster despite more static instructions.

The cost of his form is the truncation: `MN / swizzle_w` is integer division, so MN must be a multiple of 64 (§H74/§H76). His dispatcher guarantees that by padding on the host.

## So the trade is now fully understood, with numbers

| | HIS 4-D | OURS rank-3 |
|---|---|---|
| TMA per k-step (128x160) | **2** | 7 |
| executed instructions | **32.1 M** | 104.8 M |
| tensor pipe active | **91.1%** | 62.6% |
| L1 throughput | 69.1% | **98.3% (saturated)** |
| MN granularity | 64 (needs host padding) | **8** |
| residue | dispatcher must pad | **works by construction** |

**We bought MN%8 generality and paid ~15% throughput for it.** That's a real engineering trade, and until this profile nobody had priced it.

## The fix that takes both

Exactly the A1B0 pattern: **add the 4-D MN-major descriptor as a second path, picked at launch when `MN % 64 == 0`**, keeping rank-3 for everything else.

- aligned shapes — which is **every production GEMM** (§H76: 0 of 15/18/17 need padding) — get his 2-TMA path and the tensor pipe back
- ragged shapes keep our rank-3 correctness, no host padding, no `cudaMalloc`
- no dispatcher change

That is the single highest-value item found today, and it's the one thing that would close most of the 8.3% mean gap.

**Card is free, clocks reset, artefacts pulled.** Shall I implement the dual-descriptor path?

## The fix, as built

**`init_4d_tma_MN_sm90`** — makes the swizzle atom a gmem dimension `{atom, K, MN/atom, batch}`, so the TMA engine walks the atoms and **one instruction covers the whole MN extent** instead of `MN/atom` instructions.

```cpp
a_mn_ok  = !A_IS_MN || (M % A_ATOM == 0);
b_mn_ok  = !B_IS_MN || (N % B_ATOM == 0);
use_mn4d = a_mn_ok && b_mn_ok;
```
Tested on the **global** extent, not the tile — the rank-4 descriptor's `MN / MN_ATOM` truncates, so a ragged M or N must not take it. A K-major operand doesn't constrain the choice.

Four instantiations now (A1B0 × MN4D), each folding to one path, plus `BLUBLAS_NO_MN4D` as an A/B kill-switch so one build serves both arms.

## Two things worth flagging

**I checked the descriptor cache** — `use_mn4d` changes *which* descriptor gets built, so it looks like it belongs in the cache key. It doesn't: it's a pure function of M, N and compile-time swizzles, and M/N are already in the key. I documented that reasoning in the code so nobody "fixes" it into the key later.

**The risk I can't rule out yet:** the rank-4 descriptor lays smem out differently from rank-3. The wgmma descriptor (`make_gmma_desc_mn_major`) has to agree with it. If the smem arrangement differs, results will be **wrong, not slow** — and a throughput benchmark won't catch that.

So before I quote any speed number, the first test is **correctness**: run both paths on the same shape and compare outputs. If they don't match bit-for-bit, the speed is irrelevant.

While it builds, the reasoning behind the test design:

## Why bit-identical, not "close enough"

Both paths feed the **same wgmma instructions the same data in the same order** — only the TMA descriptor rank differs. So the outputs must match **exactly**. If I allowed a tolerance, a subtly mis-laid-out smem tile could pass while being wrong, which is precisely the failure this test exists to catch.

## Why two processes, not one

The kill-switch is a function-local `static` inside the launcher, so it latches on first use. Running both arms in one process would silently measure the same arm twice — the exact "two runs of the same backend" trap that bit us earlier today with the library relink. Hence: run the binary twice, compare digests.

## The test also catches a subtler failure

It reports `nonzero` count. If the rank-4 descriptor covers fewer rows than it should — the truncation we're guarding against — part of C stays zero and the count drops, even if the non-zero part looks right. A checksum alone could miss that; the count won't.

## Shape choice

`2048×2048×1024 TN` — TN makes **both** A and B MN-major, so both operands exercise the new path. NN/NT only exercise B. If TN passes I'll check the other two, then move to speed.

# Correctness gate: **PASSED on all five cases, bit-identical**

| case | 4-D digest | 3-D digest | |
|---|---|---|---|
| TN 2048² × 1024 (both operands MN-major) | `0612b6aa…` | `0612b6aa…` | **identical** |
| NN 2048² × 1024 (B MN-major) | `d2599aaa…` | `d2599aaa…` | **identical** |
| NT 2048² × 1024 (neither — control) | `77a55203…` | `77a55203…` | **identical** |
| **TN M=2056 (ragged)** | `5ffb651c…` | `5ffb651c…` | **identical** |
| **NN M=2056 (ragged)** | `fbffb0a0…` | `fbffb0a0…` | **identical** |

Not "within tolerance" — the same 64-bit digest over the entire output buffer.

The ragged cases matter most: **M=2056 is not a multiple of 64**, so the gate correctly refused rank-4 and both arms fell through to rank-3. That's the truncation guard working, and it's the thing that would have silently corrupted results.

## The bug the gate caught

Running correctness first paid for itself immediately. My first version read the kill-switch **only at the kernel pick**, while the descriptor was built from the ungated flag. So `BLUBLAS_NO_MN4D=1` built a **rank-4 descriptor** and launched a **rank-3 kernel** — mismatched halves of one contract, `illegal instruction` at runtime.

A throughput benchmark would have shown that arm simply failing, and I'd likely have blamed the harness. The digest test pointed straight at it. Now one flag drives both halves, with a comment saying why it must.

## Where this leaves us

The rank-4 path is **correct**. Whether it's *faster* is still unmeasured — that's next, and it's the number that decides whether our template survives.

Item 8 is a different kind of decision, so let me put it to you rather than decide.

## His host-side padding — what it is

When a shape isn't aligned, he allocates padded copies of A/B/C, zero-fills, copies in, runs, copies out, frees:

```
cudaMalloc  x3   (synchronous)
cudaMemsetAsync
cudaMemcpy2DAsync  x3-4
cudaFree    x3   (synchronous)
```
per padded call.

## Why it exists

**It's a workaround for his own limitation.** His TMA descriptors truncate — `MN / swizzle_w` and `(K/BK)` are integer divisions that silently drop the tail. The padding exists to make sure a ragged shape never reaches them.

## What we do instead

We handle residue **by construction**: the rank-3 descriptor carries the real extents, so the hardware bounds-checks and zero-fills the tail. `k_iters = ceil(K/BK)`. Zero allocations, zero copies.

**Evidence it works** — from yesterday's correctness gate, ragged M=2056 (not a multiple of 64):

| case | 4-D digest | 3-D digest |
|---|---|---|
| TN M=2056 | `5ffb651c…` | `5ffb651c…` **identical** |
| NN M=2056 | `fbffb0a0…` | `fbffb0a0…` **identical** |

The gate correctly refused the rank-4 path and fell through to rank-3, and the answer was right.

## So the decision

This isn't like shared-store, where his mechanism *might* have been better and we measured it. Here, porting his padding means **adding a slow path that fixes a defect we don't have.** Ours does zero work where his does 3 synchronous allocations.

That's provable from code — not a performance opinion.

**Three options:**

1. **Skip the mechanism, record why** — note in the log that his padding is a workaround for descriptor truncation we don't share, with the ragged-shape digests as proof. *(my recommendation)*
2. **Port it as a knob, default off** — for completeness, like `SPLITK_ATOMIC`. Costs nothing when off, but it's dead code fixing a non-problem.
3. **Port and measure it** — pad-then-run vs our native residue on a ragged shape. That would give a number, and honestly I'd expect ours to win by a lot given the allocations.

Option 3 is the only one that produces proof rather than argument. It's maybe 10 minutes of GPU. **Which do you want?**

**Don't port it, don't drop it — park it as a declared dependency**, with the trigger written down:

**His "tall tile map" is plain row-major.** No curve. The Hilbert code is the `if` branch; tall grids take the `else`.

I traced both decoders instruction by instruction:

|---|---|

|---|---|

```
NN, all inputs a constant -> every element of C must be equal
  cluster 2x1 (B multicast)   rank-3: 0 bad     rank-4: 50.0000% bad
  cluster 1x1 (no multicast)  rank-3: 0 bad     rank-4: 0 bad
```

Every corrupt element was **exactly half** its true value. Cause: for an MN-major operand, multicast partitions along K, and the consumer expects atom-major smem with the k-slices nested inside each atom — destinations strided by `ATOM_BYTES`. A single rank-4 TMA writes its box **contiguously**, so it cannot scatter into strided sub-blocks. The old offset put slice 1 on top of slice 0, costing half the k-accumulation. **No offset fixes it** — the single-TMA shape and the K-sliced layout aren't expressible together.

You're right, I chased the wrapper and never the curve. Here's the actual investigation.

## What Hilbert is for — found the design doc, it's in his SM103 tree

SM90's version is a **port**. The real comment lives in `Bgemm_sm103_cluster_template.cuh:1975`:

```
Three-way tile ordering based on grid shape:
  Square (grid_m == grid_n): Hilbert — balanced A+B reuse (~sqrt(gm×gn)× each)
  Tall   (grid_m >  grid_n): row-major — B footprint fits in L2 after wave 1
  Wide   (grid_n >  grid_m): col-major — A footprint fits in L2 after wave 1
                             ... much less than Hilbert's ~32MB working set for
                             wide grids like 4k×8k
```

So Hilbert is **not** a tall-grid thing at all. It's the **square** case. Row-major and col-major each optimise **one** operand's L2 reuse. When the grid is square neither operand dominates, so he uses a space-filling curve to keep consecutive tiles close in **both** axes and get balanced reuse of A *and* B.

That's the answer to "how is it connected" — it's one third of a three-way policy, and I'd been staring at a different third.

## And here's the thing I'd have missed entirely: his SM90 port is incomplete

| | SM103 (the full design) | SM90 (what he ported) |
|---|---|---|
| square | Hilbert | Hilbert |
| tall | row-major, `gm > gn` | row-major, **`gm > 4*gn`** |
| wide | **col-major** | **nothing — falls back to supergrouped** |

Across our 15 shapes × his 11 tiles: **59 of 165** combinations are wide grids where SM103 would use col-major and SM90 has no branch at all. That hole is bigger than Hilbert.

## Is it wired? Yes. Is it called? Rarely, and it's never been measured.

- Wired and live: built at `:1861`, passed at `:1915/:1918`, kernel indirects at `:1077/:1188`. Not dead code.
- Needs `grid_m == grid_n` **exactly**. Over 15 shapes × 11 tiles, **9 of 165** hit it (e.g. wQ-wgrad on 192x192 → grid 11×11).
- **No test, no benchmark, no doc anywhere outside the source comments.** I grepped his whole tree.

So: it's a genuine design he believes in, ported from SM103, but on SM90 it's unproven and one third of it is missing.

## The part that matters for us: two of his three branches are already our knobs

I checked our `decode_mega_tile` against each branch:

| his branch | our knob | new code? |
|---|---|---|
| tall → row-major | `RASTER=1, RASTER_SWIZZLE=0` | **no** |
| wide → col-major | `RASTER=0, RASTER_SWIZZLE=0` | **no** |
| square → Hilbert | — | **yes, genuinely new** |

`RASTER=0, SW=0` gives `mega_row = t % mgm`, `mega_col = t / mgm` — sweep all rows per column. That is exactly SM103's `for hx: for hy:`. So we already have his col-major, including the third he never ported to SM90.
