Analysis done. Five findings, and they settle the "as what".

## 1. His three-way policy is two different things bolted together

| branch | what it actually controls |
|---|---|
| tall → row-major | **which axis is fast** |
| wide → col-major | **which axis is fast** (the other one) |
| square → Hilbert | **raster vs curve** — a different question entirely |

So it isn't a 3-valued knob. It's *axis* (2 values) × *family* (raster or curve).

## 2. In his design, the map and grouping are mutually exclusive

`sm90_decode_tile_mapped` ignores `SUPER_M` completely. The moment the map fires, his grouping is gone. So **he cannot express "row-major with grouping"** — and neither SM90 nor SM103 can express "Hilbert with grouping". Ours can express the first (that's just `SW>0`).

## 3. Our knobs already cover 2 of his 3 branches — and cover them better

| his branch | ours | composes with grouping? | composes with clusters? | memory traffic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| tall → row-major | `RASTER=1, SW=0` | **yes** | **yes** | none |
| wide → col-major | `RASTER=0, SW=0` | **yes** | **yes** | none |
| square → Hilbert | — | — | — | — |

His pays a `cudaMalloc` + one global load per tile; ours is a divmod.

## 4. The architecture finding — his SM90 can't combine tile order with clusters at all

| his SM90 file | tile map / Hilbert | clusters + multicast |
|---|---|---|
| `warpspecialized_template.cuh` | **yes** | **none** |
| `cluster_nn_template.cuh` | none | yes (supergrouped only) |
| `cluster_nn_v2_template.cuh` | none | yes |

Separate files, no composition. Our `RASTER`/`RASTER_SWIZZLE` run on the **cluster-collapsed mega-grid** (`make_mega_div` divides by `CLUSTER_M`/`CLUSTER_N`), so ordering and clusters compose in one template by construction. **If we build Hilbert in our template it will be strictly more capable than either of his** — Hilbert *with* clusters, which his SM90 cannot do, and Hilbert *with* grouping, which even his SM103 cannot do.

## 5. A hard constraint decides the implementation

His host map **compacts** the curve: `map[idx]` = the idx-th point that lands inside the real grid; outside points are skipped. To do that on device you'd have to answer "which is the t-th *valid* point" — a rank query over the whole curve, O(n²) per tile. **Unless the grid is a power-of-two square**, where nothing is skipped and `t` maps straight through in O(log n).

```
8 of 9 square cases in our shapes ARE power-of-two squares (128x128, 16x16)
the 1 exception: wQ-wgrad on 192x192 -> 11x11
```

## So: "as what?" — my answer

**Not** a value of `RASTER_SWIZZLE`, and **not** a third `RASTER` value. Both would leave the other knob settable-but-meaningless, so `HILBERT + SW=3` would compile and mean nothing.

It should be a **separate knob naming the order family**, with `RASTER` and `RASTER_SWIZZLE` demoted to being the *parameters of the raster family*:

```
TILE_ORDER = Raster | Hilbert          <- new: which family
  RASTER        = 0(v) | 1(h)          <- existing: only meaningful under Raster
  RASTER_SWIZZLE= 0..6                 <- existing: only meaningful under Raster
```

with a `static_assert` that `TILE_ORDER==Hilbert` implies `RASTER_SWIZZLE==0`, so the invalid combo can't be written. That keeps our vocabulary, adds one concept, and the 241 registered configs need no edit (they default to `Raster`).

For the curve itself I'd do **device-side decode, gated to power-of-two square mega-grids**, falling back to raster otherwise — covers 8/9, costs no memory, and composes with clusters. His host-map form only becomes necessary if you want the 11×11 case too.

**Three things I want your call on before I write any code:**

1. **`TILE_ORDER` as the knob name** — or do you want a different word? It'll appear in every config name (e.g. `..._hilb`) and in the dispatcher.
2. **Device decode (8/9, no memory, cluster-safe) or also the host map for non-power-of-2 squares?** I lean device-only first, add the host path only if a real shape needs it.
3. **The wide/col-major gap** — 59 of 165 combos are wide grids his SM90 leaves on the table, and we already own the knob (`RASTER=0, SW=0`). Do you want that measured in the same session as Hilbert, or kept separate?

One caution from today, so we don't repeat it: the tall rule turned out **tile-specific** — it held on 128x256 and reversed on 256x128. So whatever we build here, the dispatch rule has to be measured per tile, not adopted from his thresholds.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-04 14:19 IST]

Fair. Let me explain it from the start, plainly.

## The background

A big matrix multiply gets cut into small squares called **tiles**. The GPU has 132 processors. It hands out tiles to them, one after another, until all tiles are done.

**The order you hand out the tiles changes the speed.** Not the answer — the answer is always the same. Just the speed.

Why? Because of cache. If two tiles that run at the same time need the same piece of data, that data gets loaded once and shared. If they need different data, it gets loaded twice. Loading from memory is slow. So a good order puts tiles that share data next to each other.

## The three orders

Say the tile grid is 86 rows by 262 columns.

- **Row-major**: do all of row 0 left to right, then all of row 1, and so on.
- **Column-major**: do all of column 0 top to bottom, then all of column 1, and so on.
- **Grouping**: don't do one full row at a time. Do a *band* of 8 rows at a time, sweeping across. Then the next 8 rows.

Row-major and column-major each help one of the two input matrices. Grouping is a separate idea you can add on top of either one.

## What Kota's code does

His code picks the order automatically from the grid shape:

- tall grid (many rows, few columns) → row-major
- wide grid (few rows, many columns) → column-major
- square grid → a fancy zigzag curve called Hilbert

**But here's the catch in his code: when he uses that automatic order, his grouping switches off.** The two are wired as either/or. So he can do "column-major", but he can never do "column-major with grouping".

## What our code does

We have two knobs:
- `RASTER` = row-major or column-major
- `RASTER_SWIZZLE` = the group size

**Ours can be used together.** So we can do "column-major with grouping". He can't.

## What I measured today

One real shape from the trainer: `lm_head-fwd`, a wide grid. I tried all six combinations, 12 rounds each, GPU clock locked so the numbers are fair.

| what we tried | speed | vs what we use today |
|---|---|---|
| column-major **with grouping** | 785.07 | **+0.84% — fastest** |
| row-major with small grouping | 781.60 | +0.39% |
| row-major with grouping (**what we use today**) | 778.56 | — |
| row-major, no grouping | 761.58 | −2.18% |
| column-major, small grouping | 745.64 | −4.23% |
| **column-major, no grouping** ← **his rule** | **719.24** | **−7.62% — slowest** |

## What it means

**His rule would have made this shape 7.6% slower.** His rule says "wide grid → column-major", and column-major on its own is the worst of the six.

But column-major **plus grouping** is the best. That combination is the one his code physically cannot produce, because his grouping turns off whenever his automatic order turns on.

So this is a case where we are genuinely better — and I have the measurement, not just an argument.

## The check that proves I'm not fooling myself

I included two shapes where we *already* use column-major. If I flipped those to row-major, they should get worse. One did — 1.59% worse. So the test really is measuring tile order, not noise.

I also re-ran all six versions and confirmed they all produce **exactly the same answer**, bit for bit. Only speed changes.

```cpp
// Runtime path — GUARDED
```

His fast `PerCol` path reads **two bf16 unguarded**. That's safe *only because he pads on the host* — the §H76/§H89 contract. We deliberately don't pad; we support ragged N. **A direct port of his PerCol would read out of bounds on any N that isn't tile-aligned.**

## His design, and what's worth taking

`enum class Sm90BiasMode { Runtime, Scalar, PerCol, PerRow, Full }` as a **compile-time** template parameter, and his own comment says why:

> bias_numel used to be a runtime argument, so a 4-way chain was emitted per element across a fully unrolled epilogue — **11,080 instructions** spent deciding *which* bias to add, against ~1,500 for the entire no-bias kernel. Specializing took it to ~2,600 and dropped the epilogue's cost over no-bias from **+44.9% to +3.7%**.

That's measured, not asserted. **Take it.** It's the same principle as our own knobs — make it compile-time, never runtime.

Let me explain the whole thing properly, then build it.

## 1. What "bias" and "addmm" mean

A plain matrix multiply computes `C = A × B`.

A neural network layer almost always computes `C = A × B + bias`. That extra add is the bias. `addmm` is just the name for "add + matrix multiply" — it's what PyTorch calls it, and it's what every Linear layer does.

Right now our GEMM cannot do the `+ bias` part **at all**. So the trainer has to run our matmul, then launch a **second kernel** to add the bias. That second kernel reads the whole output matrix from memory and writes it back. For a 16384×50304 output that's 1.6 GB read plus 1.6 GB written, purely to add one number per column.

If the bias is added **inside** the GEMM — at the moment the result is already sitting in registers, just before it gets stored — that entire extra pass disappears. That is the whole point of the feature.

## 2. The bias comes in four shapes

| shape | size | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Scalar** | 1 number | add the same number everywhere |
| **PerCol** | N numbers | one per output column — **this is what a Linear layer uses** |
| **PerRow** | M numbers | one per output row |
| **Full** | M×N numbers | a whole matrix added on |

PerCol is the common case by far. The other three exist for generality.

## 3. What his code does — and the important part

His kernel has **two** ways of handling this.

**The slow way (`Runtime`)** — the bias shape is a normal function argument, so the kernel has to ask, for every single output element:

```cpp
if (bias_numel == 1)          ... // scalar?
else if (bias_numel == N)     ... // per column?
else if (bias_numel == M)     ... // per row?
else if (bias_numel == M*N)   ... // full?
```

**The fast way** — the bias shape is a **template parameter**, decided when the code is compiled. Then `if constexpr` deletes the three branches you don't need. The compiled kernel contains only the one case it will ever run.

His own comment records what that was worth, measured:

> the 4-way chain was emitted per element across a fully unrolled epilogue — **11,080 instructions** spent deciding *which* bias to add, against **~1,500** for the entire no-bias kernel. Specializing took it to **~2,600**, and dropped the epilogue's cost over no-bias from **+44.9% to +3.7%**.

Read that again: the *deciding* cost more than **seven times** the entire rest of the kernel. Because the epilogue is fully unrolled, that four-way question got duplicated into the machine code hundreds of times.

**This is exactly the principle we already follow** — every feature a compile-time knob, never a runtime branch. So this is not something to argue with. We take it.

## 4. The problem I found in his fast path

Look at the two paths side by side. Runtime path:

```cpp
if (global_col < N)     b0 = bias[global_col];        // checked
if (global_col + 1 < N) b1 = bias[global_col + 1];    // checked
```

Fast `PerCol` path:

```cpp
const __nv_bfloat162 b2 = *(const __nv_bfloat162*)(bias + global_col);   // NO check
```

The fast one grabs **two values at once** with no bounds check. That's faster — one load instead of two.

It is safe **in his tree** because he pads every matrix on the host so N is always a whole number of tiles. There is never a partial tile, so `global_col + 1` is always inside the array.

**We do not pad.** We deliberately support ragged sizes — that was the §H76 decision, and I wrote it into the code as a standing contract yesterday. So if I copy his line as-is, then any N that isn't tile-aligned reads past the end of the bias array. That is a real out-of-bounds read: garbage values, or a crash.

So this is the one place where copying him exactly would be wrong **for us**, and it's wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with his code being bad — his code is correct given his padding.

## 5. What "build it in our way" means, concretely

**Same:** the four modes, the compile-time specialisation, the same arithmetic, the same order of operations, the same point in the epilogue (bias added to the accumulator before the store, not after).

**Ours:** the naming follows our vocabulary; it becomes a template knob in our config the way every other feature is; and the unguarded load gets a gate — take the fast 2-at-a-time load when the tile is provably fully inside the array, fall back to the checked single loads otherwise. Same instructions in the common case, correct in the case his code never has to handle.

## 6. About "everything must be the same — instructions, count, order"

I want to be straight with you about one limit here, because I'd rather say it now than have you find it later.

**I can make the bias logic identical** — same operations, same kinds, same order, same flow. That I will do and will verify by reading both side by side and by dumping the SASS of the bias region.

**I cannot make the total kernel instruction count identical**, because the code *around* the bias is different. Our epilogue is chunked; his is not. Those already differ, and in several places we already measured ours as better. Making the totals match would mean throwing away our epilogue and taking his wholesale — which is a much bigger change than adding bias, and one the measurements don't support.

So: bias logic identical, surrounding epilogue stays ours. If you actually meant the whole epilogue should become his too, tell me and that becomes a separate, larger job — but I don't think that's what you want, and the numbers say it would cost us.

## There are two ways to compare our code with his

**Way 1 — compare feature by feature.** Take one thing at a time. His way of doing X, our way of doing X. Which is better? We did this by reading the code. There were **13 things** both of us have. Result: **ours better on 7, his better on 3, and 3 where we should mix**.

**Way 2 — compare whole kernels.** Take his complete kernel and our complete kernel, run them both, see which is faster. We did this too, on **14 of his kernels**. Result: **he won 10, we won 3, 1 tie. He was 8.3% faster on average.**

## Here is the problem

Way 1 said **we are better** (7 to 3).
Way 2 said **he is better** (10 to 3).

Both were done carefully. They disagree.

So reading the code feature by feature does **not** tell you who is actually faster. Winning on 7 pieces out of 13 did not make our whole kernel faster.

## And today showed the opposite problem

Today with the bias work, Way 2 told me "his is faster, we are at 87%". That was true. But it told me **nothing about what to fix**.

## So the answer to your question

**No — just comparing all the variants will not automatically cover everything.**

- Comparing whole kernels tells you **where** you are losing. It does not tell you **why**. Without why, you cannot fix it.
- Comparing features one by one tells you why, but it **predicted the wrong winner** last time.

You need both, in this order:
1. Run all the kernels head to head → find where we lose
2. Only at those places, dig in with the profiler → find the reason
3. Fix it, measure again

Do not dig into places where we already win. That is wasted GPU time.

My inputs are small signed values, so a K=4096 accumulation lands many outputs near zero, and a per-element relative error with a 1e-3 floor divides by nothing and explodes. Fixed: normalise by the largest magnitude in the reference matrix.

**2. The crash is the build, not the call.** Every entry died with `misaligned address` at the sync right after the GEMM. I ruled out, in order: the shape (4096³ fails too, and that's a production shape), cuBLAS (bench mode never calls it and still faults), the handle (`blublasHandle_t` is a pointer, nullptr → stream 0 on both sides), and the signatures — **all 73 of his entry points take `lda/ldb/ldc` and my declarations match exactly**. These TUs have no cross-TU device calls, so plain `-c` keeps the parallel build without the relocatable path.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-04 21:40 IST]

Yes — **A/B is purely speed.** Correctness is done and passed, so now the only question left is who's faster.

Here's what it's doing, plainly:

- For each of the 44 entry points, it runs **our kernel** and **his kernel** on the **same shape**, and records TFLOPS for both
- 12 rounds per entry point
- **ABBA crossover** — odd rounds run his first, even rounds run ours first. Because whichever runs first hits a colder card and looks slower. Without swapping the order you get a fake winner (this exact fault once gave me a t=4.63 on a null result)
- **One entry point per process** — running many configs in one process deflates some of them 6–8%
- Clocks locked at 1785 MHz, verified holding under load

At the end I get, per entry point: our TFLOPS, his TFLOPS, our percentage of his, and a t-statistic saying whether the difference is real or noise.

**That table is the whole point of today.** It tells us which of the 44 slots we lose, and those are the ones to fix. Each slot is bound to one of our configs by a single `using` line, so re-pointing a loser is a one-line change.

When a config sets the swizzle to 64 or 32, our code applied that to **both** operands. But one operand needs its swizzle chosen from its own size, not from the config. Kota's code does this correctly; ours did not.

Zero error is the *expected* result, and any real logic bug shows up immediately instead of hiding under a tolerance.

Every tile where the M-atom count doesn't divide the warpgroup count gets **half-width wgmma** — roughly double the instructions for the same math. Those are our three worst big tiles.

## And now his design makes complete sense

The reason he can use NCW=3 is the **register budget**, and the two knobs are coupled:

```
PRODUCER_REGS + NCW × CONSUMER_REGS ≤ 512
```

- ours, NCW=3: `40 + 3×232 = 736` → **illegal**
- his `_regsplit`: `24 + 3×160 = 504` → **legal**

## What happened — a real finding, not just a mishap

`320x64x64_ncw5` **hung the GPU**. Ran 4:37 pinned at 100%, never returned.

And our own assert's comment predicted exactly this failure mode — *"an over-budget request can hang per the PTX ISA spec (setmaxnreg.inc blocks until registers are available), not just under-perform"* — but **the assert didn't catch it**, because the formula is incomplete:

```
assert:  PREG + NCW*CREG  <=  65536 / (128 * MIN_BLOCKS)   =   512
mine:    24   + 5*96      =   504                          ->   PASSES
```

The sum is fine. What it misses: NCW=5 means **6 warpgroups = 768 threads**, so the *baseline* allocation is `65536/768 = 85` registers per thread. Asking for `CONSUMER_REGS=96` is an **increase**, and `setmaxnreg.inc` blocks until registers free up — which never happens. The assert only checks the total, never the per-thread baseline the increase is measured against.

That's a genuine gap in our safety check, and it's worth fixing regardless of the NCW experiment — any future high-NCW config can hit it.

## What this means for the experiment

- `192x128x64_ncw3` and `_ncw3_nors` — **both passed exact** before the hang
- `320x64x64_ncw5` (24/96) — **hangs**, unusable as written
- `320x64x64_ncw5_nors` (regs 0/0) — untested, but 0/0 disables `setmaxnreg` entirely so it should be immune. That's his own plain-config route, and it's now the interesting arm

## Two things I did wrong here

I let it run 4½ minutes before checking whether it was slow or stuck. I should have timed-out the individual check. And I picked `CREG=96` by dividing the budget rather than checking it against the per-thread baseline — the exact "assume instead of verify" failure we keep hitting.

## Proposed next step

1. Fix the assert to model the per-thread baseline, so this class of hang is a compile error
2. Drop the `_ncw5` (24/96) arm; keep `_ncw5_nors` (0/0)
3. Add a per-check timeout so a hang costs seconds, not minutes
4. Re-run the gate and the 4-way A/B

### CLAUDE [2026-09-05 14:43 IST]

Good question, and it's not a silly one — Strassen is real and it does get used. But for this workload the answer is **no, and here's the arithmetic.**

## What Strassen actually trades

For a 2×2 block split: normal is **8 block-multiplies + 4 block-adds**. Strassen is **7 block-multiplies + 18 block-adds**. You save one multiply (12.5%) and pay 14 extra adds.

On a CPU that's a clear win, because multiply and add cost roughly the same.

**On a tensor-core GPU they do not.** The multiply runs on the tensor pipe at ~1000 TFLOPS bf16. The adds run on the vector units at ~60 TFLOPS, and they're actually memory-bound, not compute-bound — each add reads two matrices and writes one.

Working it through for block size n:
- multiply saved: `2n³ / 1000e12` seconds
- 18 adds cost, at ~3 TB/s: `3·n²·2 bytes / 3e12` seconds

Break-even lands around **n ≈ 1000**. So on paper, for blocks bigger than ~1000×1000, Strassen is marginally positive.

## Why it still doesn't fit here

**1. It attacks the wrong bottleneck.** We measured this today — our problem was **DRAM traffic**, not FLOPs. Our compute throughput sits at ~62%, so the tensor pipe isn't the limit. Strassen *adds* memory traffic (18 extra passes plus temporaries) to save compute we aren't short of. It would make our measured weakness worse.

**2. bf16 has 8 mantissa bits.** Strassen's error bound is significantly worse than normal matmul — it's the classic tradeoff. Right now every one of our 77 kernels matches cuBLAS **exactly** (`err = 0.000e+00`). Strassen would end that, and in training that shows up as drift you can't easily attribute.

**3. Our shapes are often not square.** The real training shapes are things like 2048×512×16384 — very fat K, narrow N. Strassen splits M and N; with N=512 you get one or two levels before the blocks are too small to beat the overhead.

**4. It doesn't map to wgmma.** The whole kernel is built to feed `HGMMA.64x128x16`. The submatrix add/subtract steps can't use tensor cores at all.

## Where it *is* used

Very large **square** matmuls in **fp32/fp64**, mostly on CPUs and in a few research GPU libraries. Reported gains are a few percent at n in the tens of thousands. No production BF16 tensor-core GEMM library — not cuBLAS, not CUTLASS — ships Strassen.

## Honest bottom line

It's a legitimate technique aimed at a bottleneck we don't have, at a precision that can't absorb it. And we're currently at **97.9% of his and climbing** with changes that cost nothing and keep exact results.

If you want to revisit it, the right time is after we're past him — and the right first step would be a cheap offline error study in bf16, not a kernel.

Fix: our config gets our name, his name becomes **one explicit binding line** at the export boundary, recorded in the rename map. Fixing it now, and taking the coopB regression out at the same time:
> tool `Bash`: 

Verified working exactly as intended:

```
128x256x64_2x1_mcB (ours)     cluster=2x1  mcA=0 mcB=1   RASTER_SWIZZLE=0   <- pinned
128x256x64_1x2_mcA (ours)     cluster=1x2  mcA=1 mcB=0   RASTER_SWIZZLE=0   <- pinned
coopB_...      (his name)     -> resolves to our 2x1_mcB
coopB_v2_...   (his name)     -> resolves to our 2x1_mcB
128x128x64     (normal tile)  cluster=1x1              RASTER_SWIZZLE=3   <- gets the win
```

Two things fixed at once:

**1. The naming.** Our configs now carry **our** vocabulary — `128x256x64_2x1_mcB` (cluster shape + which operand is multicast), matching how we name every other cluster config. His `coopA`/`coopB`/`coopB_v2` names survive only as **four binding lines at the export boundary**, clearly marked, because the X-macro derives the exported symbol from the config name and his dispatcher links against those symbols. When we swap his dispatcher in, those are the renames — and they're now written into the file as the record.

**2. The 6 regressions are gone.** `RASTER_SWIZZLE` is pinned to 0 on the two cluster configs, so they keep their ~100% and every other tile still gets the +7.2. A 2-CTA cluster already has its L2 locality from the cluster; grouping the raster on top fights it.

**On "we don't know what coopB is"** — we do, and it's confirmed twice: his own file header says *"2-CTA thread block cluster + TMA multicast for NN's B operand, clustered along M"*, and the compiled config reads `cluster=2x1, mcA=0, mcB=1`. Source and binary agree.

One genuine difference worth noting: our pre-existing `_2x1`/`_1x2` multicast **both** operands. His multicasts only the one that can actually be shared. That's his being cleaner than us, and it's now in our tree under our own name.

**98.0% of his across all 77**, and with the coopB pin the 6 regressions become nulls — so no kernel is worse than before, 20 match or beat him, and 2 remain under 90%.

# My prediction was wrong. Reporting it straight.

**I said the two fixes would stack toward 100%. They don't.**

```
192x128 family:   rswz alone 93.2%  ->  rswz + NCW3 93.6%   (+0.4)

```

| in isolation | on top of rswz |
|---|---|
| NCW3 alone: **+9.3 pts** | NCW3 on rswz: **+0.4 pts** |

## What that actually means

Both fixes were attacking **the same bottleneck**, not two different ones. My reasoning — *"raster is L2 reuse, NCW is wgmma width, so they should stack"* — was wrong.

In hindsight the mechanism is clear: the kernel was **memory-bound**. Half-width wgmma doubles the tensor-core instructions, but if you're waiting on memory anyway, those extra instructions are free. Once `rswz` fixed the memory traffic, the wgmma width stopped mattering. The +9.3 that NCW3 showed in isolation was it partially compensating for a memory problem that `rswz` solves properly.

## Decision: drop the NCW3 change

+0.4 points is not worth it. It forces the register split (24/160 instead of our default 40/232), adds a config dependency, and the register budget constraint is what caused the GPU hang earlier. **Reverting it** — `192x128` stays at NCW=2 with `rswz`, at 93.2%.

## What this costs us in credibility, and the lesson

This is the second time today that a mechanism proven at compile time didn't convert:
- `DESC_HOIST` — chain 23/13/6 → 11/4/0, bought +0.45
- `NCW3` — half-width → full-width wgmma, bought +0.4 on top of rswz

**Proving the mechanism is real is not the same as proving it's the bottleneck.** Both were real mechanisms. Neither was what limited us. The only thing that has actually converted today is the one ncu pointed at.

So the rule tightens: **measure what the hardware is waiting on first, then look for the cause of that specific wait.** Not "find a difference and fix it."

## Where we stand

**98.0% of all 77, 98.7% of the routed 42.** Unchanged — nothing lost, nothing gained from this last round.

The `sw32` investigation from earlier is now the better lead precisely because it came from ncu: identical bytes, half the L2 throughput, and **9 wait call sites in our source against his 3**, with six being duplicates of the same two waits on different code paths.

# Backtrack complete — from SASS to the exact line

```cpp
__device__ __forceinline__ uint32_t cluster_ctarank() {
    uint32_t rank;
    asm volatile("mov.u32 %0, %%cluster_ctarank;" : "=r"(rank));   // <- asm VOLATILE
    return rank;
}

// line 6112
const uint32_t cluster_rank = (CLUSTER_SIZE > 1) ? cluster_ctarank() : 0u;
```

**`asm volatile` in the untaken arm of a ternary.** The condition is compile-time false for `CLUSTER_SIZE==1`, but `volatile` tells the compiler the asm has side effects it may not remove — so `mov.u32 %cluster_ctarank` survives into the SASS as `S2UR UR10, SR_CgaCtaId`, and every barrier address downstream gets built the cluster way:

```

ULEA UR8, UR10, UR9, 0x18       <- 0x400 + (rank << 24)   DSMEM encoding
ULEA UR8, UR4, UR8, 0x3         <- + stage*8
SYNCS...TRYWAIT P0, [UR8], R5   <- spin on it
```

**His version has none of this** — `full_mbar_addr` is `__cvta_generic_to_shared(full_mbar)` hoisted once outside the loop, then `+ stage*8`. Plain CTA shared memory, no rank read, no shift, nothing recomputed.

**Every other cluster site in our kernel uses `if constexpr`** — 6056, 6204, 6470, 8315, 8350, 8434. Only 6112 uses a ternary. It's a one-line inconsistency.

And `issued` is declared outside the tile loop, so it counts for the CTA's entire life. The guard skips 24 waits **once**, then costs a branch and an address rebuild on **every** iteration forever.


This also explains why it hurts `sw32` specifically and not `128x128x64`: the cost is per wait, and BK=16 means 24 stages × 1 wgmma versus BK=64's 6 stages × 4.

# I introduced a hang. Reporting it straight.

**`320x64x64` with `NCW=5` deadlocks.** Entry 51 (`nn 320x64x64`) spun for 29 minutes on the card and never returned. The change is bad and is being dropped.

**Why the guard didn't save us:** my correctness gate checks for *wrong answers*, not for *no answer*. A hang isn't a failure — it's an absence of one, so the gate just blocked forever instead of aborting. That's a real hole in my harness and it cost ~29 minutes of card time.

**Likely cause** (to investigate, not assume): `NCW=5` makes 6 warpgroups = **768 threads**, where every other config in the tree runs 384 or 512. Something in the mbarrier arrive-counts or the epilogue's warpgroup partitioning doesn't hold at that width. Our register-budget assert passed (24 + 5×96 = 504 ≤ 512) so it isn't the register pool — the assert was satisfied and the kernel still hung, which means the assert doesn't cover this case.

**Two fixes going in before anything else runs:**
1. **`timeout` on every check and bench invocation**, so a hang aborts instead of blocking.
2. **Drop `BLUBLAS_320_NCW`** from the arm — `320x64x64` is unrouted anyway, so it was the lowest-value item in the queue.

The `128x32x64` swizzle (entry 10 — the *worst routed* entry, cause measured at 4.64× conflicts) never got tested because the hang happened at entry 51, before the A/B. That's the part worth re-running.

You're right, and let me be precise about what I actually failed to do rather than just apologise.

**What I verified:** the config *values* — PREG, CREG, NCW, EPI_SWZ, PFSKIP — by compile-time probe. All correct.

**What I never did:** run a single kernel. I confirmed `NCW=5` produced the right numbers on paper and went straight to an 81-entry gate. `NCW=5` means **768 threads**, a warpgroup count *no other config in the entire tree uses* — that is a structural novelty, and the one thing I should have done was execute one entry before batching 81. I checked the paperwork three times and never checked that it ran.

**Two rules now in the harness, not just in my head:**

Ours is well-built: float4 128-bit loads, four independent accumulator chains, grid-stride, deterministic fixed-order accumulation, alpha/beta applied once. Your instinct is reasonable. Now his:
> tool `Bash`: 

# Found it — and you were right, it's not the algorithm

Same workspace layout (`scratch + s*n`), same float4 loads, same accumulation order. The difference is the **output store**:

```c
// HIS — one packed 64-bit store of 4 bf16
out[0] = __floats2bfloat162_rn(acc.x, acc.y);
out[1] = __floats2bfloat162_rn(acc.z, acc.w);
reinterpret_cast<float2*>(C)[q] = *reinterpret_cast<const float2*>(out);

// OURS — FOUR separate 16-bit scalar stores
for (int v = 0; v < 4; ++v) C[base + v] = from_f32<T>(o[v]);
```

**We issue 4× the store instructions he does, at 2 bytes each instead of one 8-byte packed store.**

And ours also carries work his doesn't:
- an **alpha multiply** per element (his v4t has no alpha at all)
- a **beta / C_in read-back** branch (his has none)
- a **3-condition alignment guard** per grid-stride iteration (`base+4<=n && (base&3)==0 && (n&3)==0`)

So your read is correct: **our algorithm isn't worse — it's more general.** His `v4t` is a stripped special case: bf16 only, no alpha, no beta, no C_in, no ragged tail. Ours handles all of that and is deterministic. It pays for that generality, and the store width is the biggest part of the bill.

**The actionable bit:** the 4-scalar-store is pure loss — we can pack to `bf162` and do one 64-bit store exactly like him **without giving up alpha, beta, determinism or the tail path**. That's fixing our own inefficiency, not copying his design.

Verifying in the SASS rather than trusting my source reading:

## Your four questions, answered

**1. Does he have determinism without alpha/beta?** Yes. Determinism comes from the **fixed accumulation order** (`s = 0…S-1`, one thread per element, no atomics) — nothing to do with alpha/beta. Both of us are deterministic. Confirmed in SASS: 0 atomics on both sides.

**2. So what's the use of our extra alpha/beta/`C_in`?** It's not decoration — it's **capability**. We can run split-K with `beta ≠ 0`; he cannot and falls back to a kernel that's slower on exactly the shapes split-K exists for. So on `beta ≠ 0` small-K shapes, **ours is the more capable path**. That's a real advantage, not baggage.

**3. Is he using a different algorithm?** **No — identical algorithm.** Per-element serial sum over slices, fixed order, grid-stride, no atomics, no tree reduction, no shared memory. Same maths, same order, same instruction *kinds* (`LDG` + `FADD` + `F2FP` + `STG`).

The difference is purely **width**:
```
his:   LDG.E.128 (128-bit)  ->  FADD  ->  STG.E.64 (one packed 64-bit store)
ours:  LDG.E     (32-bit)   ->  FADD  ->  STG.E.U16 x4 (four 16-bit stores)
```

**4. Should we copy him?** **Partly — take the width, keep our generality.** Two fixes, neither of which costs us anything:
- **fix the gate** so the `VEC=4` path actually fires (it currently needs ≥135,168 elements, and split-K targets *small* outputs, so it almost never triggers)
- **pack the stores** — build `bf162` pairs and do one 64-bit store instead of four 16-bit ones

That gives us his memory efficiency **and** keeps alpha, beta, `C_in`, the ragged tail, and determinism — strictly better than either version today.

ncu **serialises and profiles a single launch** — the GPU never reaches sustained thermal/power state. The A/B runs 30 iterations back-to-back, 12 rounds, where the 700W cap actually binds. And the one counter where we're clearly worse is exactly the one that costs power:

**More instructions → more power at equal work → cap binds → clock drops → slower in sustained running, while every per-launch counter looks better.**

That would also explain why the residual is so *uniform* (98.1–99.4% across 18 entries of different shapes and layouts) — a clock deficit scales everything by the same factor, which no per-tile mechanism would.

Here's what the investigation actually produced — this is the answer to what you asked for:

**The root cause, found by reading his code against ours (not guessing):**

His epilogue swizzle is `template<int BN> Sm90CEpilogueSwizzle` with `SWIZZLE_BYTES = sm90_c_swizzle_bytes(BN)` — **derived from BN, so every config he writes gets it automatically and none can ever miss it.** Ours is a template parameter `_EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES = 0`, i.e. **off by default, opt-in per config**. §H116 opted in 7 configs; every variant config written since got nothing.

**Audit result: 40 of 77 entries are missing it, and they hold 65.8 of the 94.2 remaining points — 70% of the whole gap.**

| config | % | shortfall | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 320x64x64 ×3 | 90.9% | **27.4** | H132 (queued) |
| 128x192x64_regsplit ×3 | 93.2% | **20.4** | H131 (running) |
| 128x128x64_2cta ×3 | 98.0% | 6.1 | H131 |
| 128x192x64_ring | 95.6% | 4.4 | H132 |
| cluster_v2 / coopB / coopB_v2 ×9 | 99.2–99.7% | 5.3 | H131 |

**The clincher:** `128x192x64_regsplit` and plain `128x192x64` are the **same tile, same raster** — one has the epilogue stack (99.0%), one doesn't (93.2%).

**Second defect found on 320x64x64:** BM=320 → 5 M-atoms, our NCW default is 2, so `EPI_SPLIT_M = (5 % 2 == 0)` is **false** → half-width wgmma. Identical to the §H120 defect that gave 192x192 +1.7. Only NCW 1 or 5 divide 5, and NCW=5 is what deadlocked — so I'm testing the epilogue fix alone first, one variable.

**Things I ruled out** (so nobody re-chases them): most `_regsplit` entries are non-issues — `BLUBLAS_RS_PREG/CREG` resolve to 40/232, the defaults, so they inherit the fixes and do no register split; `192x128x64_regsplit` is literally an alias of the plain config. And raster is *not* the regsplit gap's cause — same raster, still 6.8% down.

Also found and staged: his plain `128x192x64` uses `SUPER_M=32`, ours uses 8 — a knob that's been sitting in our source since §H105 marked *"no-op until `-DBLUBLAS_192_RSWZ=5`"* and was never measured.

## What was wrong, and it was my mistake

The trainer builds the vendored BLAS with **its own** Makefile, which never defines `BLUBLAS_HAS_SM90`. Our BF16 dispatcher wraps its whole SM90 routing block in `#ifdef BLUBLAS_HAS_SM90` — so the **call site was preprocessed out** and every BF16 GEMM fell to the **SM89** legacy path. nsys named it outright: our arm ran `bgemm_backward_template_kernel` (from `BF16/SM89/`) where his ran `bgemm_sm90_kernel`. Same 139,200 launches, 36.7 s vs his 14.0 s.

**Why my link check missed it — the part I've now written into memory:** I reported 4628 SM90 kernels present, 3 `_kota` exports, 0 unresolved symbols. All true, all irrelevant. The variant TUs compile their kernels regardless of that define; only the *caller* was deleted. The kernels were present and unreachable. **Symbol presence is not reachability.** The check that catches it is `nm -u` on the caller's object — `blublasBgemmSM90_dispatch_*` refs were **0** broken, **3** fixed. Two other delays came from the same family: a regex needing 3 chars where the names are 2 (`nn`/`nt`/`tn`), and `echo "[$(date)] exit=$?"` resetting `$?` so failures reported exit=0.

**Here's what the line-by-line comparison actually found — three separate defects, not one:**

**1. Signature mismatch (the crash).** His `dispatch_nn/nt/tn` take **16** params ending in `lda, ldb, ldc`. Ours took **13**. Because `extern "C"` has no name mangling and no cross-TU type checking, the linker bound a 13-arg call to a 16-arg callee **without a single warning**. His code then read garbage leading dimensions, built a TMA descriptor on a junk stride, and the driver rejected the launch — `invalid argument` on `nn M=8192 N=512 K=1536`.

**2. Missing leading-dimension logic (a latent correctness bug in ours).** His BF16 dispatcher derives them and gates on them:
```
lda_nat = (transA==N) ? K : M ;  ldb_nat = (transB==N) ? N : K ;  ldc_nat = N
packed  = (lda==lda_nat && ldb==ldb_nat && ldc==ldc_nat)
ld_ok   = packed || (lda>=lda_nat && ldb>=ldb_nat && ldc>=ldc_nat)
sm90_ld* = packed ? 0 : ld*
```
Ours had **none of it** — no derivation, no `ld_ok` gate. A non-packed layout would have been computed as if packed: **silently wrong results**, not a crash. I've adopted his logic verbatim rather than hardcoding `0` as I first did.

**3. Four separate declaration sites.** These functions are declared in the BF16 dispatcher, the SM90 dispatcher, `Bgemm_sm90_bf16.cuh`, and his Kota file. I fixed all four and verified programmatically that every one agrees at 16 params. **The compiler then caught the header I'd have otherwise missed** (`more than one instance of overloaded function ... has "C" linkage`) — which is precisely the type check `extern "C"` denied us across TUs.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-07 15:50 IST]

Good question, and the answer hinges on a safety property I should check before recommending anything. PDL has **two halves**: the launch attribute *and* a device-side `griddepcontrol.wait` before the kernel touches data the previous kernel wrote. Enabling the attribute on a kernel that lacks the wait is a **data race**, not a speedup.

Let me research both designs properly:
> tool `Bash`: 

**Research answer: yes, his design is genuinely more robust, and here's the technical reason.**

**His design — both halves unconditional, one env kill-switch:**
- `griddepcontrol_wait()` at line 1053: **no `if constexpr`, no guard** — always compiled into the kernel prologue
- `griddepcontrol_launch_dependents()` at line 1301: emitted when the last tile completes
- launch attribute: always set unless `BLUBLAS_NO_PDL`

**Why unconditional is safe** — and this is documented in *our own* source: *"Both instructions are no-ops unless the launch carries `cudaLaunchAttributeProgrammaticStreamSerialization`."* So compiling the wait in always costs nothing, and it makes the two halves **impossible to disagree**.

**Ours has three independent conditions that must agree**: the `USE_PDL` template knob, `CLUSTER_SIZE > 1` for the attribute, and the env switch. They *don't* agree — which is precisely the bug.

Let me map exactly what changing it would touch, and check the safety obligation:
> tool `Bash`: 

Proper answer, and it's **not** a simple "copy his" — the research turns up something our design does *better*, plus a genuine reason our knob exists.

**Three separate things, and they need separating:**

**1. A clear bug — fix unconditionally.** The launch attribute lives inside `if constexpr (CLUSTER_SIZE > 1)`. So a config with `USE_PDL=true` and `CLUSTER_SIZE=1` compiles the device-side `griddep_wait()` in (line 6346) but **never gets the attribute** — PDL silently does nothing. That's a defect with no upside. The two halves must be reachable together.

**2. His robustness pattern is better, and here's why it's safe.** His `griddepcontrol_wait()` is unconditional. Ours is behind `USE_PDL`. Since the instruction is a **no-op without the attribute** (documented in our own source), making the wait unconditional costs nothing and makes the halves *impossible to desync*. That's strictly more robust than our three-condition arrangement. Worth adopting.

**3. But our design has a correctness refinement his may not — we should NOT drop it.** Our own comment documents it:

> *"Under SPLIT_K we have such a dependent, and it is ours: `splitk_reduce_kernel` opts into PDL and its first act is `sk_griddep_wait()` before reading the fp32 partials. Those partials are written by the epilogue BELOW this line, so firing here let the dependent start reading them early."*

So we deliberately move `launch_dependents` **after** the tile loop under split-K, with a `__threadfence()` (line 8346). His fires at last-tile (line 1301). Copying him wholesale could reintroduce a **silent wrong answer** on split-K.

**And the reason our knob exists is measured, not arbitrary:**

> *"COST IS NOT ZERO WHEN THERE IS NOTHING TO OVERLAP: the dependent lands on free SMs and contends with the still-draining producer. On B300 the net was strongly positive; on a shape with no gap to recover it is a small negative."*

**So my recommendation:**

- **Do** fix the attribute reachability (both launch paths) — pure bug fix
- **Do** make the device-side wait unconditional like his — zero cost, removes the desync class of bug
- **Keep** our split-K-aware `launch_dependents` placement — his pattern is riskier there
- **Default the attribute ON** for these configs but keep the kill-switch, then **measure** — because our own record says PDL is occasionally negative, so "always on" is a policy claim I should not assert without the A/B

That gives us his robustness without discarding a correctness fix we already paid for. Expected value is the **+0.333 s idle** we measured (~0.3%) — real but modest, so I'd rather implement it correctly than fast.

## First — your shape question, proven from the script

**`global_batch` changes nothing about the shapes.** [bluscript_zero(2).cpp:492](bluscript_zero(2).cpp#L492) is the only place it is used:

```cpp
const int64_t tokens_per_micro = cfg.B * cfg.T * world_size;
const int GRAD_ACCUM = cfg.global_batch / tokens_per_micro;
```

524288 / (2·4096·1) = **64**. It only sets how many times each shape runs per step.

**`mini_batch` (B) does change them — in two different slots:**

| layout | what B·T is | B=1 | B=2 (ours) | B=4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nn, nt (fwd + dgrad) | **M** | 4096 | 8192 | 16384 |
| tn (wgrad) | **K** | 4096 | 8192 | 16384 |

N is always a model dim (E, KV, 2F, F, V) and B never touches it. I reconstructed all 15 4B shapes from (B·T, model dims) and compared against the measured rows — **15/15 exact match**. So at B=2 the 45 are locked; if we ever move to B=4 every one of them changes and the whole measurement is void.

The permanent fix is in:

```cpp
static inline int h92_sk(int i)
{
    static const char* e = std::getenv("H92_SK");
    static const int   v = (e && std::atoi(e) > 0) ? std::atoi(e) : -1;
    return (v > 0) ? v : H92[i].split_k;
}
```

All four `_splitk` cases (33/34/35/36) now read it, and the sweep passes the factor **the dispatcher would actually choose** for each shape, taken from my validated `sm90_tn_splitk_plan` re-implementation. Sweep is 135/135.

Good morning. Here's the full picture, and one new finding from the 4B data that changes what I'd prioritise.

## Where we are

| | cuBLAS | his production BLAS | **ours (hybrid)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **600M, 1×** | 73,583.8 | 72,918.0 (99.10%) | **72,336.0 (98.30% of cuBLAS, 99.20% of his)** |
| **4B, 2×** | 36,139.3 | 35,364.2 (97.86%) | **35,367.6 (97.86% of cuBLAS, 100.01% of his)** |

**We caught him on 4B.** And it isn't luck — on GEMM alone we're **ahead**: our GEMMs are 100.73% of his (935 ms faster over the run), 97.80% of cuBLAS where his are 97.09%.

## What shipped yesterday

The tile-order **axis** fix. Our kernels walk one grid axis, his walks the other; on the 1.7B gate_up wgrad (a 16×88 grid) that was worth **79–89% → 98–99.7%** of his across all three mini-batches, with non-overlapping distributions. Pinned to that one config only — the global flip is refuted, and I tested the "wide grids always win" generalisation on nine other shapes and it's a null, so that's closed off.

## Where the remaining gap actually is

Our 4B deficit to cuBLAS is **4,408 ms**: GEMM **2,799 ms (63%)**, collateral **1,610 ms (37%)**.

GEMM side — 19 shapes still behind him, but they're a long thin tail. Only one is meaningful: **`TN_256x128x64` on lm_head wgrad, 96.29 / 98.94 / 99.38%**. Everything else is 99.3–100%, i.e. inside the noise floor of the measurement.

## The new finding — and it's not what I expected

Breaking the 4B collateral down per kernel:

| kernel | ours vs cuBLAS | his vs cuBLAS | ours − his |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gqa_bwd_vj1d` | +876.7 ms (103.26%) | +932.0 ms (103.47%) | **−55.4 ms (we win)** |
| `gqa_v62_sm90` | +388.9 ms | +392.8 ms | −3.9 ms |
| **`ncclSymkDevKernel_ReduceScatter`** | **+288.5 ms (134.78%)** | **−169.2 ms (79.59%)** | **+457.7 ms (we lose)** |

I had assumed the collateral was `gqa_bwd_vj1d` again. **It isn't.** We actually beat him on that one. The entire +355 ms collateral gap — and more — is the **NCCL reduce-scatter**: his runs it at 79.6% of cuBLAS (*faster* than cuBLAS), ours at 134.8%. A 457 ms swing on an 829 ms kernel.

That's a communication kernel that only exists at NP≥2, so we have never seen it before yesterday. Something about our GEMM stream timing is destroying its overlap with compute.

## Ideas for beating cuBLAS in all three models

Ranked by measured size, not by guess:

1. **The NCCL reduce-scatter overlap — 458 ms, biggest single item, and his tree already solves it.** He's *faster than cuBLAS* there; we're 35% slower. Whatever he does, it's reachable. This is a scheduling/stream question, not a kernel-rewrite, so it should be cheap. Multi-GPU only — but that's the configuration that matters for 4B.
2. **`TN_256x128x64` lm_head wgrad — the only real GEMM target left.** 96.29% at 4B, and it's on the same tile family across all three models, so one fix pays three times.
3. **The collateral is the ceiling, not the GEMMs.** Even at *perfect* GEMM parity with cuBLAS we'd still be 1,610 ms behind on 4B — about 0.78%. So GEMM work alone cannot beat cuBLAS. The two have to move together, and per §H142 they're coupled through the 700 W power cap: our GEMMs draw more power, the cap clamps, the next compute-heavy kernel runs slower.
4. **The honest lever nobody has pulled: the convert kernels.** `vec4_convert_to_fp32` is 13.5 s and `vec8_convert_to_bf16` is 10.4 s on the 4B — **23.9 s, ~11% of all GPU time** — and we're within 0.3% of cuBLAS on both because it's the *same code*. That's not a BLAS win, but it's the largest single block of removable work in the trainer, and a vec8 replacement already exists in our tree gated to sm_103.

- Single reduce-scatter kernels lasting **0.18–0.26 seconds**. That is not data movement — that is a rank **blocked waiting for its peer**.
- **rank 0 and rank 1 differ by 6–10×** in the same arm, moving identical bytes. Pure skew.
- I only looked at rank 0, so I read one side of a see-saw as a cost.

And the deeper error: **summed kernel time is a bad proxy for wall time here.** Ours is 580 ms "faster" than his in summed kernels but only **21 ms** faster on the host clock — **4% passes through**. NCCL overlaps with compute, so its duration is absorbed, not added.

So scratch that item. It was a measurement artifact, not a lever.

## The corrected picture — and it's all matmul, exactly as you said

Re-attributing our 4B gap against **wall** time (4,748 ms over 15 steps):

| | ms | share | is it ours to fix? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GEMM** — our kernels vs cuBLAS's | **2,799** | **59%** | **yes, directly** |
| `gqa_bwd_vj1d` + `gqa_v62` slowed down | 1,266 | 27% | **yes, indirectly** |
| NCCL reduce-scatter | — | — | no, it's a wait |
| everything else | ~60 | 1% | noise |

The second row is the part worth being clear about, because it looks like it contradicts you but doesn't. Those two `gqa` kernels are **identical code in all three arms, with identical launch counts** — I verified that. They run 3.3% and 5.0% slower under a BLAS than under cuBLAS. They don't slow down by themselves; they slow down because **our matmuls draw more power, the 700 W cap clamps, the SM clock drops, and the next compute-heavy kernel pays for it** (that's the §H68/solved-clock mechanism, measured end-to-end before).

So it is still the matmul kernels. It's just that leaner matmuls buy us **twice** — once in GEMM time directly, once in the collateral they stop causing. Note the memory-bound kernels (`vec4_convert`, `vec8_convert`, 23.9 s of work) show **+0.06% to +0.33%** — essentially nothing. Only the power-hungry ones move, which is the signature of a power effect rather than anything structural.

## What that means for the plan

Everything routes to one place: **make the matmul kernels leaner** — fewer instructions and less power per FLOP, not just fewer cycles.

The targets, all matmul, ranked by measured size:

1. **The 2,799 ms GEMM gap to cuBLAS on 4B** (97.80% → 100%+). That's the direct 59%.

3. **Power per FLOP.** This is what unlocks the 1,266 ms of collateral, and it's the piece we've never attacked head-on. §H142 established the mechanism; the instruction-excess work list (§ the 7 groups) is the concrete route.

And one measurement correction I'll carry forward: at NP≥2 I have to compare on **host step time or the critical path**, never summed kernel time — 4% pass-through makes that metric actively misleading. It's a good thing you challenged it; I'd have spent the morning chasing a barrier.

**The problem is not kernel speed. We already have faster kernels than cuBLAS.** The problem is that our kernels lose far more of their speed when run inside a real training step — which is exactly the power/clock mechanism §H142 documented: our GEMMs draw more power, the 700 W cap clamps, the clock drops, and everything after pays.

Three consequences:

1. **The standalone sweep cannot pick trainer targets.** It systematically flatters us by ~3.5 points because it removes the shared power environment. Every per-shape optimisation decision made from it would be aimed at the wrong thing.
2. **"Beat cuBLAS in all 3 models" is not a kernel-speed problem.** It's an **energy-per-FLOP** problem. Making a kernel faster in isolation may make this *worse* if it costs more power.
3. The one real standalone outlier — `TN_192x128x64` at 85.07% / 85.40% on `1536×1536×K` — is genuine and worth fixing (he's also bad there at 86%, so it's a shared weakness, not his margin).

Two honest caveats: the cuBLAS retention figure is **n=1** (only one kernel had an unambiguous launch-count match), and the 6 split-K shapes remain excluded pending the workspace question. The n=1 needs strengthening before I'd build a plan on the exact 6.5-point figure — though the direction is corroborated by the 3.5-point standalone-vs-trainer gap arriving independently.

## The fix, and how it was derived

**Cause, isolated by a control arm:** cuBLAS runs `tn 1536×1536` on a **128×160 tile with a 2-wide cluster**; we ran it unclustered on 192×128.

| step | K=8192 | attribution |
|---|---|---|
| `128x160` unclustered | 589.5 | — |
| + RASTER=1 *(control)* | 642.9 | raster axis: **+9.1%** |
| **+ cluster 2×2** | **741.7** | **cluster: +15.4%** ← the cause |
| cuBLAS | 749.6 | |

Without that control I'd have credited the whole gain to the cluster. Orientation matters too: 2×2 = 741.7, 4×2 = 733.5, **2×4 = 327.7**. Our 2×2 beats cuBLAS's own 4×2.

**The trap it walked into:** a straight rebind fixes three shapes and **wrecks** the other three on the same entry point — `3072×1024` falls from 100.7% to **42.6%** of cuBLAS. Caught by the blast-radius test, not by reasoning.

**The rule — measured on 30 points, not fitted to 2:**

> use `128x160 + cluster 2x2` **iff** wave-utilisation of the current tile **< 0.78** **and** `ceil(N/160)` is **even**

The threshold sits in an **empty gap**: every cluster win has utilisation ≤ 0.727, every loss ≥ 0.833. Nothing to tune. And the second condition is mechanism, not correlation — a 2×2 cluster pairs tiles along N, so an odd `ceil(N/160)` leaves a half-empty cluster column and wastes a CTA pair. That is exactly why N=768/1024/2048 collapse. **30/30 correct.**

**Implementation:** a `Sm90RuntimeSel` hook in the entry-point emitter. Default is a pass-through that launches the bound config, so **every non-specialised entry keeps byte-identical codegen** — I'm verifying that with a SASS comparison against the pre-change object right now. His dispatcher is untouched; it picks the entry point, we pick the config underneath.

**Expected production effect:** `tn 1536×1536×K` (600M Q/O wgrad, **48 calls/micro-step**) 85.1% → 98.5–99.9% of cuBLAS, with `3072×1024` protected by both conditions.

Once the build lands I'll re-run the blast radius over all six shapes through the shipped binary — the win doesn't count until it survives that.

## 1. `Sm90RuntimeSel` — no, it adds no meaningful overhead. Here's the actual code path

It's a **compile-time** template struct, not a runtime branch. Two cases:

**Every config that doesn't specialize** gets the default at [Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh:9459](src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L9459):
```cpp
{ launch_bgemm_sm90<Cfg, LAY>(A,B,C,M,N,K,batchCount,alpha,beta,stream,bias,lda,ldb,ldc); }
```
A pure `inline` forward. The compiler picks the specialization at compile time — **there is no test at runtime, no branch, no lookup**. Proven, not assumed: §H152 compared SASS hashes before/after and got `9cdd9b7d768e3e08` **identical** for every non-specializing config.

**The one config that does specialize** runs ~15 host-side integer ops before the launch — 2 ceil-divides, a multiply, a wave count, a modulo, 3 compares. That's **on the CPU, once per GEMM call**, not per tile and not per thread. Scale it: 600M calls that site 48×/micro-step → **48 × ~15 ns ≈ 0.7 µs** against **40,280 µs** of GEMM. That's 0.002%.

And empirically: h154's control shape ran the same kernel through the **full dispatcher chain** (of which this hook is a small part) vs direct — **741.8 vs 741.4 TF, +0.06%**, i.e. noise.

So the mechanism is safe. It's also the *right* place for this, which matters for your future-proofing point — see §4.

## 2. You're right, and I stated it badly

I am **not** proposing "swap the variant" as the answer. The sweep is **reconnaissance, not the decision** — it costs 25 min, needs no rebuild, and answers one cheap question: *is there already an arm that beats 84.99%?* That number is the **floor any optimization has to beat**. Without it I'd be optimizing blind.

But your ordering instinct is correct, and I skipped a step. The real question splits in two, and they need **different fixes**:

| if… | then the bug is | and the fix is |
|---|---|---|
| the split-K **kernel** is inefficient (e.g. the separate reduce kernel eats the gain) | kernel | fix the kernel — helps **everywhere** split-K is used, now and future |
| split-K is the **wrong strategy** for this shape | dispatch | fix the rule — 4B already proves a plain tile can win here |

The sweep only answers the second. **So I'm adding the autopsy for the first**, which I should have planned from the start:
- **nsys**: split the timeline into the *main* kernel vs the *reduce* kernel. If reduce is a big share, that's the bug outright — and it's a 2-minute measurement.
- **ncu** on the main kernel: compare it against the 4B non-split-K kernel on the same site.

Even if a plain tile wins the sweep, **we still fix split-K**, because we need it working for genuinely low-occupancy shapes in future models. Dropping it because one shape dodges it is not future-proof.

## 3. The "39 of 135" — what I got wrong

Two different ways to average the same 135 numbers. I quoted one and implied the other.

- **Per-variant mean** (what I said before): group the 135 cases by which of the 16 variants ran, average inside each group. **15 of 16 groups are ≥100%.** Only `TN_128x128x64_splitk` fails.
- **Per-case**: look at each of the 135 individually. **39 are below 100%.**

The gap is averaging hiding losers. Concretely:

| variant | cases | MEAN | worst case | cases below 100% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NT_128x256x64_regsplit | 38 | **101.89%** | 97.95% | **10 of 38** |
| NN_128x256x64_regsplit | 29 | **101.23%** | 97.08% | **6 of 29** |
| TN_128x256x64_regsplit | 15 | **100.06%** | 99.04% | **9 of 15** |
| TN_256x128x64_2WG | 9 | **100.40%** | 97.37% | 3 of 9 |
| TN_128x128x64_splitk | 6 | **85.14%** | 74.28% | 6 of 6 |

`NT_128x256x64_regsplit` averages 101.89% and looks healthy — but 10 of its 38 shapes lose to cuBLAS. **The trainer runs specific shapes, not variant averages**, so the per-case number is the one that matters. "No variant below 100%" was true and useless. My mistake.

The good news: the 39 losers are mostly shallow — after the 5 split-K ones, the worst is **95.61%** and most are 97–99.9%.

## 4. Strategy — and the future-proofing rule

**Sequencing:**
1. **Ceiling sweep** (running) — what's the best any existing arm does on these 6?
2. **Autopsy** — nsys main-vs-reduce split, then ncu. *Why* is it slow?
3. **Decide** using both: fix the kernel, the rule, or both.
4. Then trainer nsys on your word.

**The design rule I'll hold to, so this doesn't rot:**

- **Never hardcode a shape list.** The fix must be a predicate on shape properties — occupancy, N, K, bias-present — so a new model config gets it automatically. §H152's rule is `util < 0.78 && ceil(N/160) even && bias==nullptr`; it was validated 30/30 with the threshold sitting in an **empty gap** (wins ≤0.727, losses ≥0.833), not fitted to the data.
- **`Sm90RuntimeSel` is the right home** precisely because it's zero-cost for everything else and additive: a new specialization touches one struct and cannot perturb any config already measured (SASS-proven).
- **Fix the kernel even if the rule wins**, so split-K is healthy for future shapes.
- **Every rule ships with its falsification arm** — the case that looks identical on failure, per the vacuous-check lesson.

Screen results in ~15 min. I'll bring the ceiling and then the autopsy plan with real numbers, not a recommendation before the data.

## The sweep refuted my own hypothesis — that's the headline

I said this was probably a dispatch bug because 4B avoids split-K and wins. **Wrong.** Of 34 arms × 6 shapes, all correct, the incumbent is **already the best or near-best on 5 of 6**:

| case | incumbent | best alternative found | gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| 600M B1 | 74.26% | 128x64x64_regsplit → **76.45%** | +2.94% |
| 600M B2 | 84.38% | splitk **sk=3** → 85.90% | +1.80% |
| 600M B4 | 83.52% | splitk sk=3 → 83.78% | +0.31% |
| 1.7B B1 | 77.05% | 128x64x64_regsplit → **83.56%** | **+8.44%** |
| 1.7B B2 | 90.39% | splitk sk=3 → 91.09% | +0.77% |
| 1.7B B4 | 99.36% | *incumbent is best* | 0 |

Best case we'd claw back ~2 of the 20-point gap. **Swapping the variant does not fix this — it's a kernel-level problem.** Good news: that's a far more useful finding than a cheap dispatch win, and it cost 25 min.

## What the numbers point at (a lead, not a conclusion)

Absolute time deltas behave **oppositely** in the two models, which rules out one single cause:

- **1.7B**: 4.31 → 2.84 → **0.31 µs** as K grows (converges to cuBLAS)
- **600M**: 4.57 → 4.36 → **7.76 µs** as K grows (diverges)

The CTA arithmetic separates them exactly:

| | M-tiles | N-tiles | ×sk=2 | CTAs / 132 SMs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.7B (M=2048) | 16 | 4 | 128 | **97.0%** |
| 600M (M=1536) | 12 | 4 | 96 | **72.7%** |

1.7B nearly fills the machine and reaches 99.36%; 600M leaves **36 SMs idle** and never gets past 85.9%. That 27% waste matches the deficit size. But it does **not** explain 1.7B B1 (97% occupancy, still 77%) — at K=4096 the whole kernel is 18.76 µs, so prologue/epilogue amortisation is a second, separate effect.

**I also found a hole in my own sweep**: I included no `BN<64` tn arms (`128x32`, `128x16`, `128x8` exist) and there are **no BM=64 tn arms at all**. For M=1536, N=512 a smaller tile is exactly what would fill 132 SMs. That gap needs closing before I claim the ceiling is real.

## Plan for the 39 — tiered, and the tiering comes from the data

The 39 collapse into **14 families** (same site + layout + variant). One fact decides the strategy for each:

**Only ONE family loses on every shape it runs — the split-K one (6 of 6). Every other family wins on some shapes and loses on others.**

| family | cases | recoverable | wins/loses | ⇒ fix type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TN_128x128x64_splitk | 6 | 1.124 ms | **0 win / 6 lose** | **kernel defect** |
| TN_128x128x64_regsplit (1.7B gate_up wgrad, N=11264) | 1 | 0.939 ms | 2 win / 1 lose | dispatch/rule |
| TN_128x256x64_regsplit (gate_up wgrad) | 4 | 0.203 ms | 2 win / 4 lose | dispatch/rule |
| NN_128x256x64_regsplit (K/V fwd, N=512–1024) | 4 | 0.142 ms | 3 win / 4 lose | dispatch/rule |
| TN_256x128x64_2WG (lm_head wgrad, N=50304) | 3 | 0.137 ms | 6 win / 3 lose | dispatch/rule |
| NT_128x256x64_regsplit (lm_head dgrad, K=50304) | 7 | 0.100 ms | 5 win / 3 lose | dispatch/rule |
| 8 smaller families | 14 | 0.324 ms | mixed | dispatch/rule |

**Tier 1 — kernel work (1.124 ms, 38% of all recoverable).** The split-K family. Next actions, all measurement, no guessing: (a) **nsys the cuBLAS arm** to see what kernel it actually runs on `tn 1536x512x8192` — we have never looked; (b) nsys ours to size the separate reduce kernel; (c) close my sweep hole with the small-BN arms; (d) ncu the main kernel against 1.7B B4, the one case that *does* reach parity.

**Tier 2 — one big rule target (0.939 ms, 32%).** `1.7B gate_up wgrad tn 2048x11264x16384` at 95.61% on a **128x128 tile with N=11264**. The same variant hits 104.9% and 101.4% on other shapes, so the kernel is fine and the *choice* is wrong. This is a `Sm90RuntimeSel` rule, the cheap kind.

**Tier 3 — the shallow tail (~0.9 ms across 32 cases, all 97–99.9%).** Work these **as families, not one by one** — each family shares a variant and a shape feature, so one rule fixes several cases and generalises to future model configs.

## The honest arithmetic, so we're not surprised later

Fixing **all 39** is worth, in the configs we actually run at B=2:

| config | GEMM/step | losers | recover | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 600M B=2 | 40.28 ms | 4 | 0.283 ms | **+0.70%** |
| 1.7B B=2 | 68.14 ms | 4 | 0.251 ms | **+0.37%** |
| 4B B=2 | 207.99 ms | 4 | 0.176 ms | **+0.08%** |

Most of the 2.969 ms sits in **B=1 and B=4 configs the scripts don't currently run**. And the trainer gap on 4B is **3.67 points ≈ 7.6 ms/step** — roughly 40× what fixing 4B's shape losses buys.

So: the 39 are worth fixing for completeness, and I'll fix them. But they will not close the trainer gap, and I won't let a green shape table imply otherwise. When you're ready for GPU time, the first thing I'd ask for is **one short nsys capture of the cuBLAS arm on the split-K shapes** — it's the single measurement that unblocks Tier 1.

## The split-K deficit is the *reduce kernel*, and our main kernel is fine

nsys, 30 launches each, ours vs cuBLAS:

| case | K | cuB main | cuB reduce | our main | **our reduce** | total % | **main-only %** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 600M B1 | 4096 | 11999 | — | 13412 | **2280** | 76.5% | **89.5%** |
| 600M B2 | 8192 | 22269 | — | 23040 | **2357** | 87.7% | **96.7%** |
| 600M B4 | 16384 | 33870 | 3903 | 41639 | 2317 | 85.9% | 81.3% |
| 1.7B B1 | 4096 | 13376 | — | 14026 | **2546** | 80.7% | **95.4%** |
| 1.7B B2 | 8192 | 25020 | — | 23890 | **2696** | 94.1% | **104.7%** |
| 1.7B B4 | 16384 | 42442 | 4346 | 42612 | 2679 | 103.3% | 99.6% |

Our GEMM kernel is **89.5%–104.7%** of cuBLAS's — it was never the problem. The whole deficit is `splitk_reduce_kernel_fast<false,2>` at a **near-fixed ~2.3–2.7 µs**, which is 15% of runtime at K=4096 and only 5% at K=16384. That's exactly why 1.7B converged with K and 600M didn't.

**And the reduce cannot be optimised away as a kernel** — it's already at the memory wall: 6.29 MB read + 1.57 MB write in 2280 ns = **3.45 TB/s** (600M), **4.12 TB/s** (1.7B), against an H200's ~4.8 TB/s peak. There is no kernel work left to win there. The only fix is **not to do it**.

## What cuBLAS does instead — and we already have the tile

| shape | cuBLAS kernel | splits K? |
|---|---|---|
| 600M B1/B2 | `nvjet_sm90_tst_**64x128**_64x8_**4x2_h**_bz_NTN` | **no** |
| 1.7B B1/B2 | `nvjet_sm90_tst_**64x128**_64x8_**2x1_v**_bz_NTN` | **no** |
| 600M B4 | `128x192_64x5_2x1_v_coopB_splitK` | yes |
| 1.7B B4 | `128x128_64x6_1x2_h_splitK` | yes |

cuBLAS uses **64×128 with no split-K** at low K, and only splits at K=16384 — where it pays a *bigger* reduce than ours (3.9–4.3 µs) but wins on the main kernel.

**`Sm90Config_64x128x64` already exists** in our tree, and all 14 cluster variants — including `64x128x64_4x2_h` and `64x128x64_2x1_v`, cuBLAS's exact two — are already in the build list and **linked into the binary** (`nm --defined-only` = 1 for each). They were simply never put in the harness table, so my sweep never tried them.

Why this should work, by arithmetic: 128×128 at sk=2 gives 48 tiles × 2 = 96 CTAs each doing `128·128·K/2`. 64×128 unsplit gives 96 tiles × 1 = 96 CTAs each doing `64·128·K` — **identical work per CTA, identical occupancy, but no fp32 partials to HBM and no reduce**. Removing the reduce alone is 76.5% → **89.5%** (600M B1) and 80.7% → **95.4%** (1.7B B1); dropping the 6.29 MB partial-write from the main kernel should add a few more points.

## Also closed: my sweep hole

Narrow-BN arms are not the answer — `128x32` lands at 34–47%, `128x16` at 27–36%, `128x8` at 11–17%. The §H155 ceiling holds. The missing dimension was **BM**, not BN.

| 600M B4 | 83.70% | 54.44% | 57.61% | 48.02% | **−31.2%** |

## Why full-width made it *slower* — the structural reason

`BM=64` holds exactly **one** m64 atom. That forces a choice, and both options are worse than BM=128:

- **NCW=2** → M-split illegal → split N → half-width wgmma, but **2 consumer warpgroups** (256 threads)
- **NCW=1** → full-width wgmma, but **1 consumer warpgroup** (128 threads)

Two warpgroups issuing half-width beat one issuing full-width — latency hiding wins. **BM=128 gets both**: 2 warpgroups *and* full width, which is exactly why `128x128` sits at parity with cuBLAS. My earlier "half-width = crippled" inference was right about the mechanism and wrong about the consequence.

cuBLAS gets 595 TF on this tile where our best BM=64 gets 434. They are not bound by our one-atom constraint — their 64×128 must map consumers to a 64-row tile differently. Closing that is a **kernel redesign**, not a knob.

## Where Tier 1 stands — 80 arms, all correctness-gated

| investigation | arms | result |
|---|---|---|
| §H155 variant sweep | 34 | incumbent best on 5/6 |
| §H156 nsys | — | deficit is the reduce kernel; **at the memory wall** (3.45–4.12 of ~4.8 TB/s) |

| `_SPLITK_ATOMIC` | — | already measured: workspace form **+13.76% on 16/16**, and non-deterministic |

**The incumbent is our ceiling with the current kernel architecture.** Not because I stopped looking — because 80 measured arms and a root-cause nsys profile all point the same way.

## What I'd do — your call

Two real paths remain, both **kernel projects, not knobs**: redesign the BM=64 consumer mapping, or implement stream-K. Either is multi-session.

The prize is **0.198 ms on 600M B=2 (0.49% of GEMM)** and **0.133 ms on 1.7B B=2 (0.19%)**.

**Tier 2 is worth 0.939 ms — 5× more — and is a dispatch fix**, where the same variant already hits 104.9% and 101.4% on neighbouring shapes. That's my recommendation. But you said don't quit on these 6, and if you want the BM=64 redesign I'll take it on — I'd just want you to pick it knowing it's a multi-session kernel rewrite for ≤0.5%.

Read it. **Short answer: no — that's not it, and the word "cooperative" is a false friend here.**

## Why it isn't

The page is purely a **thread-synchronization** API — `thread_block`, `tiled_partition()`, `sync()`, `reduce()`. It has **zero** mentions of matrix multiply, GEMM, tiles, operands A/B, multicast, TMA, or wgmma. `coopA`/`coopB` sit in cuBLAS's nvjet *kernel-name grammar*, in the same slot as `splitK` / `bias` / `plain` — they're cuBLAS-internal variant tokens, not a reference to a CUDA API.

## But we did already solve this — twice, and it's in our own tree

**§H17**, from 60,733 captured cuBLAS kernel names:
> `1x2_h_bz_coopB` exists — 23,325 shapes, the most common kernel. A 1x2 cluster multicasts A. If coopB meant "B-multicast", this could not exist. **⇒ coopA/coopB is NOT the multicast operand.**

The proven correlation is **tile shape**: `coopA` → 128x256, 256x128 (both dims even multiples of 64); `coopB` → 192x192, 320x128, 192x128, 128x192 (a dim is an *odd* multiple of 64).

And our own template at [line 971](src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L971) states it outright:
> *"coopA = blocks/WG even, coopB = odd. Same emitted code either way — an exhaustive 18-kernel opcode census found no instruction that differs."*

## The real "cooperative" — and it lands right on today's problem

There *is* a genuine concept behind the name, but it's **CUTLASS's Cooperative schedule**, not CUDA Cooperative Groups:

- **Cooperative** = 2 consumer warpgroups split **one** tile's M (`AtomLayoutMNK Shape<2,1,1>`), **requires TileShape_M ≥ 128**, and **falls back to Pingpong at M=64**
- **Pingpong** = each warpgroup owns a **separate** tile, with an OrderedSequenceBarrier to alternate

That is exactly the wall we hit in §H157/§H158. CUTLASS's own builder says the cooperative 2-warpgroup schedule **is not available at BM=64** — you switch schedules. We don't have Pingpong, so we forced a cooperative-style mapping onto a tile shape where CUTLASS and cuBLAS use a different one. That's the mechanism behind "NCW=2 gives half-width, NCW=1 gives half the warpgroups, both lose."

So your find didn't answer the coopA/coopB question, but it pointed at the right neighbourhood — and **Pingpong is the named, documented thing we're missing** if we ever want BM=64 to work.

One correction I owe you: I have two contradictory notes on this, one saying coopA/coopB *are* multicast. §H17's 60,733-kernel evidence beats it. Fixing that now:

**Card is free (0%, 0 MiB) — your colleague can use it.** Everything is rebuilt and staged. Here's where we are, simply.

## What I found when you stopped the run

The run had done 373 rows. When I checked them, **every single checksum was `0.000000`.**

That means your idea — get correctness free from the performance run — **would not have worked**. The checksum was useless. It printed the same value for cuBLAS and for every kernel, good or broken.

**Why:** the harness summed 1024 *signed* values. Our test inputs are small and signed, so at K=8192 the output lands near zero, and 1024 signed numbers cancel each other out to nothing.

Good thing we stopped — otherwise I'd have run 65 minutes and had zero correctness information at the end.

## The fix

Changed the checksum to two numbers that cannot cancel:

| | old | new |
|---|---|---|
| what | sum of signed values | **sum of \|values\|** + an **index-weighted sum** |
| elements | 1024 | **4096** |
| format | `%.6f` | `%.6e` |

- Sum of |values| catches a wrong-magnitude result.
- The index-weighted sum catches a result with right numbers in the **wrong places** (shifted or permuted stores) — which a plain sum would miss.

Both `bench` and `bcublas` print the same two numbers, so they compare directly.

## Status

- Both arms patched, rebuilt, linked clean, synced
- Sweep scripts updated to capture both numbers
- **Resume script tested against the real partial file** — it correctly saw 2 rows for finished arms and 0 for unreached ones
- The 373 old rows are archived, not deleted. I'm starting clean rather than mixing two formats.
- **392 arms still to run, ~66 min**

1. **A 5-second smoke test** to confirm the new checksum is actually non-zero and that ours matches cuBLAS. I don't want to burn 66 minutes again on an unverified fix. Can I run that when the card is free?

Three separate bugs, any one of which would have wasted the full 66 minutes:

Verified. Both numbers hold — nothing to correct in the EOD.

## The units are terabytes per second, and 4.8 TB/s is right

**NVIDIA's own H200 page:** 141 GB HBM3e, **"4.8TB/s"** memory bandwidth — and our own records confirm the card was the 141 GB / 143771 MiB H200.

**The measured figures, recomputed from the raw nsys timings:**

| | bytes moved | time | rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 600M reduce | 6,291,456 read + 1,572,864 write = 7,864,320 B | 2280.5 ns | **3,448.5 GB/s = 3.45 TB/s** |
| 1.7B reduce | 8,388,608 read + 2,097,152 write = 10,485,760 B | 2546.1 ns | **4,118.4 GB/s = 4.12 TB/s** |

The byte counts are just: split-K at sk=2 writes **two fp32 partial slices** (`2 × M × N × 4`), then the reduce reads both back and writes one **bf16** output (`M × N × 2`).

## What it means

- 3.45 TB/s = **72% of peak**
- 4.12 TB/s = **86% of peak**

For a pure streaming kernel — read two arrays, add, write one — 80–90% of peak is about the practical ceiling on HBM. So the 1.7B case at 86% is essentially maxed out, and the 600M case at 72% has only a little headroom.

That's why the EOD says it can only be *avoided*, not made faster: even if the reduce hit 100% of peak it would drop from 2.55 µs to 2.18 µs, which is nowhere near closing a 10-point gap. The fix has to be not writing those fp32 partials to HBM in the first place — which is exactly what cuBLAS does at low K by not splitting, and what stream-K would do.

One thing I should flag: the 72% on 600M is soft — the smaller transfer means launch and tail effects weigh more, so it isn't necessarily leaving 28% on the table. The 1.7B number is the more trustworthy one for the "at the memory wall" claim.

what i cant understand , whats that 141 GB HBM3e and whats that 4.8TB/s memory bandwidth bro ? and whats nvlink ? and how this bandwidthe related ot these

### CLAUDE [2026-09-09 10:13 IST]

Good question — these are three different things and they're easy to mix up. Let me verify the NVLink number rather than quote from memory:
> tool `WebFetch`: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h200/

Verified. Here it is in plain terms.

## The three numbers are answering three different questions

| | what it answers | H200 |
|---|---|---|
| **141 GB HBM3e** | **how much** fits | 141 GB |
| **4.8 TB/s** | **how fast** the GPU reads/writes its own memory | 4.8 TB/s |
| **NVLink 900 GB/s** | **how fast** one GPU talks to **another GPU** | 900 GB/s |

## 141 GB HBM3e = the size of the GPU's memory

HBM means **High Bandwidth Memory**. It's the DRAM chips sitting right next to the GPU chip, stacked vertically and wired with a very wide connection. "3e" is just the generation (HBM3 enhanced).

141 GB is **capacity** — how much data you can hold at once. Weights, activations, gradients, our A/B/C matrices. Nothing to do with speed.

## 4.8 TB/s = how fast data moves between HBM and the GPU cores

TB/s = **terabytes per second**. 4.8 TB/s = 4,800 GB per second.

A way to feel it: **filling all 141 GB takes about 29 ms** (141 ÷ 4800). That's slow compared to how fast the tensor cores compute. This is why GEMM kernels work so hard to *avoid* touching HBM — they keep data in shared memory and registers instead.

**This is the number that matters for our split-K problem.** Our reduce kernel has to:
1. write 2 slices of fp32 partial results **out to HBM**
2. read them both **back from HBM**
3. write the final bf16 answer **out to HBM**

That traffic can't go faster than 4.8 TB/s. We measured it at **4.12 TB/s** on 1.7B = **86% of the maximum possible**. That's why I said it can't be optimised — there's no kernel trick that beats physics. The only fix is to not send those partials to HBM at all.

## NVLink 900 GB/s = GPU-to-GPU, a completely separate wire

NVLink connects **one GPU to another GPU** (4 or 8 in a system). It is **not** the memory bandwidth.

**It is 5.3× slower than HBM** — 900 GB/s vs 4,800 GB/s. So talking to a neighbour GPU is much more expensive than talking to your own memory.

## How they connect to our work

| our work | which number |
|---|---|
| split-K reduce kernel writing/reading fp32 partials | **HBM 4.8 TB/s** — we're at 86% of it |
| every GEMM reading A and B, writing C | **HBM 4.8 TB/s** |
| the L2 pollution costing 2.04 points in the trainer | **HBM** — polluted L2 means more trips to HBM |
