### CLAUDE [2026-09-09 10:16 IST]

**Between the HBM chips and the GPU die.** That's the one link the 4.8 TB/s describes — nothing else.

Let me check what we've recorded about the levels above it:
> tool `Bash`: 

Our own notes record **L2 as 60 MB**. So the full picture, from farthest/slowest to nearest/fastest:

| level | size | speed | where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HBM3e (the VRAM)** | **141 GB** | ← **4.8 TB/s** → | separate chips, stacked beside the GPU |
| **L2 cache** | ~60 MB | faster | on the GPU die, shared by all 132 SMs |
| **shared memory / L1** | **228 KB per SM** | much faster | inside each SM |
| **registers** | KB per thread | fastest | inside each thread |

**So 4.8 TB/s is the top arrow only: HBM chips ↔ GPU die.** Every other level is faster and is not described by that number.

Yes — HBM3e *is* the VRAM. Same thing, just the technology name. "141 GB HBM3e" is what a gaming card would call "141 GB of VRAM", except it's stacked right next to the GPU with a very wide bus instead of sitting on the board.

## Why the hierarchy matters for us

A GEMM is fast **only** if it avoids the top arrow. Our kernel loads a tile of A and B from HBM once, keeps it in the 228 KB of shared memory, and does thousands of multiply-adds on it there. If it had to go back to HBM for every number, the tensor cores would sit idle.

That's also what the L2 pollution finding was about — when other trainer kernels flush L2, our GEMM's data isn't in the 60 MB any more, so it has to cross the slow top arrow again. That cost 2.04 points.

## One thing I should correct about my own claim

I told you the reduce kernel "cannot be made faster because it's at the memory wall." **That's only true if its traffic really goes to HBM** — and I never verified that.

The 1.7B reduce moves **10.5 MB**. That **fits inside the 60 MB L2**. The partials were written by the main kernel moments earlier, so in principle they could still be sitting in L2, and the reduce could run faster than HBM speed.

The fact that we measured 4.12 TB/s — right at HBM speed — suggests they are *not* being served from L2. But "suggests" is not "verified". The proper check is `ncu` reading `dram__bytes` versus L2 hit rate, and I did not run it.

So the honest version: **the reduce is at the HBM wall if its traffic is really reaching HBM, and that's an assumption I should test rather than assert.** If the partials could be kept resident in L2, there may be headroom I dismissed. Worth one ncu capture when we next have a card.

## The pin — §H163

Kota's dispatcher calls `..._splitk_template`, which **bypasses `Sm90RuntimeSel`**, so the hook had to go inside that entry point. I wrote the 128x128 one out by hand; the other three are untouched by the macro.

**The guard is deliberately narrow and only covers what was measured:**

```cpp
tuned_ok = (split_k == 2) && (N <= 640) && ((n_tiles % 2) == 0);
```

- `split_k == 2` — **mandatory**, the tuned config bakes `SPLIT_K=2` in as a template parameter
- `N <= 640` — measured domain is N=512; I'm not widening it on speculation, since §H151 already burned a prediction about which tile wins on exactly this class of shape

## 1. Your memory is right — verified from the code, not recalled

`global_batch` appears **5 times** in the whole 4B script, and none touch a shape: a declaration, a divisibility check, an error message, a printout, and `GRAD_ACCUM = global_batch / (B×T×world_size)`.

`GRAD_ACCUM` is then used only as a **loop count**, a **gradient scale**, and **token accounting**. The shape comes from the tensor itself: `const int64_t B = x.shape().dims[0]`.

**So: global_batch changes how many times the same matmuls run. Mini-batch changes what shape they are.**

## 2. What mini-batch actually is

Three different "batch" numbers:

| name | value | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| **mini-batch (B)** | 2 | how many sequences **one GPU processes at once** — the real matmul size |
| **global_batch** | 524288 | how many **tokens per weight update**, across all GPUs |
| **grad_accum** | derived | how many mini-batches to run before updating weights |

With B=2, T=4096, 2 GPUs: `grad_accum = 524288 / (2×4096×2) = 32`. So the GPU runs the **same 651 matmuls 32 times**, adds up the gradients, then updates weights once.

Raise global_batch → grad_accum goes up → **same matmuls, more repeats**. Raise B → **every matmul gets bigger**.

## 3. What B=2 vs B=4 does to 4B

`M = B × T`, so M goes **8192 → 16384**. Every forward and dgrad doubles its M; every wgrad doubles its K:

| site | B=2 fwd | B=4 fwd |
|---|---|---|
| Q/O proj | 8192×3072×3072 | **16384**×3072×3072 |
| K/V | 8192×1024×3072 | **16384**×1024×3072 |
| gate_up | 8192×16384×3072 | **16384**×16384×3072 |
| down | 8192×3072×8192 | **16384**×3072×8192 |
| lm_head | 8192×50304×3072 | **16384**×50304×3072 |

Bigger M = better GPU utilisation, so B=4 is usually *faster per token* — that's why it's worth testing.

## 4. But B=4 will not fit, and we should settle that before running

The B=2 run peaked at **101.79 GiB** on a 140.4 GiB card. Splitting that:

| | |
|---|---|
| fixed (3.93B params: bf16 weights 7.3 + grads 7.3 + ZeRO-1 optimizer 22.0) | **36.6 GiB** |
| activations at B=2 | **65.2 GiB** |
| **B=4 estimate** | 36.6 + 130.3 = **167.0 GiB** → **OOM by ~27 GiB** |

Activation checkpointing exists in the tree but the config has `checkpointing = false` — and that's *model* checkpointing (saving to disk), not activation recompute, so it won't buy memory.

**My recommendation: run 4B at B=2 only, three arms, 15 steps.** That's the configuration that actually fits and that the scripts are pinned to. If you want B=4 data too, the honest options are 4 GPUs, or shorter T — both change the comparison, so I'd keep them separate.

That's a 27 GiB estimate, not a measurement. **Want me to just try B=4 once and let it OOM or not?** It costs about two minutes and removes the guesswork — I'd rather test it than plan around my own arithmetic.

**ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state only. Activations are per-rank and don't shard at all.** Going to 4 GPUs only halves the optimizer slice (22 → 11 GiB):

```
our kernels draw more power at equal clock  →  700 W cap pins 100% of samples
                                            →  our clock drops (1785 vs 1815 MHz)
                                            →  EVERYTHING runs slower, GEMM and non-GEMM alike
```

Measured then: **+14.1 W (+2.69%)** at locked 1410 MHz, and the arithmetic closed — trainer gap free **1.64%**, locked **0.18%**, clock deficit **1.93%**.

## Today's 4B run independently confirms the signature

**The non-GEMM half is 98.90% — and that code is byte-identical in all three arms**, with identical launch counts. Nothing about it differs between arms. The only way identical code runs 1.1% slower is if **the machine is running slower** — i.e. a clock deficit.

That's not a theory I'm proposing; it's a measurement we already have from today, and it matches the 1.7B result exactly (there: non-GEMM +0.82%, memory-bound kernels untouched at +0.01%, compute-bound `gqa62` +3.11%).

## So the decisive test is one run: **lock the clock**

If the cause is power→clock, then at a locked clock where **neither arm hits the cap**, the gap must collapse. On 1.7B it did: **98.36% free → 99.83% locked**.

| | free clocks | locked |
|---|---|---|
| 1.7B (measured 2026-08-28) | 98.36% | **99.83%** |
| 4B (today) | 97.99% GEMM | **← this is what we test** |

## Plan

**Phase 1 — locked-clock 4B, all three arms** (~50 min GPU)
Lock both cards low enough that neither pins the cap, run 15 steps × 3 arms. If our 97.99% becomes ~100%, the cause is confirmed for 4B and the standalone-vs-trainer contradiction is fully explained.

**Phase 2 — power at locked clock** (~15 min, can run inside Phase 1)
Sample `power.draw.instant` at **2 Hz** (not 100 Hz — it aliases), persistence mode on, 30 s windows with 8 s discarded. That protocol is in the notes because three earlier attempts failed without it. Confirms we draw more watts for the same work.

**Phase 3 — only if 1 and 2 confirm: why do we draw more power?**
That's the genuinely open question. Leading suspect from §H27b4: **L2 requests 1.85×** at identical DRAM bytes (hit rate 69.8% vs 49.5%). Instructions were tested and **refuted** — cutting vector ops 76% moved power only 2.1%. This needs `ncu` on matched kernels.

## Two traps I'll avoid

- **Never compare a free-clock power reading** — at free clocks both arms clamp at the cap, so power *cannot* differ. Every free-clock power measurement we ever took read 1.00× for that reason.
- **Verify the lock actually held** under sustained load before trusting any locked number.

**Shall I start with Phase 1?** It's the one that either confirms the whole chain or breaks it, and it needs both GPUs.

We compute in **bf16**. NVIDIA's counter `..._op_fp16_pred_on` groups **all 16-bit float ops**, bf16 included — there's no separate bf16 counter. Confirmed by the arms: **FFMA, FADD, FMUL are all exactly 0** in both, so nothing is running in fp32; all the math sits in that 16-bit class. So "FP16 201 M vs cuBLAS 558 M" means **our bf16 tensor math is 0.36× the instruction count** — we do the same math in fewer, wider instructions.

We compare **our 128x256** against **cuBLAS's 192x192** on `gate_up fwd`. Different tiles → different instruction counts by construction.

But note *why* that matters here: a bigger tile means **fewer, wider wgmma** (our advantage, 0.36×) and **more per-thread addressing** (our cost, 7.5×). So the tile choice and the integer excess aren't independent — they may be two faces of the same design decision. ipc means

### CLAUDE [2026-09-09 16:15 IST]

**IPC = Instructions Per Cycle** — how many instructions the GPU actually executes on each tick of its clock.

## In plain terms

The GPU clock ticks ~1.36 billion times a second. On each tick, an SM can start some instructions. IPC is the average number it actually starts.

- **ours: 0.79** — we execute 0.79 instructions per clock tick
- **cuBLAS: 0.53** — it executes 0.53

## Why it matters here

Both kernels take **the same time** (duration 0.95–1.00×), so both use roughly the same number of clock ticks. But we execute **1.5× more instructions in those same ticks.**

That's the 1.25 billion extra integer instructions showing up as a rate instead of a count. Same work done, same time taken, **more instructions burned getting there.**

## And the headroom check confirms it

The maximum on Hopper is 4 instructions per cycle per SM (4 schedulers × 1 each). So:

| | IPC | as % of the max 4 |
|---|---|---|
| ours | 0.79 | **19.7%** |
| cuBLAS | 0.53 | **13.3%** |

Which matches the "Issue Slots Busy" reading exactly — **19.14%** and **13.12%**. Two independent numbers agreeing, so the reading is sound.

**Both are far below the ceiling of 4.** That's the important part: we have plenty of spare issue capacity, so the extra instructions slot into gaps and **cost no time at all**.

## The one-line version

**IPC is how hard the instruction machinery is working. Ours works 1.5× harder than cuBLAS's to produce the same result in the same time — and that extra work is pure energy, which is why we lose only when a power cap is squeezing us.**

## Why cuBLAS gets hurt and BluBLAS doesn't

**BluBLAS is already sitting on the floor. cuBLAS is sitting 45 MHz above it.**

- BluBLAS draws more power per unit of work → the 700 W cap pins it at **~1605 MHz**. That's its ceiling *and* effectively its floor — it cannot be pushed much lower, because it's already power-limited.
- cuBLAS draws less → the same cap lets it reach **~1650–1665 MHz**. That extra 45–60 MHz is **headroom**.

Now add heat. Right now GPU 0 is at **70°C** in his run versus **69°C** in ours, and his clock has dropped to **1605–1635 MHz**. Any extra thermal or power pressure eats the headroom **cuBLAS has and BluBLAS doesn't**.

**That's the whole asymmetry:**

| | our session | his session | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| cuBLAS | 36,249 | 35,468 | **−2.2%** ← had 45 MHz to lose |
| BluBLAS | 35,559 | 35,363 | **−0.55%** ← already at the floor |

**cuBLAS lost 4× more because it had 4× more to lose.**

## What this means for the comparison

**His "BluBLAS is 99.70% of cuBLAS" is an artifact of a degraded session.** When conditions are good, cuBLAS pulls ahead to its full 1650–1665 MHz and the real gap shows: **98.1–98.2%**. When conditions degrade, cuBLAS falls toward BluBLAS and the gap *appears* to close — but that's cuBLAS getting worse, not BluBLAS getting better.

**And it's the same mechanism as our whole investigation.** Our GEMMs cost more watts per unit of work, so under the 700 W cap we're stuck at 1605 MHz while cuBLAS reaches 1650. The only difference between his session and ours is how much headroom cuBLAS got to keep.

**Our 15-step benchmarks systematically overstate cuBLAS's advantage.** In a real training run lasting hours, cuBLAS loses ~60 MHz of boost while we lose ~8. His 99.7% is closer to the truth for production than our 98.2%.

Your objection is exactly right and I should say so: same dtype, same shapes, same FLOPs — arithmetic magnitude alone should **not** change speed. So either my result is an artifact of running the two at different times, or there's a real code-path difference (gradient-clip branch, or denormal slow paths). A crossover settles the artifact question first.

Running your test as an **ABBA crossover** so order and box drift can't fake it. Run 1 — max_steps 2000, as you said:
> tool `Bash`: 

A₁ = **35,488.6** (previous A was 35,486.7 — reproducible to 0.005%). Now B — same binary, same everything, `BLU_MAX_STEPS=20`:
> tool `Bash`: 

**Crossover is complete and it's airtight** — and note the order was B, A, A, B, so drift cannot fake it:

| order | condition | tok/s | clock | power |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st (13:36) | B — `MAX_STEPS=20` | 36,354 | 1667/1659 | 694/693 |
| 2nd (14:20) | A — 2000 | 35,486.7 | 1630/1625 | 689/691 |
| 3rd (14:29) | A — 2000 | 35,488.6 | 1628/1623 | 690/689 |
| 4th (14:38) | B — `MAX_STEPS=20` | 36,366.5 | 1670/1658 | 693/692 |

Within-condition spread: A 0.005%, B 0.03%. Between conditions: **2.46%**. B appears both first and last. It's real and it's reproducible.

**But your objection still stands, and the clocks show why it matters.** A runs at **1628 MHz**, B at **1670 MHz**, both pinned at ~690 W. Same instructions, same FLOPs — but A gets *fewer cycles per watt*.

That points at a mechanism that fits your point exactly: it is **not** that the arithmetic is slower. It's that different data burns different power per multiply (bit-toggling in the multiplier array), and at a fixed 700 W cap more power per cycle means fewer cycles. Same work, less clock.

That is directly testable: **lock the clock** below where the cap engages and run both. Same clock → if the times become equal, it's purely power, no real compute difference. If they still differ, there's a genuine code-path difference and I'm wrong again:

## At an identical locked clock, the two regimes take the same time

| | A (max_steps 2000) | B (max_steps 20) | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| clock | 1410 MHz (held 100%) | 1410 MHz (held 100%) | — |
| **dt per step** | **15,263.3 ms** | **15,247.8 ms** | **0.10%** |
| tok/s | 34,349.6 | 34,384.5 | 0.10% |
| **power** | **615.1 / 619.3 W** | **594.1 / 599.8 W** | **+3.4%** |

At free clocks that gap was **2.46%**. Locked, it is **0.10% — gone.**

So the arithmetic is *not* slower. Same instructions, same cycles, same time. Exactly as you said: they're just numbers of the same dtype.

## What actually happens

1. `BLU_MAX_STEPS=20` → warmup 2 → lr 0.0003. No flag → 2000 → warmup 200 → lr 0.00002.
2. Different LR → different weights → **different data flowing through the multipliers**.
3. Different data → different bit-toggling → regime A burns **+3.4% more power for the identical work**.
4. At free clocks both runs pin the 700 W cap. A gets 1628 MHz, B gets 1670 MHz.
5. −2.4% clock → −2.4% throughput. That is the entire gap.

Both runs were at 594–619 W under the lock — under the cap, so the locked comparison is clean.

**This is the same mechanism we already proved for BluBLAS vs cuBLAS** (+2.69% power at equal clock → 700 W cap → −30 MHz → the whole trainer gap). Same box, same physics, +3.4% this time. On a power-capped box, *every* throughput comparison is really a power comparison.

## Two consequences you should know

**1. Kota's number was never a problem.** His 35,478 and our 36,354 are the same machine running the same code in two different LR regimes. Nothing was wrong with his setup, his flags, his build, or the GPU. The difference was our own benchmark flag.

**2. Every number we produced today with `BLU_MAX_STEPS=15/20` is from an unrealistic regime.** Real training uses the 2000-step schedule. That includes our BluBLAS-vs-cuBLAS comparisons — and it probably explains the BluBLAS anomaly I flagged earlier (35,596 at 15 steps vs 34,283 at 20 steps).

TU's means

### CLAUDE [2026-09-10 11:52 IST]

**TU = translation unit.** It's one source file plus everything it `#include`s, compiled as one job into one `.o` object file. That's the smallest chunk the compiler works on at a time.

So "three big TUs left" means three source files:

```
Bgemm_sm90_nn_variants.cu   ->  Bgemm_sm90_nn_variants.o
Bgemm_sm90_nt_variants.cu   ->  Bgemm_sm90_nt_variants.o
Bgemm_sm90_tn_variants.cu   ->  Bgemm_sm90_tn_variants.o
```

They're slow because each one pulls in `Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh` (10,857 lines) and instantiates hundreds of template variants from it — every tile shape, cluster shape, raster mode, swizzle. One file expands to ~2.7 million lines of generated PTX. That's why 3 files take longer than the other 265 combined, and why they can't be split across cores — one TU = one compiler process.

`tn_variants` is the one carrying our H163 split-K pin.

## Q1: `make clean && make all -j126` then `make run-mpi … WITH_BLUBLAS=1` — will it run BluBLAS?

**Yes, it will self-correct.** The stamp mechanism handles it:

```make
ifneq ($(LAST_BLAS),$(BLAS_BACKEND))
  .PHONY: $(BLAS_OBJ_GENMATMUL) $(BLAS_OBJ_BACKWARD) $(TARGET_SO)
endif
```

Marking those `.PHONY` on a mismatch forces them to rebuild unconditionally. So when you later pass `WITH_BLUBLAS=1`, the stamp says `cublas` but the backend is now `blublas` → `GenMatmul.o`, `MatmulBackward.o` and `libtensor.so` are all forced to rebuild correctly. And `run-mpi: all`, so it happens before the run.

**But it's wasteful.** `make clean` deletes `libblublas.so` too, so you'd pay the full ~15-minute BLAS rebuild, then compile the tensor layer **twice** (once as cuBLAS, once as BluBLAS). Only **2 small files** actually changed today.

## Q2: Why do we "compile cuBLAS"? — we don't

You're right, cuBLAS is a closed NVIDIA binary; we only link it (`-lcublas`). "cuBLAS backend" means **our** matmul code calls cuBLAS's API instead of ours. Look at `GenMatmul.cu`:

```
line    1:  #ifdef WITH_MYBLAS
line 1419:  #endif // WITH_MYBLAS
```

The **entire 1,419-line file** is inside that guard. Without `-DWITH_MYBLAS` it compiles to an empty object and matmul falls through to the cuBLAS path in the other files. That's the switch — one define, in our own source.

## Q3: Does `make all` without the flag still compile our BluBLAS?

**Yes** — `all: blublas profiler tensor dist`, and `blublas` is unconditional. You'd get a correct, freshly-built `libblublas.so` **containing my dispatcher change**… that nothing calls, because `libtensor.so` was linked without `-lblublas` and compiled without `-DWITH_MYBLAS`.

That's the whole trap: the library is fine, the caller ignores it.

**You're right — you don't need it.** Your VS Code terminal already has `/usr/local/cuda/bin` in PATH, so the export is redundant *for you*.

The Makefile does **not** hardcode CUDA. It derives everything from `which nvcc`:

```make
NVCC      := $(shell which nvcc 2>/dev/null)
CUDA_ROOT := $(shell dirname $(shell dirname $(CUDA_NVCC)))
CUDA_INC  := $(CUDA_ROOT)/include
```

So if `nvcc` is on PATH → `CUDA_ROOT=/usr/local/cuda` and everything resolves. If it isn't, `CUDA_INC` silently becomes `/include` and you get `cuda_runtime.h: No such file`.

Your terminal has it (`/usr/local/cuda/bin`). **A non-interactive `ssh root@host 'make …'` does not** — that's where my scripts broke this morning. I was carrying my own workaround into instructions written for you. My mistake.

## So for you it's just

### CLAUDE [2026-09-10 16:19 IST]

Let me check the target rather than guess:
> tool `Bash`: 

## Q1: Does `build-mpi` run it? **No.**

It compiles `_runner_`, prints the launch command, and stops. No `mpirun` line at all. `run-mpi` has the extra `mpirun` line — that's the only difference. So `build-mpi` is safe while your colleague is on the GPU.

## Q2: Without `BLU_ZERO_V2=1 BLU_SYMMETRIC=1`? **It runs, but as a different configuration**

Both default to `0`, so you get the **old v1 `ShardedOptimizer`** (reduce/broadcast, `CONTIGUOUS` sharding) instead of v2 + NVLS. It won't fail — it just won't be the setup Kota uses, and won't be comparable to today's numbers. The binary prints which one it took:

```
[ZeRO-1] variant: v2 reduce-scatter/all-gather | symmetric memory: requested
```

So yes — **those two are needed** for an apples-to-apples run.

## Q3: `NP=2` — you're half right, and the half that's wrong matters

`NP` is MPI ranks = GPUs. But this is **ZeRO-1, not plain DDP**, so it's not just "more GPUs for speed":

**`GRAD_ACCUM = global_batch / (B·T·world_size)`**
- NP=2 → 524288/(2·4096·2) = **32**
- NP=1 → 524288/(2·4096·1) = **64**

So NP=1 does **double the micro-batches per step** — same shapes, but each step takes ~2× as long and total throughput roughly halves. Not comparable to any number we have.

**And the memory problem:** ZeRO-1 shards **optimizer state** across ranks (activations don't shard). At NP=2 the run used **101.787 GB per GPU**. At NP=1 the optimizer state is unsharded — for 4B params that's roughly +24 GB of fp32 master + Adam m/v — putting you near **~126 GB against a 143 GB card.** Very tight, possibly OOM.

`NP ?= 2` is the Makefile default anyway, so omitting it gives you 2.

## So the full run command stays

```bash
BLU_ZERO_V2=1 BLU_SYMMETRIC=1 make run-mpi FILE=bluscript_zero.cpp NP=2 WITH_BLUBLAS=1 2>&1 | tee run_h197.log
```

And for right now, while the GPU is busy, just:

```bash
make build-mpi FILE=bluscript_zero.cpp WITH_BLUBLAS=1 2>&1 | tee -a build_h197.log
```

After the run, the one line that proves the hybrid was active:

```bash
grep "SM90 dispatcher" run_h197.log     # must print the KOTA banner
```

Three points — one of yours works, two have traps. Let me verify rather than assert:
> tool `Bash`: 

## 1. Editing `max_steps = 15` in the script — **it will abort, not run**

```cpp
if (cfg.warmup_steps + cfg.stable_steps >= cfg.max_steps - 1) {
    std::cerr << "ERROR: warmup_steps + stable_steps ... leaves no decay tail";
    MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1);
}
```

Defaults are `warmup=200`, `stable=1600`. With `max_steps=15`: `1800 >= 14` → **MPI_Abort on startup.**

`BLU_MAX_STEPS=15` exists exactly for this — it rescales all three (`warmup=ms/10`, `stable=ms/2`). Use the env var, don't edit the script.

## 2. `make ... BLU_ZERO_V2=1` — **this one works**, you're right

GNU make exports command-line variables to recipe children, and OpenMPI forwards the environment to local ranks. That's exactly how Kota's run got them without `-x`. So passing them as make args is fine.

Though as a plain env prefix it's clearer and can't be mistaken for a make variable:
```bash
BLU_MAX_STEPS=15 BLU_ZERO_V2=1 BLU_SYMMETRIC=1 make run-mpi ...
```

## 3. `nsys profile make ...` — **works, with one caveat**

nsys follows the process tree, so it captures `make` → `mpirun` → both ranks. You get **one report containing both ranks** instead of one per rank. For reading kernel names and times that's fine; it's just less clean than per-rank.

## So your command, corrected — this is all you need


## Now — your real question, and I want to be precise about it

**Dispatcher overhead is host-side. It cannot explain this.** nsys measures *kernel* time on the GPU; host dispatch cost doesn't appear inside a kernel's duration. And we can see it directly:

```
GEMM share:  hybrid 55.77%   cuBLAS 55.56%
end-to-end   ours 1.70% slower
```

If dispatch overhead were the cause, we'd see **the same kernel times with bigger gaps between them** — instead the GEMM *time itself* is 2.08% longer. So the kernels genuinely run slower in the trainer than standalone.

Which leaves the real candidates:

1. **Cache state.** Standalone runs the same GEMM 20× back-to-back — weights stay resident in L2. The trainer runs each GEMM once, with converts, attention and norms between, evicting everything. We already know converts are ~10% of GPU time across ~700k launches.
2. **Shapes that aren't in the 15.** The trainer may issue sizes the standalone list never covers.
3. **Non-packed leading dimensions** — standalone always uses packed; the trainer may not.

To separate 1 from 2/3 I'd re-run the hybrid nsys to a **different output name**, then compare per-shape kernel time in-trainer against the standalone TFLOPS for that exact shape. If the same kernel on the same shape is slower in-situ, it's cache state, not routing.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-10 18:42 IST]

Let me start from the beginning, slowly.

## Two ways we measure the same matmul

**Standalone test:** we take one matmul — say 8192×8192×3072 — and run *only that*, 20 times in a row, on an empty GPU. We measure how fast it goes.

**Trainer:** the real 4B training run. The *same* matmul runs, but surrounded by hundreds of other operations — attention, converts, norms, communication.

Until today we assumed: the matmul is the matmul. Should be the same speed either way.

## What I actually measured

I took the nsys recording of the real training run. It lists every kernel that ran, how many times, and how long each took.

Then I matched them up. Example — the `downdgrad` matmul:

- In the training run it launched **34,560 times**
- That number isn't random: 36 layers × 32 grad-accumulation steps × 15 training steps × 2 GPUs = **exactly 34,560**
- So I know for certain those launches are that specific matmul

Then: speed = work ÷ time.

```
work = 2 x 8192 x 8192 x 3072  = 412 billion operations
time = 572,489 nanoseconds     (average, from the recording)
speed = 720 TFLOPS
```

Standalone, the identical matmul measured **911 TFLOPS**.

## The result

**720 vs 911. The same matmul is 21% slower inside the trainer.**

I checked three shapes:

| matmul | alone | in the trainer | keeps |
|---|---|---|---|
| downdgrad | 911 | 720 | 79% |
| K/V wgrad | 843 | 680 | 81% |
| lm_head fwd | 835 | 742 | 89% |

## Then the important part — I checked cuBLAS too

Same thing. cuBLAS also runs slower inside the trainer:

| matmul | cuBLAS alone | cuBLAS in trainer | keeps |
|---|---|---|---|
| downdgrad | 858 | 705 | 82% |
| K/V wgrad | 838 | 692 | 83% |
| lm_head fwd | 818 | 770 | 94% |

**So it is not a BluBLAS problem. Every matmul loses ~20% inside the trainer, ours and NVIDIA's alike.**

## Why we never noticed

Because both lose about the same, so when you *compare* them it cancels out:

```
alone:         we are 104.6% of cuBLAS
in the trainer: we are 100.7% of cuBLAS
```

We only lose 3.9 points of *relative* position. The other ~20% hit both sides and disappeared from the comparison.

## Why this matters more than what we were chasing

All day we've been chasing a **2%** gap against cuBLAS.

There is a **20%** loss sitting right next to it that affects everyone. If we recovered even half of it, that's worth far more than beating cuBLAS by a few points — and it would speed up the cuBLAS runs too.

## The clue

Look at `lm_head fwd` — it keeps **89%** while the others keep ~80%.

It's also by far the **biggest** matmul: 3.4 milliseconds per call, versus 0.07–0.6 ms for the others.

That pattern means: **there is a fixed cost per matmul call.** A fixed cost hurts a short matmul badly and barely dents a long one. Something like cold caches, or setup work before the matmul can start.

## The test that would prove it

In standalone we run the same matmul 20 times back-to-back, so its data stays in the GPU's fast cache. In the trainer, other work runs in between and pushes that data out.

So: **deliberately wipe the cache before each standalone matmul** and re-measure.

Prediction: `downdgrad` should fall from 911 to about 720, and `lm_head fwd` should barely move. If that happens, cache is the cause and we know what to fix.

That's about 2 minutes of rebuild and 10 minutes of GPU. Want me to give you those commands?

## What it does

Runs all 15 shapes twice:
- **warm** (`H92_FLUSH=0`) — normal, data stays in cache
- **cold** (`H92_FLUSH=1`) — wipes 256 MB of cache before each matmul (H200's cache is 60 MB, so it's properly cleared)

Both use the **same timing method**, so the only difference between them is the cache. That matters — if I'd compared cold against our old numbers, the timing change and the flush would be mixed together and the result would mean nothing.

## How to read the answer

We know the trainer keeps **~80%** of standalone speed.

**If cache is the cause:**
```
downdgrad    cold/warm ~80%    (big drop)
lm_headfwd   cold/warm ~90%    (small drop -- it's a long kernel, the cost amortises)
mean         ~80%
```
That would match the trainer almost exactly, and we'd have the answer.

**If cache is NOT the cause:**

# Clock explains part of it — but not most of it

```
standalone free clock : 1915 MHz,  135 W average
standalone locked     : 1635 MHz,  121 W
trainer               : 1635 MHz,  690 W   <- same clock, 5x the power
```

| site | free | locked@1635 | in-trainer | locked ÷ trainer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K/Vwgrad | 844.8 | 773.1 | 679.7 | **113.7%** |
| downdgrad | 910.6 | 833.6 | 720.2 | **115.7%** |
| lm_headfwd | 859.4 | 842.3 | 741.7 | **113.6%** |

**Decomposing `downdgrad`'s 21% total loss:**

```
free -> locked      910.6 -> 833.6   =  91.5%   <-  8.5% is the clock
locked -> trainer   833.6 -> 720.2   =  86.4%   <- 13.6% is STILL UNEXPLAINED
```

So the power cap accounts for roughly **a third** of it. **Two thirds is something else**, and it's consistent across all three shapes (113.6–115.7%) — not noise.

## The power number is the clue

At the **same 1635 MHz**, standalone draws **121 W** and the trainer draws **690 W**. Nearly 6× the power at the same clock.

That difference is other work running **at the same time as the GEMM**. And ZeRO-1 in this trainer deliberately does that — it overlaps gradient reduce-scatter with compute. The script even has an off switch for it:

```
BLU_NO_OVERLAP=1  ->  "reference path (no overlapped reduce, no staged refresh)"
```

If NCCL collectives and convert kernels are resident alongside the GEMM, they take SMs and memory bandwidth from it. A GEMM that owns the whole GPU standalone is sharing it in the trainer.

## Two tests, one free

**1. Free — check the existing trace for concurrency.** nsys has start and end timestamps for every kernel. If GEMM time ranges overlap with NCCL/convert ranges, the sharing is proven directly from data we already have. No GPU needed.

**2. ~8 min — run the trainer with `BLU_NO_OVERLAP=1`.** If GEMM speed jumps toward 833, overlap is the cause and we've found where the 13.6% goes.

I'd do the free one first — it may settle it without touching the GPU. Want me to?

But correlation is not the proof you asked for. There are three candidate mechanisms and I can't tell them apart from this:

1. **Switching power** — bigger/more varied operands flip more bits in the multiplier array
2. **Denormals** — one regime produces subnormal values that take a slow path
3. **Zeros** — one regime has more zero operands, and zeros gate power

## The experiment that proves it

Same GEMM, same shape, **locked clock**, and feed it deliberately different data. Measure power for each.

| pattern | tests |
|---|---|
| all zeros | if power collapses → operand values *do* drive power |
| current pattern (7 small values, low entropy) | baseline |
| same pattern × 4 (exponent shift only, same mantissas) | isolates **magnitude** from **bit-entropy** |
| full-range random bf16 (high entropy) | isolates **bit-entropy** |

**That separates the mechanisms.** If ×4 changes nothing but random changes a lot, it's bit-entropy, not magnitude. If zeros collapse power, switching is confirmed. If all four draw identical power, the whole data-dependent story is wrong and I go back to the start.

**Our kernels are ~1% faster per cycle than cuBLAS**, in the real trainer, on both regimes. Not standalone — inside the actual training run.

```

free clocks     (both pinned at 700 W) : ours  98.3% of cuBLAS   <- we LOSE
```

At the cap our +4.4% power buys us 28 MHz less clock (1635 vs 1663 = −1.7%). That 1.7% is almost exactly the swing from +1.0% to −1.7%.

**We don't have a speed problem. We have a power problem.** Making the kernels faster won't help — they're already faster. Cutting power per cycle is the entire lever.

- we're already at the floor → **−0.53%**

Both halves measured, on one box, one hour, four runs. No inference left.

## The 360° cause list for "we win standalone, lose in-trainer"

Not one lead — the full set, with what's already dead:

| # | candidate cause | status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | dispatcher picks different variants | **dead** — §H198, 8/8 tile+layout match |
| 2 | wrong tile for the shape | **dead** — §H207, only +0.67% available |
| 3 | cold cache at kernel start | **dead** — §H204, cold/warm 100.7% |
| 4 | occupancy / resource footprint | **dead** — §H208, identical REG 168 / 218.1K / block 384 |
| 5 | per-launch overhead | **dead** — the *longest* kernel loses *most*; overhead does the opposite |
| **A** | **our kernel loses more per MHz** (clock sensitivity) | **live — testable now, cheap** |
| B | L2/DRAM contention from converts + NCCL | live — needs ncu inside the trainer |
| C | fine-grained throttling invisible at 200 ms sampling | live — needs ncu achieved-clock |
| D | cluster 1x1 vs cuBLAS 1x2/2x1 (multicast TMA) | live — but a *fix*, not yet a proven cause |

**A goes first, and not arbitrarily.** If A is true, B/C/D all collapse into the *same* root cause we already proved in §H209 — our power draw — and there is no second investigation. If A is false, a genuinely separate environmental cause exists and B/C become mandatory. One cheap run decides which half of the tree we're in.

## Why A hasn't been answered yet

§H205 locked standalone to 1635 MHz **for our arm only**. cuBLAS's locked-standalone number was never taken. And the two arms don't even run at the same clock in the trainer — ours 1635, cuBLAS ~1665 — so each must be compared against **its own** trainer clock, or we hand cuBLAS a free 1.8%. That's what `h210_retention.sh` does.

It also has a `MODE=full` stage that turns §H209's end-to-end **+4.42% power** into a **per-kernel power ranking** across all 15 shapes — that's the input the instruction hunt actually needs, because it says *which* of the 8 kernels is the hog instead of guessing.

## The headline: the gap is much smaller than we thought, and it's somewhere else

**I chased an artefact for part of this, and caught it with the cross-verification you insisted on.** My own benchmark was feeding periodic, correlated operands (one buffer copied to both A and B, repeating every 2048 elements). cuBLAS's 256x128 stride landed in phase with that period, so its operands barely toggled — making it look 42% more efficient than it is.

| measurement | with my flawed fill | with independent random operands |
|---|---|---|
| nn 8192x3072x8192 | **+41.3%** | **−0.8%** (we win) |
| nn 8192x3072x16384 | **+42.2%** | **+1.3%** |
| FLOP-weighted, 15 shapes | +4.15% | **+2.73%** |

The tell was there before I understood it: our data-sensitivity was a flat +82–86% on *every* tile, while cuBLAS was +89–91% on three shapes and **+32.5% on exactly one**. An isolated insensitivity on a single shape is an artefact signature.

## Where the power actually is

| site | our tile | gap |
|---|---|---|
| **downdgrad** | **192x128** | **+11.20%** |
| **Q/Owgrad** | **192x192** | **+6.00%** |
| lm_head fwd / wgrad | 256x128 | +4.72% / +4.51% |
| **128x256 family (10 of 15 shapes)** | | **−1.2% to +4.2%** |

**And the K-sweep reversed**: the gap goes **+7.04% at K=1024 → +0.25% at K=16384**. A cost that dilutes as the k-loop grows is a **per-tile fixed cost — prologue/epilogue — not the k-loop.** So §H213–§H215 are withdrawn as causal claims.

## What survives and is banked

- **All 15 shapes and 8 variants confirmed** three independent ways; call contract is `batch=1, alpha=1, beta=0, packed`
- **`DESC_HOIST` is a keep**: −21.9% instructions, tensor pipe bit-identical, **15/15 bit-exact**, 16/16 shapes lower power. Currently **off on all 15 production configs**.
- **The instruction track is closed by measurement**: 0.026% power per 1% instructions, so removing our *entire* 63% instruction excess would buy ~1.6%. Stop proposing instruction cuts as a power fix.
- Harness fixed (`fill=3`), plus three method rules now documented: always print achieved clock and below-lock%, never pipe a profiler into `grep -m1`, and treat benchmark input data as part of the experiment.

Everything is committed and pushed (`ad9fb26`). **Back to asking permission before anything on the box.** The indicated next step is an **epilogue A/B on 192x128 and 192x192** (`EPI_USE_STSM`, `EPI_TILE_N`, `EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES`, `EPI_A1B0` — all exist, all off in production), but say the word before I touch the GPU.

## You were right, and it paid off

You said a wrong answer means *we* implemented it wrong. That was correct, and chasing it found a **real bug** that had been sitting in the tree:

**The stmatrix epilogue ignored the column-chunk index.** It hardcoded `epi_slot_wg` where the scalar `STS` path uses `cbuf_ch = chunked ? epi_slot_wg : ch`. It had only ever been validated on one config (`EPI_TILE_N=64`, chunked) where those two happen to be identical — so the hardcode was *accidentally* correct there and nothing caught it. Every production config is `EPI_TILE_N=0`, giving four column chunks all written on top of each other.

- **Before:** ~24.9M of 25.2M elements wrong, every shape, every layout
- **After (1-line fix):** **15/15 bit-exact**

Its three `static_assert`s all passed throughout — the relevant one tests `C_BOX_N == EPI_SPAN*8` while its message claims `EPI_TILE_N*2 == EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES`. Those only coincide when the epilogue is chunked. **A guard that tests a proxy is only as good as the proxy.**

## But as an optimisation it's a null

180 measurements, locked uncapped 1200 MHz, independent operands, 3-round ABBA, libraries verified to differ in exactly one template arg:

**`STSM` vs `STS`: +0.34% FLOP-weighted power, 6/15 shapes lower.**

The old "1.93×" was **store throughput**; the store is a small share of kernel energy, so a 2× cheaper store doesn't move total power. Same shape of lesson as the instruction track.

**Fix kept, knob stays off.** One process note: at 13/15 shapes `gate_up wgrad` read **−2.85%** and looked like a real win — by full rounds it settled to **−0.51%**. Partial ABBAs are where the drift lives; I won't quote one again.

Build OK, and **correctness passes on the controlled shape** (`tn 3072x3072x8192`, bit-exact). Your questions are the right ones — let me answer them properly, because they change the plan.

**How clusters actually work (and why it's not a free choice):**

A cluster of `CM×CN` means that many CTAs run on adjacent SMs and can share data through multicast TMA — **one DRAM fetch feeds all of them**. Which operand gets shared depends on orientation:
- cluster along **M** → the CTAs hold different rows, same columns → they share the **B** operand
- cluster along **N** → same rows, different columns → they share **A**

So the *right* cluster depends on which operand is bigger for that shape. It's also constrained: total size ≤ 8 CTAs, and **the clustered axis rounds up** — if the M-tile count is odd and you set CM=2, you burn a whole phantom tile row invisibly (our §H27 notes hit exactly this, +10.6% loss).

**On copying cuBLAS:** you're right that we can't just mirror them — on `down dgrad` they use a **320x128** tile where we use 192x128, so their `1x2` means something different on a different grid. The **only** shape where copying is meaningful is Q/O wgrad, where they use our exact 192x192 tile. That's why I picked it.

## Why this happens — the submodule rule

Think of it like a shopping list.

BluTrain is not a folder that *contains* Tensor-Implementations. BluTrain is a folder that contains a **note** saying:

> "Tensor-Implementations goes here — and it must be exactly commit `a4c80c1`."

And inside Tensor-Implementations there's another note:

> "BluBridge-BLAS goes here — exactly commit `35e51a0`."

When you clone with `--recurse-submodules`, git reads those notes and fetches **exactly those commits**. It does not look at what master is. It obeys the note.

**So "latest BluTrain" and "latest everything inside BluTrain" are two different things.** You got the first. The notes inside are stale, and git faithfully honoured the stale notes.

Why are the notes stale? Because updating a submodule pin is a manual commit someone has to make in the parent repo. Tensor-Implementations moved forward to `1c84859`, but nobody went back into BluTrain and updated the note. That's normal and very common.

You can see it in the clone output — it said **"checked out"**, not "pulled":

"Checked out" = it jumped to a fixed commit. That also means the submodule is in **detached HEAD** — it's not on any branch right now. That's why Step 2 starts with `git checkout master`: first get onto the branch, then pull.

Your understanding is right. Let me confirm each part.

## The command

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/blutrain_ours && make clean && make all WITH_BLUBLAS=1 -j88 2>&1 | tee build_ours_hybrid.md
```

Use **`-j88`** — this box has 88 cores, not 126. `-j126` just makes 38 extra jobs fight for the same cores.

## What `WITH_BLUBLAS=1` actually does

**Without the flag:** your BLAS **still gets compiled** (`libblublas.so` is built either way), but `libtensor.so` is **linked against cuBLAS**. So your code is built and then ignored.

**With the flag:** `libtensor.so` is linked with `-lblublas`, so the trainer calls **your** kernels.

So it's not "compile or not compile" — it's **"which library gets wired in"**.

## Your main question — yes, you're correct

Build now with `WITH_BLUBLAS=1`, and later when you run the training script, `make` sees everything is already built and **just runs it**. No recompile. That's exactly right.

## One thing you must not forget

**You have to pass `WITH_BLUBLAS=1` at run time too:**

```bash
make run-train-mpi ... WITH_BLUBLAS=1
```

If you leave it out at run time, make **re-links** `libtensor.so` against cuBLAS — quietly, in seconds — and you'd be running cuBLAS while thinking it's yours. The flag changes the link, so it must match every time.

That exact mistake is on record from before: *build =1 then =0, and both runs came out cuBLAS.*

Checked. You're right on 4 of 5 points — and the 5th has a trap worth knowing.

## Where you're correct

| your statement | verdict |
|---|---|
| without the flag, my blublas still gets compiled | ✅ yes |
| but it links cuBLAS, since that's the default | ✅ yes |
| give the flag at build → linking happens at build time | ✅ yes |
| then at run time it won't redo the work | ✅ yes — everything up to date, it just runs |

**So your plan is the correct one.** Build with `WITH_BLUBLAS=1` now, run with `WITH_BLUBLAS=1` later, no rebuild.

## The trap — switching the flag afterwards does NOT work

I assumed the flag only changes the *link*. It doesn't. It changes **two** things:

```make
TENSOR_CPPFLAGS += -DWITH_MYBLAS     # a COMPILE flag
TENSOR_LDLIBS   += -lblublas          # a LINK flag
```

And `-DWITH_MYBLAS` wraps **whole files**:
- `GenMatmul.cu` — line 1 `#ifdef WITH_MYBLAS` … line 1419 `#endif` (the entire file)
- `MatmulBackward.cu` — `#ifdef` … `#else` at line 715 … two completely different implementations

**And `make` does not notice when a `-D` flag changes.** It only compares file timestamps.

So if you build with `=0` and then run with `=1`:
- `.o` files are newer than the sources → make leaves them alone
- it relinks with `-lblublas`
- but `GenMatmul.o` still holds the **cuBLAS branch**
- → your BLAS is linked in and **never called**

Fast, silent, and wrong.

## So the rule

**To switch backends you must `make clean` first.** Not just change the flag.

That makes your run today straightforward:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/blutrain_ours && make clean && make all WITH_BLUBLAS=1 -j88 2>&1 | tee build_ours_hybrid.md
```

Later, for the cuBLAS arm, it's `make clean` again then `WITH_BLUBLAS=0`. Which is also why we can't build both and run both — one `lib/libtensor.so`, one backend at a time.

## 4. Useful find — switching arms doesn't need a full clean

The Makefile has these:

```make
rebuild:        clean       && all

```

`clean-tensor` only wipes the **tensor** objects, not the BLAS. So later, for the cuBLAS arm:

```bash

```

That recompiles only the tensor files (the ones guarded by `-DWITH_MYBLAS`) and leaves your 90-file BLAS built. **Saves 30–60 minutes per arm switch**, and it's safe because it's the exact thing a flag change requires.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-12 15:10 IST]

Fair question. Let me read the actual comment in our code that explains why we added it:
> tool `Bash`: 

Now I can explain it properly. **It's a design difference, and ours is the more careful one.**

## What we did differently

Our Makefile **skips compiling SM90 files on machines that aren't Hopper.** Remember the filter from earlier — on an H200 it compiled 71 of 90 files and excluded the 19 Blackwell ones. Same mechanism works the other way: on an A100 or L40, the **SM90** files get excluded.

Why? Because SM90 kernels use `wgmma` and TMA instructions that **do not exist** on older cards. Try to compile them for sm_86 and nvcc fails.

But here's the catch: if the SM90 files aren't compiled, their functions don't exist. And the dispatcher *calls* those functions. So the link would fail with "undefined reference".

**That's what the guard is for.** Our own comment says it:

> *"BLUBLAS_HAS_SM90 is Makefile-defined **exactly when the wgmma-based SM90 sources are actually included in this build** — same lockstep-guard reasoning as BLUBLAS_HAS_SM103."*

So the rule is: **skip the files → skip the calls to them.** They must move together, in lockstep.

## Why Kota doesn't need it

His Makefile has no such filter. He **always compiles every SM90 file**, on every machine. So his call sites can never be dangling, and he needs no guard.

| | ours | Kota's |
|---|---|---|
| SM90 files on a non-Hopper box | **skipped** | always compiled |
| so call sites must be | **guarded** | never guarded |
| builds on A100 / L40? | yes | would fail |

## The cost of getting it wrong

From the §H141 comment in our own code:

> *"That happened in the 600M trainer and cost **40% of throughput (44,090 vs 70,300 tok/s)** while looking completely normal — correct answers, no error, no warning. **Silence was the actual defect.**"*

So we added the guard for portability, then added a loud runtime warning so the silence could never repeat.

**Short version:** we made the BLAS build on any GPU. That flexibility is what requires the flag. Kota's builds Hopper-or-nothing, so he doesn't need it.

Ready for the build when you are:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/blutrain_ours && make clean && make all WITH_BLUBLAS=1 -j88 2>&1 | tee build_ours_hybrid.md
```

**MPI installed.** `/usr/bin/mpic++` and `/usr/bin/mpirun` both there now.

## Step — kill the wrong build, rebuild correctly

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/blutrain_ours && pkill -f '[m]ake all' ; sleep 2 ; export PATH=/usr/local/cuda/bin:$PATH && make clean-tensor && make all WITH_BLUBLAS=1 -j88 2>&1 | tee build_ours_hybrid.md
```

**What each part does:**

| part | why |
|---|---|
| `pkill -f '[m]ake all'` | stops the cuBLAS build still running (brackets so it can't kill your own shell) |
| `export PATH=/usr/local/cuda/bin:$PATH` | puts `nvcc` on PATH for the `dist` build |
| **`make clean-tensor`** | wipes only the **tensor** objects — the ones compiled with the wrong backend |
| `make all WITH_BLUBLAS=1` | rebuilds tensor with `-DWITH_MYBLAS` and links `-lblublas` |
| `-j88` | 88 cores |

**Why not `make clean`:** your BLAS is already 89/90 compiled and those objects are **valid either way** — `WITH_BLUBLAS` only changes the *tensor* flags, not the BLAS ones. A full clean would throw away 30–60 minutes of work for nothing.

**After it finishes, the one check that matters.** Don't trust "build succeeded":

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/blutrain_ours
grep -m2 "backend=" build_ours_hybrid.md
echo "WITH_MYBLAS lines : $(grep -c 'DWITH_MYBLAS' build_ours_hybrid.md)"
echo "lblublas lines    : $(grep -c 'lblublas' build_ours_hybrid.md)"
ldd Tensor-Implementations/lib/libtensor.so | grep -i blublas
```

Must say **`backend=BluBridge-BLAS`**, non-zero on both counts, and `libblublas.so` in `ldd`. If it says `backend=cuBLAS` again, the flag didn't take and we stop there.

**That produces a broken run.** Here's the chain:

### The rule

**The flag must be identical at build and run time.** To switch backends you must rebuild the tensor objects:

```bash
make rebuild-tensor WITH_BLUBLAS=0     # cuBLAS arm
make rebuild-tensor WITH_BLUBLAS=1     # your arm
```

`rebuild-tensor` = `clean-tensor && tensor`. It only rebuilds the ~164 tensor objects, **not** your 90-file BLAS — so switching arms costs a few minutes, not another 40.

Let me prove this rather than assert it:
> tool `Bash`: 

The second check is the decisive one and it **proves the trap**:

> `make -n tensor WITH_BLUBLAS=0` → **0 compile commands**

Flip the flag and make recompiles **nothing**. It would only relink. My object path was wrong though — let me complete the proof:
> tool `Bash`: 

**Proof complete.** Concrete numbers:

| object | baked-in blublas symbols |
|---|---|
| `cuda/matmul/GenMatmul.o` | **11** |
| `cuda/matmul/MatmulBackward.o` | **6** |
| `cpu/GenMatmul.o` | 0 (CPU path, no BLAS) |

Those 17 references are **compiled into the object files**. And:

```
make -n tensor WITH_BLUBLAS=0  →  0 compile steps
make -n tensor WITH_BLUBLAS=1  →  0 compile steps
```

**Flipping the flag recompiles nothing.** So if you ran with `=0` now, those 17 blublas references would still be in the objects while `-lblublas` is dropped from the link → undefined symbols. And in the other direction (build `=0`, run `=1`), the objects would have **zero** blublas references and your BLAS would be linked but never called.

*(The `rebuild-tensor → 0` line is a dry-run artifact — `make -n` doesn't execute the `clean-tensor` sub-make, so the objects still look present. The real command does delete them first.)*

## So, the simple rule

**Never flip the flag without rebuilding the tensor objects.**

```bash
# your BLAS
make rebuild-tensor WITH_BLUBLAS=1 && make run-train-mpi ... WITH_BLUBLAS=1

# cuBLAS
make rebuild-tensor WITH_BLUBLAS=0 && make run-train-mpi ... WITH_BLUBLAS=0
```

Build flag and run flag must always match. `rebuild-tensor` touches only the ~164 tensor objects, not your 90-file BLAS — so an arm switch is minutes, not another 40.

Three findings, one you'll want to know about.

**1. Checkpointing is ON but harmless here.** `checkpointing = true`, **`ckpt_freq = 1800`** — with only 30 steps it never fires a save. But it *does* call `load_latest()` at startup, so a stale checkpoint dir could silently resume mid-training. Need to confirm none exists.

**2. Validation won't run.** `val_freq = 50` > 30 steps, so no val overhead. Good.

**3. Config confirmed** — `global_batch = 524288`, `B=2`, `T=4096` → grad_accum **32**, 30 steps = **15.7M tokens**. Matches the 09-10 run exactly, so the two are comparable.

Last checks:
> tool `Bash`: 

Two things you'll want to fix — and you were right to ask.

## 1. Checkpointing is NOT disabled, and it WILL fire

Line 1247:
```cpp
((step + 1) % cfg.ckpt_freq == 0 || step == cfg.max_steps - 1)
```

The `|| step == max_steps - 1` means **it saves at the last step regardless of `ckpt_freq`**. So at step 29 it writes a full 4B checkpoint — model + optimizer state, several GB — inside the profiled window. That costs time, disk, and pollutes the nsys trace.

## 2. Validation will also run — twice

Line 953:
```cpp
if (step % cfg.val_freq == 0 || step == cfg.max_steps - 1)
```
- step 0 → `0 % 50 == 0` → **val runs**
- step 29 → last step → **val runs again**

Each val is `val_loss_steps = 20` forward passes. So **40 forward-only passes** land in the profile that aren't training steps.

## Good news on the LR schedule

I was wrong to worry — `BLU_MAX_STEPS` scales it properly:
```
warmup = max(1, 30/10) = 3
stable = max(1, 30/2)  = 15
decay tail = 12
```
Sensible, not all-warmup.

Also: **no stale checkpoint dir**, so `load_latest()` finds nothing. Clean start. ✅

---

## What I'd suggest

Both behaviours were present in the 09-10 run too, so leaving them keeps things comparable. **But** the checkpoint write at step 29 is genuinely worth removing — it's several GB of disk I/O inside the measurement.

The fix is a small edit to `bluscript_zero.cpp` making it env-controllable, in the same style as the existing `BLU_*` vars:

```cpp
bool checkpointing = getenv_int("BLU_CKPT", 1) != 0;
```

Then run with `BLU_CKPT=0`. `make run-mpi` recompiles only `_runner_` (~1–2 min), not the libraries.

**Your call — three options:**

**A.** Make that edit, run with `BLU_CKPT=0` — cleanest profile
**B.** Run as-is — matches 09-10 exactly, but has a multi-GB checkpoint write at step 29
**C.** Edit *and* set `val_loss_steps = 0` — cleanest possible, but diverges most from the 09-10 baseline

I'd go with **A**. Which do you want?

Now I have the full answer, and it's a **real bug in the Makefile** — not an opinion.

## The mechanism exists and is exactly what your colleague described

Kota built it deliberately (lines 98–106, 220–222, 278–280):

```make
BLAS_STAMP := $(OBJDIR)/.blas_backend
LAST_BLAS  := $(shell cat $(BLAS_STAMP) 2>/dev/null)

ifneq ($(LAST_BLAS),$(BLAS_BACKEND))
  .PHONY: $(BLAS_OBJ_GENMATMUL) $(BLAS_OBJ_BACKWARD) $(TARGET_SO)
endif
```

It records the last backend in a stamp file, and when you flip the flag it force-rebuilds **exactly those two files** — `GenMatmul.o` and `MatmulBackward.o`. That is precisely your colleague's model. So he's describing the intended design correctly.

## But it is not firing — measured, just now

I set the condition to definitely TRUE and ran it:

```
stamp     = [cublas]
flag      = WITH_BLUBLAS=1  ->  BLAS_BACKEND = blublas
condition = ifneq([cublas],[blublas]) = TRUE  -> should force rebuild

result:
  mtime : 11:41:59  -> UNCHANGED
  syms  : 0         -> UNCHANGED
  stamp : still "cublas"  (write-blas-stamp never ran)
```

**Nothing recompiled, with the invalidation condition true.**

## Why it fails

`.PHONY` is the wrong tool here. GNU make **does not run implicit/pattern rules for phony targets** — and `GenMatmul.o` is built by a pattern rule (`$(OBJDIR)/%.o: %.cu`). So marking it `.PHONY` **removes its recipe** instead of forcing it. Make then has nothing to run and silently does nothing.

The `TARGET_SO` in that same line has an *explicit* rule, so `.PHONY` works there — which is why the **link** flips while the **objects** don't. That's the asymmetry, and it's why `=1 → =0` looked like it worked for you: libtensor got relinked, and `GenMatmul.o` happened to rebuild for its own reasons (its size changed 309,328 → 634,824, so it genuinely did recompile that time).

## So, who's right

- **Your colleague is right about the design.** The Makefile is built to do what he says, and I was wrong to claim no such mechanism existed — I grepped for the wrong name.
- **But it doesn't currently work**, and I can demonstrate it on demand.

## What this means practically

**Right now the tree is cuBLAS**, and asking for `WITH_BLUBLAS=1` will not change that. A hybrid run started now would be cuBLAS wearing our label.


**Non-GEMM is 1.17% slower in our arm — running identical kernels.**

Those are the same convert/attention/norm kernels, same code, same counts. They cannot be intrinsically slower. The only mechanism that makes *unchanged* kernels slower is **the GPU clocking down** — our GEMMs draw more power, the 700 W cap bites, and everything on the device pays.

And our own records say this effect is **BLAS-specific, and it favours us**: *"cuBLAS loses 2.28% at ms2000, ours only 0.53%; at the PRODUCTION regime we are 96.07% of cuBLAS (not 94.38%)."*

## So: don't change warmup — run ours at the same full schedule

**Why not `warmup_steps=0`:**

1. **Warmup doesn't change the load.** Every step does identical FLOPs regardless of LR. What changes is gradient *magnitude*, which shifts data-dependent switching power. So `warmup=0` won't "give you real load from the start" — the load was never different.
2. **It creates a third regime.** Production *is* `warmup=200, steps=2000`. Setting warmup to 0 moves further from production, not closer.
3. **It breaks comparability.** Your cuBLAS full-schedule run used warmup=200. Changing the script now means ours isn't comparable to it, and you'd need to redo cuBLAS too.

**nsys cannot give you tensor-core usage.** It gives kernel names, durations, call counts — nothing about what the SM's pipes were doing inside. Tensor-core occupancy needs **`ncu`** (`sm__pipe_tensor_op_hmma_cycles_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active`).

Two options, your call:

**A — ncu on just K/Vdgrad, both arms.** ~2 minutes. Gives tensor-pipe %, stall reasons, and settles whether it's amortisation or something else.

**B — ncu on all 15, both arms.** ~20–30 min. Gives the full tensor-core table you asked for, and tells us which shapes are tensor-bound (where only better kernels help) versus overhead-bound (where structure helps).

I'd do **B** — it's the same run cost as A repeated, and "which shapes are actually tensor-bound" decides where variant work is worth doing at all. It also answers the power question: a shape drawing more watts at the *same* tensor throughput is doing non-tensor work we could remove.

## 2. Peak FLOPS for H200 — and an honest discrepancy

**Datasheet:** H200 SXM BF16 Tensor Core = **1,979 TFLOPS with sparsity → 989.5 TFLOPS dense**. That's what the trainer prints (`bf16 peak 1979.00` for 2 GPUs).

**But our measurement doesn't fit it.** At 1200 MHz locked, scaling the datasheet gives `989.5 × 1200/1980 = 599.7 TF`. We measured **631.9 TF** on lm_headwgrad — **105% of that**, which is impossible.

Working backwards from our data instead: 100% tensor occupancy ≈ **~642 TF at 1200 MHz**, which scales to **~1059 TF at 1980 MHz**. That matches the hardware arithmetic `132 SMs × 4096 BF16 FLOP/clk × 1.98 GHz = 1070 TF`.

So the 989.5 figure is probably quoted at a lower reference clock than 1980. **I'm not going to assert which** — the useful, defensible number for our work is the measured one: **~642 TF at 100% occupancy at 1200 MHz**, and every shape's occupancy is measured directly. That's what MFU should be computed against here, not the datasheet.

Done bro — full sweep saved at `sft_research/00_SFT_resource_sweep.md`.

## The headline finding

**SFT's objective is identical to pretraining** — token-level cross-entropy, next-token prediction:

```
L_SFT(θ) = − Σ_t log p_θ( y_t | y_<t )
```

What changes is **the data, the masking, and the hyperparameters** — not the maths. So your kernel and autograd background isn't wasted; the training loop is the same machine.

## One thing that would have cost you time

**torchtune — the "PyTorch native" library everyone recommends — is discontinued.** Development wound down in 2025, no longer maintained. Half the 2026 blog posts still recommend it. The successor is **torchforge**.

I only caught it because the GitHub README contradicted a 2026 arxiv paper, so I checked. Verified on the [official wind-down issue](https://github.com/meta-pytorch/torchtune/issues/2883) and the [torchforge announcement](https://pytorch.org/blog/introducing-torchforge/).

**Use [TRL's SFTTrainer](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/sft_trainer) instead** — actively maintained (v1.13.0), and it carries into DPO/GRPO later.

## What's in the doc

| section | contents |
|---|---|
| Libraries | TRL, torchforge, [Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide), [Axolotl](https://docs.axolotl.ai/), [LLaMA-Factory](https://github.com/hiyouga/LLaMA-Factory), NeMo + benchmark table |
| Core concepts | 4 dataset formats, chat templates, **loss masking**, packing, full `SFTConfig` params, LoRA/QLoRA |
| Datasets | Tulu 3, SmolTalk2, OpenHermes, Magpie, LIMA + curated lists |
| Papers | InstructGPT → FLAN → Self-Instruct → Alpaca → **LIMA** → Tulu 3, plus 2026 work |
| Hyperparameters | LR, epochs, catastrophic forgetting |
| **Efficiency** | packing, Liger kernels, chunked CE, QLoRA — the part where your background applies |
| Evaluation | IFEval, MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard |
| Courses/blogs | [RLHF Book](https://rlhfbook.com/), smol-course, awesome lists |

## Two things worth your attention specifically

**1. Loss masking is nearly free and worth 5–15%.** Train only on the assistant's tokens, not the user's. `assistant_only_loss=True` or `completion_only_loss=True`.

**2. The memory monster is the `vocab × seq_len` logits tensor** — at vocab 50k and seq 4096 it dominates. TRL's default `loss_type="chunked_nll"` chunks the CE and skips ignored-label tokens in the `lm_head` projection. **That's the same problem as the sparse-CE work you already did in BluTrain.** Directly transferable.

## And the idea that reframes the whole field

**LIMA**: 1,000 carefully chosen examples beat much larger datasets. The "superficial alignment hypothesis" — the base model already has the knowledge, SFT only teaches format and style. Which means **the research is data curation, not the training loop**.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-17 14:17 IST]

**TRL = Transformer Reinforcement Learning**

Yes — it's **HuggingFace's** library. Official docs: https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/index, repo: https://github.com/huggingface/trl

## The name is misleading though

It started as an RL-only library (for RLHF). But it grew, and now it covers the **whole post-training stack**, not just RL:

| method | is it RL? |
|---|---|
| **SFT** (`SFTTrainer`) | **No** — plain supervised cross-entropy |
| DPO | No — preference learning, but no RL loop |
| Reward modelling | No |
| GRPO, PPO | Yes, actual RL |

So `SFTTrainer` — the one you'll use — has **nothing to do with reinforcement learning** despite living in a library called "Transformer Reinforcement Learning". The name is just historical baggage from when it only did RLHF.

## Where it sits in the HuggingFace stack

```
transformers   →  the models
datasets       →  the data
tokenizers     →  text → tokens
accelerate     →  multi-GPU / mixed precision
peft           →  LoRA, QLoRA
TRL            →  the post-training trainers  ← you are here
```

It's built **on top of** `transformers.Trainer` — `SFTTrainer` is a wrapper around it that adds the SFT-specific things (chat templates, loss masking, packing).

So when you use TRL you're still using normal HuggingFace transformers underneath. It's not a separate ecosystem.

## 1. PyTorch has NO SFT module. None.

I searched your local clone (PyTorch 2.10.0a0):

```
dirs named sft/finetune/rlhf/post_train under torch/  → (blank)
python files with sft/dpo in the name under torch/    → (blank)
```

Every top-level thing in `torch/` is infrastructure: `autograd`, `nn`, `optim`, `distributed`, `cuda`, `fx`, `compiler`, `amp`, `quantization`…

**There is no `torch.sft`. There never was.**

## 2. What PyTorch actually gives you — the building blocks

| SFT needs | PyTorch file |
|---|---|
| the loss | `torch/nn/modules/loss.py` — `CrossEntropyLoss` |
| **the masking** | same file, line 245: **`ignore_index: int = -100`** |
| optimizer | `torch/optim/adamw.py` |
| gradient checkpointing | `torch/utils/checkpoint.py` |
| flash attention | `torch/nn/functional.py` → `scaled_dot_product_attention`, backend `SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION` |
| multi-GPU | `torch/distributed/fsdp` |
| bf16 | `torch/amp` |
| gradients | `torch/autograd` |

**Notice the second row.** Remember I told you TRL masks tokens with `-100`? That `-100` is not TRL's invention — **it's PyTorch's default `ignore_index`**, sitting in `torch/nn/modules/loss.py`. The docs there say: *"Specifies a target value that is ignored and does not contribute to the input gradient."*

## 3. Proof that TRL sits on top of PyTorch

From the actual TRL source (`trl/trainer/sft_trainer.py`):

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
...
chunk_loss = F.nll_loss(log_p, lbl, ignore_index=-100, reduction="sum")
labels[output["attention_mask"] == 0] = -100
```

**TRL calls PyTorch's own function, with PyTorch's own `-100`.** It is not a separate engine. It's a wrapper.

## 4. So how does each side actually do it?

```
        HUGGING FACE                        PYTORCH

        TRL (SFTTrainer, DPO, GRPO)         torchtune  ← DISCONTINUED 2025
              │                             torchforge ← the successor
        transformers.Trainer                     │
              │                                  │
              └──────────► PyTorch ◄─────────────┘
                    (tensors, autograd, nn, optim, cuda)
```

**Both are separate libraries in separate repos, both sitting on the same PyTorch.**

Your question — *"is PyTorch doing the same as HuggingFace, having DPO, RL and SFT in one stack?"*

**PyTorch tried, in a separate repo, and it's the one that died.** torchtune had exactly that — SFT, LoRA, QLoRA, DPO, PPO, GRPO, distillation, QAT. It wound down in 2025. torchforge replaced it and leans RL/agents.

Meanwhile TRL has all of it and is alive. **That's why I said start with TRL.**

## 5. Your last question — and yes, you're right

> *"even though those are separate, still they use underneath tensor and autograd… same engine only right?"*

**Exactly right.** All of them — TRL, torchtune, torchforge, Axolotl, Unsloth, LLaMA-Factory — are thin layers over the same PyTorch tensor + autograd + dtype system. None of them has its own engine. When `SFTTrainer` calls `.backward()`, it's PyTorch's autograd graph, PyTorch's dtypes, PyTorch's CUDA kernels.

## 6. And this maps exactly onto what we build

```
PyTorch core            ≈   BluTrain's Tensor + autograd + dtypes + kernels
                            ← what our team writes

TRL / torchtune         ≈   the layer nobody on our team has built yet
                            ← what I'd now be researching
```

**Our BluTrain is PyTorch's layer, not TRL's layer.** We have the tensor, autograd, dtype promotion, reduction ops, the CUDA kernels — all the things I listed in that talent doc. What we don't have is the SFT trainer on top.

So the real question for the team is: **do we build BluTrain's own `SFTTrainer`, or do we run SFT on someone else's harness?** That's the thing I said I need answered before picking a direction — and now you can see exactly why it matters.

Saved (with a scratchpad backup this time). Here are your answers.

## 1. Not two stages — **three**

```
PRETRAINING  →  MID-TRAINING  →  POST-TRAINING
~trillions      ~hundreds of      ~millions of tokens
of tokens       billions
```

**Yes, mid-training is real.** The term reportedly first showed up in an **OpenAI job description in mid-2024** and is now standard.

## 2. Pretraining is **self-supervised, not unsupervised**

This trips people up. Unsupervised = *no labels at all*. Self-supervised = **labels exist, they just come free from the data**. For "The sky is ___" the label is "blue", taken from the text itself. There IS a cross-entropy loss against a real label — no human wrote it.

So pretraining vs SFT is **not** "unsupervised vs supervised":

| | pretraining | SFT |
|---|---|---|
| loss | next-token CE | next-token CE — **identical** |
| label from | the raw text | a human or stronger model wrote the answer |
| loss on | **every** token | **only answer tokens** (masking) |

**Same maths. Different data, different masking.** That's the whole difference.

## 3. Mid-training — what it actually is

Continue pretraining on a **much better data mix**. Same loss. Quantity → quality:

1. **Data quality shift** — upsample STEM/code/maths/reasoning
2. **Long-context extension** — Composer 2 went 32K → 256K here
3. **Domain / language expansion**
4. **Large-scale synthetic data**
5. **Capability additions** (e.g. Multi-Token Prediction for speculative decoding)
6. **Preparing for RL** — mid-training changes how well later RL works

Pretraining is too expensive to redo; post-training too small to teach capability. Mid-training is the middle.

## 4. Post-training has **six** things, not two

SFT · preference/RL · **distillation** · **model merging** · **safety tuning** · **quantization/QAT**

SFT and preference/RL are the main path; the rest support them.

## 5. Order: **SFT first, then RL** — and DeepSeek proved it

They published both:

| | recipe | result |
|---|---|---|
| **R1-Zero** | pure RL, **no SFT** | works, reasoning emerges — **but** poor readability, mixes languages mid-answer, unstable, degenerate outputs |
| **R1** | small **cold-start SFT** → RL | fixed all of it |

**Why RL alone fails:** base model follows tasks poorly → rollouts score near zero → no gradient signal → unstable updates → collapse.

SFT's job is to get the model somewhere its outputs *earn some reward*. That's why it's called **cold start**.

- **SFT alone enough?** Often **yes** — Alpaca, FLAN-T5, LIMA are SFT-only and useful. Start here.
- **RL alone enough?** Possible but expensive and degraded. Nobody ships it.

## 6. Inside SFT — four independent axes

| axis | options |
|---|---|
| **what you update** | full FT · LoRA · QLoRA · adapters |
| **where data comes from** | human-written · **distillation** · self-improvement · rejection-sampling (RFT/STaR) |
| **what you teach** | instruction · chat · domain · reasoning/CoT · tool-calling · multimodal · safety |
| **loss variant** | NLL · **chunked-NLL** · DFT · PSFT · ASFT · ProFiT |

**That last axis is where the open research is — and it's closest to our work.** Loss-function and numerical-stability changes, not data changes.

## 7. Inside RL — two families

**Family 1, true RL** (model generates, gets scored): **PPO** (classic RLHF, most expensive — needs a second reward model) · **GRPO** (drops the value network, what DeepSeek used) · **RLVR** (a *program* checks the answer — no reward model)

**Family 2, direct preference** (no rollouts, no reward model): **DPO** (reparameterises the RLHF objective away — **~3× less compute**) · **IPO** (fixes DPO overfitting) · **KTO** (works with thumbs-up/down, no paired data) · **ORPO** (merges SFT+preference into one loss) · **SimPO**

**One caveat worth flagging:** a 2026 controlled study found **scale-dependent ranking inversions** — which method wins *changes with model size*. So any "X beats Y" blog claim is only valid at its measured scale. **We measure at ours.** Same lesson as our locked-1200 vs free-clock finding.

## 8. What I'd plan

1. **SFT only, end to end** — a complete useful result on its own
2. **Measure properly** — IFEval + MMLU/GSM8K to catch what it *forgot*
3. **Then DPO** if we need quality beyond the SFT data
4. **GRPO/RLVR only if** we have a verifiable-reward task

Each stage is a shippable model. Start at step 4 and you have nothing for months.

I've read the whole paper. Here's what's actually in it.

## What they do — the maths, simply

Every token becomes a **complex number** `G · e^{iα}` instead of a plain real vector.

**Step 1 — the magnitude `G` (the "global semantics")**

For dimension *k*, take that dimension across **every token in the input** and L2-norm it:

```
G_k = ‖[w_1k, w_2k, …, w_nk]‖₂ = √(w²_1k + w²_2k + … + w²_nk)
```

One number per dimension, shared by all tokens. That's their "global context".

**Step 2 — the phase `α` (the "local semantics")**

```
α_jk = arctan2( √(1 − (w_jk/G_k)²) , w_jk/G_k )
```

**Here's the neat part.** Convert back with Euler's formula:
- real part = `G·cos(α)` = **`w_jk`** — the token's own value
- imag part = `G·sin(α)` = **`√(G_k² − w_jk²)`** — the energy of *everything else in the sequence*

So each token sits on a circle of radius `G_k`. Its own value is one axis, the rest of the context is the perpendicular axis. **That is a genuinely elegant decomposition.**

**Step 3 — update by wave ops instead of attention**
- **Interference** = complex **addition** of two variants
- **Modulation** = complex **multiplication**

No dot products. **O(n·d) instead of attention's O(n²·d).**

## What they actually measured (the real Table 2, not the abstract)

| model | dataset | accuracy | VRAM | time/epoch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wave (Modulation) | AG News | 91.66% | 0.32 GB | 147 s |
| **BERT base** | AG News | **94.64%** | 1.28 GB | 1035 s |
| Wave (Modulation) | DBpedia14 | 98.05% | 0.30 GB | 991 s |
| **BERT base** | DBpedia14 | **99.28%** | 1.27 GB | 2735 s |
| Wave (Modulation) | IMDB | 87.02% | 0.37 GB | 120 s |
| **BERT base** | IMDB | **93.94%** | 1.27 GB | 220 s |

2.4M params vs BERT's 100M. That part is real.

## What's genuinely good

1. **The global-statistic-instead-of-attention idea is sound.** One L2 norm per dimension gives every token a view of the whole sequence at **O(n·d)**. That's a real structural saving.
2. **The magnitude/phase decomposition is clean** — self vs context on orthogonal axes, and it falls out of Euler's formula rather than being bolted on.
3. **The efficiency numbers look real** — 4x less VRAM is consistent across all three datasets.

## What the headline hides — and you should know this before getting excited

**1. It is NOT a language model.** The title says "Ultra-Small Language Model" but every single experiment is **text classification** — 4 classes (AG News), 14 (DBpedia), 2 (IMDB). There is **no generation, no next-token prediction, no perplexity**. For SFT we need generation. This paper never does it.

**2. The gap isn't small where it matters.** The abstract says "approaching BERT". On IMDB — a **binary** task — it's **87.02% vs 93.94%, nearly 7 points behind.** That's not approaching.

**3. The Transformer baseline is weak on purpose.** A single transformer layer gets **71.68%** on AG News. Nobody uses a 1-layer transformer. "We beat it by 19%" is beating a straw man.

**4. The 85.62% speedup is the best case only.** On DBpedia14 it's 991s vs 2735s = **2.8x**, not 7x. They quoted AG News.

**5. No scaling evidence.** 2.4M params, 4-class task, one layer. Nothing shows this works at 1B params or on generation.

**6. Two years old, and the field hasn't picked it up.** Nov 2024. The only follow-up is [by the same authors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.06989) ("The Backpropagation of the Wave Network"). I found no independent reproduction.

## Can we use it for SFT? Honestly — no

SFT fine-tunes an **existing pretrained generative model**. This paper proposes a **new architecture trained from scratch for classification**. Different problem:

| | Wave Network | our SFT work |
|---|---|---|
| task | classification | generation |
| model | new architecture, from scratch | existing pretrained LLM |
| stage | replaces pretraining | post-training |

You cannot SFT a Llama with this. There's no path from this paper to our assignment.

## But there IS one real connection — and it's yours

**You implemented `complex32`, `complex64`, `complex128` in BluTrain.** This paper needs *exactly* that substrate: complex add, complex multiply, magnitude, `arctan2`, Euler's formula.

From your own datatype doc:

> `Complex32` — custom struct (float16 real + float16 imag) · `Complex64` · `Complex128` · complex multiplication · complex division

**So if anyone in our org ever wanted to try complex-valued models, we're one of the few frameworks that already has the dtypes.** Most people would have to build that first. That's a genuine, if narrow, asset — and it's yours.

The second connection: **"replace O(n²) pairwise ops with an O(n) global statistic"** is the same *family* of thinking as our kernel work. This paper doesn't prove it for generation, but the shape of the idea is one we'd recognise.

## Verdict

**As a thing to adopt:** no. Wrong task, wrong stage, unproven at scale, unreproduced in two years.

**As a thing to have read:** yes, worth the hour. The magnitude/phase decomposition is a nice idea and the "global statistic instead of attention" framing is a lens you'll see again — linear attention, state-space models, and Mamba all attack the same O(n²).

**My honest read:** the paper is oversold by its title and abstract, but the core idea isn't junk. It's a small, interesting result presented as a big one.

**Sources:** [Wave Network paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02674) · [follow-up on backpropagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.06989) · [HN discussion](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42200929)
