### CLAUDE [2026-09-17 17:09 IST]

Good question — that's the right one to ask. Let me check whether the paper addresses causal/generative use at all.
> tool `Bash`: 

Checked the paper directly. **Zero mentions of causal, autoregressive, decoder, next-token, or perplexity.** The only "generate" hits are about generating *embeddings*. And the architecture section ends with *"used as the foundation for subsequent classification tasks."*

So here's the honest answer for pretraining.

## The blocker: it breaks causality

The paper's own words: *"we sum the magnitudes of all token embedding components along each dimension"* — **all** tokens.

```
G_k = √(w²_1k + w²_2k + … + w²_nk)      ← includes tokens t+1, t+2, … n
```

For GPT-style pretraining you predict token *t+1* from tokens *1…t*. But `G` already contains token *t+1*. **You'd be feeding the model the answer.** Loss would collapse to near zero and the model would learn nothing.

This is fine for their task — classification is bidirectional, you see the whole document at once, like BERT. It is fatal for generative pretraining.

## That part is fixable — and it's the interesting bit

Make it a **running prefix norm** instead of a full-sequence norm:

```
G_k(t) = √(w²_1k + … + w²_tk)        ← only tokens seen so far
```

That's a **cumulative sum of squares** = a prefix scan. Still **O(n·d)**, still parallelizable, causality preserved. Genuinely doable.

**And notice what that computation is:** a reduction along the *sequence* axis. LayerNorm/RMSNorm reduce along the *feature* axis. You built both the reduction module and the norm kernels — you'd be implementing this in an afternoon.

## But there's a deeper problem the fix doesn't solve

**`G` is ONE vector shared by every token.**

Every token sees the *same* global summary. The only thing that differs per token is its own phase, derived from its own embedding. So the total "context mixing" in the whole layer is a single 768-dim vector.

| | what each token sees of the context |
|---|---|
| **attention** | its **own** weighted mixture of all other tokens — different for every position |
| **Wave Network** | the **same** global vector `G` for all positions |

For classification that's enough — you're producing **one label for the whole document**, so one global summary is the right shape.

For generation each position needs a **different** view. Token 500 predicting token 501 needs a different context than token 20 did. One shared vector cannot provide that.

**That's a capacity argument, not an implementation bug.** It's why I don't think this scales to generation as-is.

## What it would actually cost to find out

| step | effort |
|---|---|
| implement causal prefix-norm variant | days |
| build a GPT-style Wave model | 1–2 weeks |
| pretrain small (124M-ish) and measure perplexity vs a transformer baseline | weeks of GPU |
| if it works, scale and check it holds | months |

**Expected value: low.** Two years old, zero independent reproductions, only the authors' own follow-up, never tested on generation, and a structural bottleneck I'd expect to bite exactly where it matters.

## The better bet — same idea, already proven

The core insight — **replace O(n²) pairwise attention with an O(n) running state** — is real and important. But it's already been done properly:

| approach | what it does | status |
|---|---|---|
| **Linear attention** | kernel trick removes the n² softmax | deployed |
| **State-space models / Mamba** | a **per-position** running state, causal by construction | deployed, proven at scale on generation |
| **RWKV** | RNN-style linear-time LM | deployed |

**Mamba is what Wave Network wanted to be, done correctly** — it keeps a running state that is *per-position* (fixing the shared-`G` bottleneck) and is causal by design. Proven on real language modeling at scale.

**If the O(n) family interests you, read Mamba, not this.**

## So: does it benefit us?

**Directly, for pretraining — no.** Wrong task, breaks causality, structural bottleneck, unproven.

**Two things that are genuinely ours though:**

1. **Our complex dtypes are a real asset.** You shipped `complex32/64/128` with complex mul and div. Almost no in-house framework has that. If anyone here ever wants to explore complex-valued models, we're ready and others aren't. That's worth knowing even if we never use it.

2. **The reduction-along-sequence-axis kernel** is something we already own. Whether it's Wave Network, a linear-attention variant, or an SSM, the primitive is the same and it's in our reduction module.

**My recommendation:** file this one as "read, understood, not pursuing." If the efficiency direction is what caught your eye, spend that time on **Mamba/SSMs** instead — same idea, actually works on generation, and if we ever implement one, the kernel work would be genuinely ours.

## What they actually did — there is no pretraining

Their exact pipeline, from the paper:

```
random embeddings  →  1 wave layer  →  feedforward  →  norm  →  classification head
(torch.nn.Embedding,     (interference                          (4 classes)
 randomly initialised)    or modulation)
```

Trained **4 epochs directly on the labeled classification data** (AG News / DBpedia14 / IMDB, 80/20 split). That's the whole thing.

**No pretraining. No mid-training. No post-training.** The embeddings start random and are learned *during* the classification training itself.

## Where this sits in the stages we discussed

```
PRETRAINING  →  MID-TRAINING  →  POST-TRAINING (SFT → RL)
                                                              ← modern LLM pipeline

Wave Network:  [ train a small model from scratch on one labeled task ]
                                                              ← this is pre-2018 NLP
```

This is **task-specific supervised training** — how everyone did NLP *before* the pretrain-then-finetune era. One model, one task, trained from scratch. It's not a stage in the LLM pipeline; it's the thing the LLM pipeline replaced.

## So why did they compare to BERT?

BERT base was **pretrained on a huge corpus, then fine-tuned** on the same classification task. So the comparison is:

| | pretraining | params | AG News |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Wave Network** | **none** — from scratch | 2.4M | 91.66% |
| **BERT base** | huge corpus + finetune | 100M | 94.64% |

Framed that way it sounds remarkable — 40× smaller, no pretraining, only 3 points behind.

## But here's the number that settles it

**fastText — a bag-of-words linear classifier from 2016 — gets 92.44% on AG News.**

| model | year | AG News |
|---|---|---|
| BERT base | 2018 | 94.64% |
| **fastText (bag of words + linear)** | **2016** | **92.44%** |
| **Wave Network (modulation)** | **2024** | **91.66%** |
| Wave Network (interference) | 2024 | 90.91% |
| single transformer layer (their baseline) | — | 71.68% |

**Their model loses to a bag-of-words classifier from eight years earlier.**

That is the honest answer to "is this impressive?" The 2.4M-vs-100M framing only looks dramatic because **AG News doesn't need a language model at all.** It's 4-way news topic classification — World / Sports / Business / Sci-Tech. Word counts basically solve it. Seeing the word "quarterback" tells you it's Sports.

So "we approached BERT with 2.4M params" mostly means "this task never needed BERT."

## What this means for your question

You asked: *can we use it for pretraining?*

**They never did pretraining, so there's nothing to copy.** There is no "their pretraining method" to adopt — the paper contains a classifier, not a language model, despite the title.

To use it for pretraining you would have to:
1. invent the causal version (the prefix-norm fix I described)
2. build a generative architecture around it
3. pretrain it
4. and hope the shared-`G` bottleneck doesn't bite

**All four of those are things the paper did not do.** You wouldn't be adopting their work — you'd be doing original research that only borrows their token representation, with no evidence it survives the transition.

## What's actually left that's real

Two things, and they're small:

1. **The magnitude/phase decomposition is elegant** — `real = the token itself`, `imag = everything else in the sequence`, falling out of Euler's formula. Nice idea, nicely derived.
2. **`G` is cheap** — one L2 reduction along the sequence axis, O(n·d). Your reduction module already computes exactly this.

**Everything else — the headline, the "language model" title, the BERT comparison — does not survive contact with a fastText baseline.**

My read: two authors from one lab, arXiv-only, no independent reproduction in two years, and the field quietly moved on. That's usually the field being right.

**Which kernel: attention. That's the only one it touches.**

|---|---|

Researched it. You're right on one thing and wrong on another — and the proof is in the source.

## First correction: TRL is **not** a full stack. It's post-training only.

Actual file listing of `trl/trainer/`:

```
sft_trainer.py          DPO      GRPO      KTO
reward_trainer.py       RLOO     distillation_trainer.py
```

**There is no pretraining trainer.** Not in TRL, not in torchtune, not in torchforge. All three are **post-training only**.

And PyTorch core has no trainer at all — we verified that in your local clone earlier.

```
PyTorch core     → tensors, autograd, nn, optim.  NO trainer.
transformers     → models + a generic Trainer
TRL              → post-training trainers ONLY (SFT, DPO, GRPO, KTO, RLOO, reward, distill)
torchtune/forge  → post-training ONLY, as standalone scripts
```

Nobody ships a "pretraining stack" as a library. Pretraining is custom code at each lab.

## Second correction: SFT doesn't modify the loss at all

You said *"SFT is all about modifying just that cross-entropy loss function"*. It's actually **stronger than that — the loss is completely unchanged.** It's the same `F.nll_loss` PyTorch has always had.

What changes is **the labels you feed into it.** You set `-100` on tokens you don't want counted. The loss function then ignores them — using PyTorch's own `ignore_index`.

So it's not a loss change. It's a **label-construction** change.

## So why a whole module? Here's the proof

I read `sft_trainer.py`:

| | lines | share |
|---|---|---|
| **data pipeline** | **~1,100** | **~88%** |
| loss computation | ~150 | ~12% |
| **total** | ~1,850 | |

**The module exists for the data pipeline, not the loss.**

## What that 88% actually does — the functions, by name

From the source:

| function | what it does | does pretraining need it? |
|---|---|---|
| `maybe_convert_to_chatml()` | convert dataset into message format | **no** |
| `apply_chat_template()` | messages → `<\|im_start\|>user…` token string | **no** |
| `add_eos()` | append the stop token | **no** — pretraining just streams text |
| `build_labels()` | **write `-100` on prompt/user tokens** | **no** — pretraining trains on everything |
| `truncate()` | keep_start / keep_end modes | sort of |
| `pack_dataset()` | best-fit-decreasing bin packing | different problem |
| `get_position_ids_from_packed_seq_lengths()` | **reset position IDs at each packed boundary** | **no** |
| `prepare_multimodal_messages()` | image handling | no |
| `DataCollatorForLanguageModeling.torch_call()` | padding, attention masks | different |

That `get_position_ids_from_packed_seq_lengths` one is a good example of why this isn't trivial. When you pack 5 short conversations into one 4096-token sequence, the position IDs must **restart at each conversation**. If they don't, the model thinks it's one long document and RoPE gives conversation 3 completely wrong positional encoding. Silent, subtle, and wrong.

## Pretraining vs SFT — the honest comparison

| | pretraining | SFT |
|---|---|---|
| **loss function** | cross-entropy | **cross-entropy — identical** |
| optimizer | AdamW | AdamW |
| forward/backward | same | same |
| **data format** | raw text stream | structured messages with roles |
| **chat template** | none | required |
| **EOS token** | mostly irrelevant | **critical** — or it never stops generating |
| **labels** | every token | **only assistant tokens** (`-100` elsewhere) |
| **packing** | trivial, just chunk the stream | must not mix docs; needs position-ID reset |
| **what a batch is** | a slab of tokens | a set of conversations |

**The compute is the same. The data path is completely different.** That's the module.

## And the same is true of the DPO/GRPO modules

`DPOTrainer` exists because DPO genuinely **does** change the objective — it needs a reference model, chosen/rejected pairs, and a different loss. `GRPOTrainer` needs generation rollouts during training.

So the modules are not all the same shape:
- **SFTTrainer** — same loss, different data path
- **DPOTrainer** — different loss, needs a reference model
- **GRPOTrainer** — different loss *and* generates during training

## Why this matters for us specifically

If we ever build SFT into BluTrain, **we would not touch the loss or the autograd.** Those already work. What we'd have to build is:

1. chat template application
2. label masking (`-100` construction)
3. packing with position-ID reset
4. the conversational/prompt-completion data formats

**All data-side.** Our kernels, dtypes, autograd and optimizer carry over unchanged. That's ~1,100 lines of Python-equivalent work, not kernel work.

**Sources:** [trl/trainer directory](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/tree/main/trl/trainer) · [sft_trainer.py source](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/blob/main/trl/trainer/sft_trainer.py) · [torchtune recipes](https://github.com/meta-pytorch/torchtune/tree/main/recipes) · PyTorch `torch/nn/modules/loss.py` (your local clone, `ignore_index: int = -100` at line 245)

Let me get the actual formulas and code rather than describe them loosely.
> tool `WebFetch`: https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/dpo_trainer

Now GRPO:
> tool `WebFetch`: https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/grpo_trainer

Got the exact formulas. Here's the difference, and then what actually happens on the GPU.

## The one-line version

| | what you give it | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| **SFT** | prompt + **the right answer** | "copy this answer" |
| **DPO** | prompt + **two answers**, one better | "prefer this one over that one" |
| **GRPO** | prompt **only** (no answer at all) | "generate 8 yourself, I'll score them, do more of the good ones" |

**That's why the loss must differ.** The loss is just "how do I turn my data into a number to minimise" — and the three have completely different data.

## SFT — loss unchanged, because you already have the answer

```
L_SFT = − Σ log p(y_t | y_<t)
```

You know the correct token. Plain likelihood works. **No new loss needed** — it's `F.nll_loss`, PyTorch's own.

## DPO — loss must change, because there is no single "right answer"

```
L_DPO = − E[ log σ( β ( log π_θ(y⁺|x)/π_ref(y⁺|x) − log π_θ(y⁻|x)/π_ref(y⁻|x) ) ) ]
```

**Why you can't just use SFT here:** your data says "answer A is better than answer B". If you SFT on A, you throw away the information that **B was bad**. DPO keeps both — it widens the *gap* between them.

Two new things appear:

1. **σ, a sigmoid** — this is a **binary classification** loss, not cross-entropy over the vocabulary. Completely different mathematical object.
2. **π_ref, a second frozen model** — the copy of the model from *before* DPO started. Without it the model could just collapse to gibberish that happens to score well. π_ref is the leash.

## GRPO — loss changes *and* the training loop generates

```
Â_i = (r_i − mean(r)) / std(r)          ← "group relative"
L_GRPO = PPO-style clipped surrogate on Â
```

**Why you can't use SFT or DPO here:** you have **no answers at all**. Just prompts and a scorer. So:

1. generate **8 completions** per prompt (`num_generations=8`)
2. score each with a reward function (a program, or a reward model)
3. advantage = how much better than the group average
4. push up the above-average ones, push down the below-average ones

The "group relative" bit is the whole trick — instead of PPO's separate value network, you just compare the 8 samples against each other.

## Now the kernel question — what actually runs on the GPU

**SFT step:**
```
1 forward  : embed → 36 layers → lm_head → logits [B,T,V]
1 CE loss  : over the full vocab
1 backward
```
**1 model in memory, 1 forward.** The memory monster is the `[B,T,50304]` logits tensor — the thing your chunked-CE work attacks.

**DPO step:**
```
forward policy on CHOSEN    → log-probs → sum to a scalar
forward policy on REJECTED  → log-probs → sum to a scalar
forward ref    on CHOSEN    (no grad)
forward ref    on REJECTED  (no grad)
→ combine 4 scalars → sigmoid → backward through the 2 policy passes
```
**2 models in memory, 4 forwards.** ~2× the compute of SFT, ~2× the weights.

*(TRL lets you `precompute_ref_log_probs=True` to run the ref model once up front and drop it — trading disk for memory.)*

**GRPO step:**
```
GENERATE 8 completions  ← autoregressive decode, KV cache, one token at a time
score them with reward function(s)
compute group advantages
forward policy on all 8   → training forwards
(optional) forward ref
backward
```

**Here's the kernel point that matters to you:** GRPO puts an **inference workload inside the training loop**. Generation is:

| | training forward | autoregressive decode |
|---|---|---|
| matmul shape | `[B×T, K] × [K, N]` — big GEMMs | `[B, K] × [K, N]` — **skinny, one token** |
| bound by | **compute** (tensor cores) | **memory bandwidth** (weight loading) |
| KV cache | none | **grows every token** |
| our BLAS | the shapes we tuned | **totally different shapes** |

That's exactly why GRPO needs **vLLM** — you cannot decode efficiently with a training-shaped GEMM path. It's why `use_vllm=True` exists and why there's a whole `vllm_mode="colocate"/"server"` machinery.

And it creates a problem they had to solve: **vLLM uses different kernels than training, so the logprobs disagree.** TRL corrects for it with importance sampling (`vllm_importance_sampling_correction=True` by default). That's a numerical-mismatch bug caused purely by two kernel paths computing the same thing differently — very much our kind of problem.

## Summary table

| | SFT | DPO | GRPO |
|---|---|---|---|
| data | prompt + answer | prompt + chosen/rejected | **prompt only** |
| loss | cross-entropy (**unchanged**) | sigmoid on log-ratio margins | clipped surrogate + advantage |
| models in memory | **1** | **2** (policy + ref) | 1–3 (+ vLLM copy) |
| forwards/step | 1 | 4 | 8 generations + 8 forwards |
| generates during training? | no | no | **yes** |
| needs a reward function? | no | no | **yes** |
| default LR | 2e-5 | **1e-6** | 1e-6 |
| kernel profile | training GEMMs | training GEMMs ×4 | **training + inference decode** |

Note the learning rates from the docs — DPO and GRPO default **20× lower** than SFT. That alone tells you how much more fragile they are.

**So: SFT is the cheap, stable one.** One model, one forward, no generation, PyTorch's own loss. Everything after it costs 2–10× more and is harder to keep stable. That's the real reason everyone does SFT first.

**Sources:** [DPO trainer docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/dpo_trainer) · [GRPO trainer docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/grpo_trainer) · [DPO paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2305.18290)

So **on average we sit at 99.4% of NVIDIA's stated per-clock rate** — sane. Only a few individual shapes exceed it by up to 5%, which is either measurement spread or a conservative datasheet figure. I'm not going to claim which.

Let me answer both precisely — checking the harness rather than describing it.

Both answered from the code.

## 1. What `peak@clk` is

It's the **theoretical ceiling for that shape at the clock it actually ran at**.

```
peak@clk = 989.5 TF × (achieved_MHz / 1980)
```

At **locked 1200 MHz** every shape shares one ceiling — 599.7 TF — so I used a single number.

At **free clocks** the GPU picks its own clock per shape, and it varied **1410–1560 MHz** because each shape draws different power against the 700 W cap. So each shape has a *different* ceiling:

| shape | ran at | its ceiling | got | = |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q/Oprojfwd | 1515 MHz | 989.5 × 1515/1980 = **757 TF** | 678.2 | 89.6% |
| downdgrad | 1410 MHz | 989.5 × 1410/1980 = **705 TF** | 659.5 | 93.6% |

Without that column you'd be comparing a 1410 MHz result against a 1560 MHz ceiling, which is meaningless. **It's the per-shape denominator.**

## 2. Is "ours TF" an average?

**Yes — an average over iterations, but a single measurement per shape.** From the harness:

```cpp
const double flop = 2.0 * g.M * g.N * g.K * g.batch;

cudaEventRecord(t0);
for (int i = 0; i < iters; ++i)
    ours_call(g, dA, dB, dC);          // same shape, back to back
cudaEventRecord(t1);

printf("%.3f ...", flop * iters / (ms * 1e-3) / 1e12);
```

So:

```
TFLOPS = (2·M·N·K·batch · iters) / total_elapsed_seconds / 1e12
```

**Total FLOPs of the whole loop ÷ total wall time of the whole loop.** Steady-state throughput, not one launch.

**What it is NOT:**
- not an average over repeated *runs* — **one process, one arm, one shape, one number**
- not a min/max/median — no distribution was collected
- not multi-shape — each shape is measured in its own process

**Iteration count:** chosen per shape so the loop takes **~6 seconds**, because power needs ~4 s to plateau on this card. So `lm_headwgrad` at 3072×50304×8192 ran ~2,700 times, while a small shape ran ~99,000 times.

## The measurement discipline behind it, and why

| rule | why |
|---|---|
| **one config per process** | many configs in one process deflated some by 6–8% and once manufactured a phantom +10.28% |
| ~6 s window | a 1 s window read cuBLAS 1.28× low — power hadn't plateaued |
| independent operands (`H211_FILL=3`) | a shared periodic buffer once produced a fake **+41.3%** |
| correctness gates timing | a faster wrong kernel isn't a result |

## 1. Forward kernel — the insert point already exists

```cpp
int64_t row = blockIdx.x;
if (row >= batch_size) return;
// ── NEW ──
if (static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index) {
    if (tid == 0) {
        losses[row]    = T(0);
        saved_max[row] = 0.0f;      // backward reads these — must still write
        saved_sum[row] = 1.0f;      // 1.0 not 0.0, so 1/saved_sum can't be inf
    }
    return;
}
```

**The bonus:** that `return` skips the entire 50,304-wide softmax reduction for masked rows. On an SFT batch where ~half the tokens are prompt, **masking makes the CE forward ~2× faster**. It's not just correctness — it's free speed.

*(Note `saved_sum = 1.0f`. The backward computes `1.0f/saved_sum[row]`. If we write 0 there we get `inf` even in a row we're about to discard — and `inf × 0` is NaN. That's the kind of thing that poisons a whole training run silently.)*

## 2. Backward kernel — same pattern

```cpp
const int row = blockIdx.x;
if (row >= batch_size) return;
// ── NEW ──
if (static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index) {
    const float4 z = make_float4(0.f, 0.f, 0.f, 0.f);
    for (int64_t v = tid; v < vocab_vec4; v += bdim) grad4[v] = z;
    return;
}
```

## 3. The denominator — both sides

Found both places:
```cpp
LossOps.cpp:349       result = result / static_cast<float>(batch_size);
LossBackward.cpp:213  float host_scale = 1.0f / static_cast<float>(batch_size_);
```

**Both must become `n_valid`.** Change one and not the other and the loss looks right while the gradients are silently scaled wrong — loss still descends, model trains worse. Exactly the bug class that cost us weight-tying and bias-gradient.

## 4. Counting `n_valid`

One `atomicAdd(n_valid, 1)` from `tid == 0` on surviving rows. **Integer atomicAdd is exact and order-independent**, so no reproducibility problem — unlike the float atomics we avoid.

## Two things that make this easier than expected

**`uint16` targets are already supported** — `LossOps.cpp:324` dispatches on `Dtype::UInt16`. So `IGNORE = 65535` works with no dtype change anywhere.

**And there's a local RTX 3060.** sm_86. We can build and validate correctness here — no Verda box needed for this stage.

- **Hardcoded 65535** — fewer lines, but bakes an SFT decision into a shared kernel.

## ✅ The DeepSeek part is real — and there's a proper ablation table

Exact quote, [DeepSeek-R1 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) §1:

> "Although DeepSeek-R1-Zero demonstrates excellent reasoning capabilities, it faces challenges such as **poor readability and language mixing**, occasionally combining English and Chinese within a single chain-of-thought response."

And they published **Table 3 — every stage of the pipeline measured separately**. This is the official ablation you asked for:

| Benchmark | R1-Zero (pure RL) | Dev1 (+cold-start SFT) | Dev2 | Dev3 | R1 (final) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AIME 2024** | **77.9** | **59.0** ↓18.9 | 74.0 | 78.1 | 79.8 |
| **CNMO 2024** | **88.1** | **58.0** ↓30.1 | 73.9 | 77.3 | 78.8 |
| GPQA Diamond | 75.8 | 66.1 ↓9.7 | 70.7 | 71.2 | 71.5 |
| SimpleQA | 30.3 | 17.8 ↓12.5 | 28.2 | 24.9 | 30.1 |
| **IF-Eval** | 46.6 | **71.7** ↑25.1 | 72.0 | 78.1 | 83.3 |
| **AlpacaEval 2.0** | 24.7 | **50.1** ↑25.4 | 55.8 | 62.1 | 87.6 |
| ArenaHard | 53.6 | 77.0 ↑23.4 | 73.2 | 75.6 | 92.3 |
| Codeforces (rating) | 1444 | 1534 | 1687 | 1746 | 2029 |

Their own words on this:

> "due to the limited size of the cold-start dataset, **Dev1 exhibits a partial degradation in reasoning performance** compared to DeepSeek-R1-Zero, **most notably on the AIME benchmark**."

## ⚠️ What this table actually says — and where I overstated

Read it carefully and it does **not** say "RL alone is not enough."

- **Cold-start SFT made reasoning worse, not better.** AIME dropped 18.9 points. CNMO dropped 30.1.
- What SFT bought was **usability** — instruction-following +25, AlpacaEval +25.
- **R1-Zero's raw reasoning was already nearly final-R1 level**: 77.9 vs 79.8 AIME. The entire multi-stage pipeline added **+1.9 points of reasoning**. Everything else it added was formatting, helpfulness, and readability.

So the correct statement is: **RL alone was enough for reasoning. It was not enough for a shippable product.** That is a different claim from the one I gave you.

There's a second official ablation in the same paper (§B.6) showing even the readability fix costs accuracy:

> "ablation experiments in Supplementary B.6 show that such alignment **results in a slight degradation in the model's performance**, this reward aligns with human preferences, making it more readable."

## ❌ "SFT must always precede RL" — this is refuted by published work

[SimpleRL-Zoo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18892) (HKUST/TikTok) ran the exact controlled experiment: SFT first, then RL, vs RL straight from base. 10 base models — Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B/24B, DeepSeek-Math-7B, Qwen2.5 0.5B→32B.

> "While high-quality CoT data can rapidly enhance a base model's performance through imitation, we find that it **significantly limits the model's ability to explore freely during RL**. This constraint **diminishes post-RL performance** and suppresses the emergence of advanced reasoning capabilities."

Their Mistral-24B result — and note it gets **monotonically worse with more SFT**:

| RL starting point | Final accuracy after RL |
|---|---|
| Base model (no SFT) | **best** |
| After 100 SFT steps | lower ceiling |
| After 500 SFT steps | lowest ceiling |

> "these limitations become **increasingly pronounced as the number of initial SFT steps grows**" — and 500-step SFT models showed "significant declines in 'enumeration' and 'verification' behaviors."

## 🔑 The variable that reconciles both — this is the real rule

[Chu et al., ICML 2025 "SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17161) found the condition. Exact section heading:

> **"SFT is necessary for RL training when the backbone model does not follow instructions."**
>
> "Figure 9 shows that **without SFT, all end-to-end RL runs fail to improve**. More specifically, we observe that without SFT, the base model suffers from poor instruction following capability."

And SimpleRL-Zoo explains why they got the opposite result:

> "Qwen2.5 models, due to their extensive use of synthetic data during pretraining, **already exhibit instruction-following abilities and reflective behaviors**"

**So it's not "SFT always first." It's: SFT is needed only if the base model can't follow the prompt format well enough for RL to get a usable reward signal.** Qwen2.5 base can → skip SFT. Llama3.2 base can't → RL fails outright without it.

Same paper also has the hard OOD numbers, which is the strongest case *against* SFT-only:

| Task | RL | SFT |
|---|---|---|
| GeneralPoints-L (OOD) | +3.5% | **−8.1%** |
| V-IRL-L (OOD) | +11.0% | **−79.5%** |

## ❌ My "80% of business applications" — that was my number, not a paper's

I need to flag this plainly: **there is no study behind that figure. I made it up.** Treat it as a rule of thumb from practice, not a citation.

The nearest *real* evidence is [LIMA (Zhou et al., NeurIPS 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11206) — 65B LLaMa, SFT on **1,000 hand-curated examples only, no RL at all**:

- Preferred or equal to **GPT-4 in 43%** of human comparisons, **Bard 58%**, **DaVinci-003 65%**
- But: "while LIMA held its ground on examples similar to training, it was **thrown off by out-of-distribution prompts or adversarial examples**"

That last line is the honest limit — and it matches Chu et al.'s −79.5% OOD collapse exactly. **SFT-only is strong in-distribution and brittle outside it.** Which is fine for a narrow internal bot, and not fine for an open-ended assistant.

## ⚠️ The important part — my kernel plan had a bug

Megatron's `pretrain_gpt.py` docstring is literally **`"""Pretrain and SFT GPT."""`** — one script, both jobs. Confirms the thesis. But look at *how* they do the loss:

```python
loss_mask = loss_mask.view(-1).float()
loss      = torch.sum(losses * loss_mask)
num_tokens = loss_mask.sum().clone().detach().to(torch.int)
return loss, num_tokens, report
```

**They never divide.** They return the *unnormalized sum* and the *token count* separately, and the framework divides after all-reducing both across ranks.

My plan said "divide by `n_valid`" inside `LossOps.cpp`. **That is wrong for BluTrain**, and here's why it bites us specifically:

The 4B config runs **2 ranks × grad_accum 32 = 64 micro-batches per step.** Every one has a *different* number of unmasked tokens in SFT. If each divides by its own local `n_valid` and we then average:

- micro-batch with 50 valid tokens → each token weighted `1/50`
- micro-batch with 500 valid tokens → each token weighted `1/500`

**Tokens in short completions get weighted 10× more than tokens in long ones.** Loss curve looks completely normal. Model just trains wrong. This never shows up in pretraining because there every token is valid, so the count is uniform and the bug is invisible.

**Correct version:** accumulate `sum(losses)` and `sum(n_valid)` separately across all 64 micro-batches *and* both ranks, all-reduce both, divide **once** at the end.

This also means the `ignore_index`-vs-`loss_mask` choice is now a real decision, not a detail:

| | in-kernel `ignore_index` (my original) | `loss_mask` multiply (Megatron) |
|---|---|---|
| kernel signature change | yes | **no** |
| skips softmax on masked rows | **yes — ~2× faster** | no, computes then discards |
| proven at 100B+ scale | no | **yes** |
| needs uint16 sentinel | yes | no, separate mask stream |

My read: **take Megatron's semantics (mask + global denominator) and keep the in-kernel early-out for speed.** We get both. But that's worth deciding with the code in front of us, which is the point of cloning.

## Your main question: no, torchtitan is not the engine

Three different layers get called "the framework". They're not the same thing:

| layer | what it really is | PyTorch world | **BluTrain equivalent** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Engine** | C++/CUDA kernels, autograd, tensors | **`pytorch/pytorch`** | **`Tensor-Implementations/`** |
| **2. Platform** | parallelism, training loop, checkpoints | **`torchtitan`** (pure Python) | **`bluscript_zero.cpp` + `dist/`** |
| **3. Recipes** | chat templates, dataset formats, trainers | **TRL**, Axolotl, LlamaFactory | *we have nothing here yet* |

**Your `pytorch_source/` folder is layer 1 — the engine.** Verified:

```
pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen   FOUND      <- the C++ kernel library
pytorch_source/c10             FOUND
pytorch_source/torch/csrc      FOUND
216 MB
```

**torchtitan is layer 2.** It's Python that *calls* the engine. It is not what you have, and it is not "PyTorch".

## And this pays off immediately — the best kernel reference is already on your disk

`pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Loss.cu`. That is PyTorch's real CUDA `ignore_index` implementation:

```cpp
index_t cur_target = target[index];
if (cur_target == ignore_index) {
    output[index] = static_cast<scalar_t>(0);
    continue;                    // <-- skips all work for this row
}
```

**That is character-for-character the design I proposed for our forward kernel.** Confirmed against the reference, not guessed. No clone needed — it's local.

And their reduce kernel accumulates the denominator in the *same pass*:

```cpp
if (t != ignore_index) {
    sh_inputs[threadIdx.x]  -= input[i*ndim + t] * cur_weight;
    acc_weight[threadIdx.x] += cur_weight;      // <-- this is n_valid
}
...
*total_weight = acc_weight[0];                  // returned as an OUTPUT
*output = sh_inputs[0] / acc_weight[0];         // or unnormalized if !size_average
```

## My answer on the three

**"Most people use it" and "closest to us" are different questions**, so don't pick one framework for both:

| role | pick | why |
|---|---|---|
| **MAIN — the one we copy design from** | **Megatron-LM** | Only one with our *shape*: own C++/CUDA kernels, tensor+data parallel, trains from scratch. Its `pretrain_gpt.py` docstring is literally `"""Pretrain and SFT GPT."""` — **one script, both jobs**, which is exactly our plan |
| **Cross-ref 1 — kernel** | **ATen `Loss.cu`** (local) + **Liger-Kernel** | The exact kernel we're writing. ATen = correctness, Liger = speed |
| **Cross-ref 2 — data** | **TRL** | What the ecosystem uses. Defines chat templates and the `-100` convention. We have to interop with it either way |
| secondary | torchtitan | A pretraining platform that *added* SFT — same transition we're making |

**Why Megatron and not HuggingFace, even though HF is far more popular:** we're not *using* any of these — we own our engine. TRL sits at layer 3 and assumes PyTorch underneath, so **none of its code is portable to us.** Megatron sits at layers 1+2, so its decisions *are*. Popularity decides the data format we interop with; architecture decides what we copy.

## Two corrections now in the doc

**1. §8 said torchforge is "the successor to torchtune."** Wrong — PyTorch started two post-training libraries and **stopped both**:

> torchtune: *"no longer actively maintained… wound down in 2025"*
> torchforge: *"Development paused. LLM training at PyTorch is being consolidated in **torchtitan**."*

**2. §5 said flatly "SFT must always precede RL."** Refuted — now replaced with the R1 Table 3 numbers, SimpleRL-Zoo's counter-experiment, and the actual condition (*"SFT is necessary for RL training **when the backbone model does not follow instructions**"*). Also retracted the invented "80%" figure in writing so nobody cites it later.

## New: §23 — a bug in my own plan, caught before we wrote code

Megatron **never divides** inside the loss:

```python
loss       = torch.sum(losses * loss_mask)     # unnormalized
num_tokens = loss_mask.sum()
return loss, num_tokens                        # division happens later, globally
```

My plan said divide by `n_valid` in `LossOps.cpp`. **That's wrong for us.** The 4B config runs **2 ranks × grad_accum 32 = 64 micro-batches**, each with a different unmasked-token count. Dividing locally then averaging weights a 50-token micro-batch's tokens **10× more** than a 500-token one. Loss looks normal, curve descends, `maxRelErr` is 0 — the model just learns the wrong objective. Invisible in pretraining because there the count is uniform.

Touch points went from 5 to 7. The new one is the global accumulate-then-divide, plus an `N == 0` guard.

## Q1: Does Liger have an SFT module? — **No.**

Proof — searching the whole source tree for "sft":

```
grep -ril "sft" src/   →   only 2 files: jsd.py, fused_linear_jsd.py
```

Both are **JSD (distillation)**, not SFT. There is no `SFTTrainer`, no training loop, no dataset handling, no chat templating.

**Liger is a kernel library, not a training framework.** Its whole source tree:

```
src/liger_kernel/ops/            <- the Triton kernels
src/liger_kernel/transformers/   <- monkey-patches into HF models
src/liger_kernel/chunked_loss/   <- post-training losses
src/liger_kernel/megatron/       <- Megatron integration
src/liger_kernel/backends/ triton/ testing/
```

What it *does* have for post-training is `chunked_loss/`:

```
dpo_loss.py  cpo_loss.py  orpo_loss.py  simpo_loss.py
kto_loss.py  grpo_loss.py  jsd_loss.py  cosine_similarity_loss.py
fused_linear_preference.py  fused_linear_ppo.py  fused_linear_distillation.py
```

**Every one of those is preference/RL — none is SFT.** Because SFT doesn't need a special loss. It's plain cross-entropy, which lives in `ops/cross_entropy.py` and `ops/fused_linear_cross_entropy.py`.

**So: Liger gives you the kernels SFT runs on, not an SFT module.** You use it *underneath* TRL or HF by monkey-patching. That's exactly why it's a cross-reference for us and not the main one.

## Q2: Own kernels, or copied? — **Mixed, and they document it honestly**

There's a `NOTICE` file and a `licenses/` directory. Verbatim, the NOTICE lists **7 sources**:

| # | source | license | what they took — their words |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Unsloth** | Apache 2.0 | *"The `calculate_settings` function to determine block size and warp is reused for Norm and MLP operations. Modifications and additions were made to the RMS Norm implementation."* |
| 2 | **Triton** (OpenAI) | MIT | *"Modifications were made based on Triton tutorials for the RMS Norm implementation."* |
| 3 | **Efficient Cross Entropy** (Mohamed Malek) | MIT | *"**The idea of gradient-in-forward and chunking was used in the Linear Cross Entropy implementation.**"* |
| 4 | **Flash Attention** (Tri Dao et al.) | BSD 3 | *"Optimization ideas such as tiling and recomputation were inspired by this work."* |
| 5 | **AutoAWQ** | MIT | *"The design of the automodel was referenced from this project."* |
| 6 | **llm.c** (Karpathy) | MIT | *"The design of end-to-end testing was referenced from this project."* |
| 7 | Tiny Shakespeare | — | convergence tests |

And `licenses/` carries the actual license texts: `LICENSE-Apache-2.0`, `LICENSE-MIT-Efficient-Cross-Entropy`, `LICENSE-MIT-triton`, `LICENSE-MIT-AutoAWQ`, `LICENSE-MIT-llmc`.

Beyond the NOTICE, grepping the code found more in-line attributions:

```
ops/utils.py:58                        reference: unslothai/unsloth .../kernels/utils.py#L43
ops/fused_linear_scaled_cross_entropy.py:8   "adapted from Verl's fused linear PPO formulas"
ops/fused_linear_cross_entropy.py:493        Reference: mgmalek/efficient_cross_entropy
ops/fused_moe_kernels.py               "Adapted from sonic-moe" (×5)
ops/cutedsl/ops/cross_entropy.py:47    "Adapted from FlashAttention-4 (flash_attn/cute/utils.py)"
```

**The key answer for us: nothing is copied from PyTorch.** Not one attribution points at PyTorch/ATen. These are **Triton kernels written to *replace* PyTorch's**, not derived from them. `ops/cross_entropy.py` opens with plain imports and no attribution header — it's their own.

So, precisely:
- **The plain CE Triton kernel** → Liger's own
- **The chunking + gradient-in-forward trick** in fused linear CE → credited to `mgmalek/efficient_cross_entropy`
- **RMS Norm** → Triton tutorials + Unsloth
- **MoE** → sonic-moe
- **PyTorch** → nothing

## The lead worth knowing about

`src/liger_kernel/megatron/` contains `cross_entropy.py`, `monkey_patch.py`, `rms_norm.py`, `swiglu.py`.

**Liger already ships a Megatron integration.** Since Megatron is our main architectural reference, that directory shows exactly how a custom CE kernel gets swapped into a Megatron-style trainer — which is the same operation we're doing in BluTrain. That's the single most useful file set in the repo for us.

There's also a `cutedsl/` backend (NVIDIA CuTe DSL, CUDA-level not Triton) with its own `cross_entropy.py` adapted from FlashAttention-4 — closer to our C++/CUDA world than the Triton path.

Let me clear the confusion first, then give you the steps.

## What JSD is

**JSD = Jensen-Shannon Divergence.** It measures how different two probability distributions are. It's used in **distillation** — training a small model to copy a big model's output. That's a different job from SFT.

I only mentioned it to show Liger has no SFT trainer. Being honest: I saw those two filenames matched a search for "sft" but I never read *why* they matched, and the repos are deleted now so I can't check. Ignore that detail. The solid proof is different: there is no `SFTTrainer` file, no training loop, and `chunked_loss/` contains only preference losses (DPO, ORPO, KTO, GRPO...) — no SFT loss.

## The thing you're actually asking — yes, Liger has SFT kernels

Two different things, and this is where the confusion is:

| | does Liger have it? |
|---|---|
| **SFT module** (trainer, data loading, chat templates) | ❌ **No** |
| **The CE kernel that SFT runs on**, with `ignore_index` | ✅ **Yes** — `ops/cross_entropy.py` |

**And here's the key point: it is the same kernel for pretraining and SFT.** There is no separate "SFT kernel". SFT uses the exact same cross-entropy — it just adds masking. That's why we only need to add `ignore_index` to BluTrain's existing kernel, not write a new one.

**You're right that we already have everything.** BluTrain has its own CE kernel. We are **not** replacing it and **not** copying Liger's code — theirs is Triton/Python, ours is CUDA/C++. We read it only to see *how* they handle `ignore_index` and chunking. Reference, not source.

So the clone list is 4 references for 4 different questions:

| repo | the one question it answers |
|---|---|
| **pytorch_source** (already local) | how does a correct CUDA `ignore_index` kernel look? |
| **Megatron-LM** | where does the divide-by-n_valid go in a distributed trainer? |
| **Liger-Kernel** | how do you make that kernel fast? |
| **TRL** | what data format must we accept? |

## What `splitk_observe/` was

19 MB from 2026-08-01, untracked. The **split-K reconnaissance on cuBLAS**: 6 probe shapes profiled to find out when cuBLAS actually dispatches split-K, and what its reduce kernel does.

## Verdict: we did **not** need it — it was already documented well

§H27z.8 and §H27z.9 already hold every conclusion:

- the **retraction** of the b300 §62.3 "smoking gun" (skinny-N was the wrong shape set — the real trigger is small M·N + large K)
- the **gating rule**: split so `output_tiles × S ≈ SM count` (132) — explains all 6 shapes, no exceptions
- the **workspace formula** `M*N*4*S + 16`, confirmed on 4 points
- the **cost**: reduce is 22.5% of total on `256x256x16384` — not free
- split-K is a **modifier on an existing variant**, not a tile family

## I verified the documented SASS claims before deleting — both hold

| claim in §H27z.8 | re-measured today | |
|---|---|---|
| `ATOM/RED instrs = 0` | 0 | ✅ |
| `LDG/STG = 48` | LDG 38 + STG 10 = **48** | ✅ |

**My first recount said 39 and was wrong** — predicated lines like `@P0 LDG` parse as opcode `@P0`, so every predicated instruction gets dropped from the histogram. Stripping `@!?P\d+` first gives exactly 48. I wrote that trap into the doc, since it silently undercounts any SASS histogram.

## What I added before deleting

An addendum to §H27z.8 with the one thing not captured — the **full opcode histogram** of `splitKreduce_kernel`:

```
IMAD 67 · LDG 38 · LDC 37 · FADD 34 · BRA 31 · ISETP 28 · ULDC 27 · LEA 22 · FMUL 15 · IADD3 14
```

Plain load-add-store: 38 LDG + 10 STG + 34 FADD. No atomics, no shared memory, no tensor ops. The rest is address arithmetic. That's the exact numerics §H27z.9 locked our own reduce against.

Also recorded: **both probe shapes produce byte-identical histograms**, so cuBLAS uses *one* reduce kernel regardless of S. That's a new observation, not in the doc before.

Not transcribed: the per-instruction stall columns (400 rows × 64 columns), which only ever existed to establish the two claims above — now confirmed.

## Why `sassloop.sh` mattered

It measures SASS instruction counts for any `Sm90Config_*` **with zero GPU** — nvcc `-c`, `cuobjdump -sass | c++filt`, then a Python pass that finds the innermost backward-branch loops containing HGMMA (the consumer k-loop) and prints per-opcode histograms plus the uniform-datapath counts:

```
UMOV ULOP3 ULEA USHF UIMAD UIADD3 BRA BSSY BSYNC SEL R2UR S2UR PLOP3 HGMMA
```

That's the exact measurement behind the instruction-excess track — and it runs **without a box**, which is what makes it worth keeping now that the Verda boxes are gone. It was untracked and existed nowhere else; `blublas/tools/` has 100+ tracked scripts but not this one.

## One thing in it worth noting

Its opcode extractor does:

```python
re.sub(r'^@!?U?P\d+\s+', '', x.strip())
```

It **strips the predicate before taking the mnemonic**. That's the same bug that bit me earlier today on the splitk SASS recount — 39 instead of the correct 48, because `@P0 LDG` was being counted as opcode `@P0`. The script had it right back in August. Both the tool header and §H233 now say so.

Two separate things here, and mixing them up is the usual trap:

| **Authentication** | whether the **push/merge is allowed** | the PAT you push with |

**They're independent.** You can author commits as `goutham.kumar@blubridge.com` while authenticating with any token that has push rights. And merge-PR permission comes from **the account whose PAT does the push** — not from the email on the commit.

**Set the author email when you clone, before the first commit.** If you commit with the personal email and fix it afterwards, every existing commit is authored wrong, and correcting that needs `rebase`/`filter-branch` — history rewriting on a branch other people may have pulled. One command now avoids all of it.

The IDE login and git credentials are separate systems. From here I only see the git side: `GOUTHAM1926` (personal). Whether Antigravity is signed in as the blubridge account, I have no way to check — you'd need to look in its settings.

**The thing to confirm before you start:** do you have a **PAT issued from the `goutham.kumar@blubridge.com` account**? That's what actually gates merging. If you only have the personal PAT, you can clone, branch, commit and push — but the merge will be refused.

Commands to inspect your git config — all read-only, nothing changes.

## The quick check — what a commit would be authored as

```bash
git config user.email
```

Run inside a repo → gives the effective value there. Run outside any repo → gives the global one.

## See each level separately

```bash
git config --global --get user.email      # global  (~/.gitconfig)
git config --local  --get user.email      # this repo only (.git/config)
git config --system --get user.email      # machine-wide
```

**Local beats global.** So if `--local` prints something, that's what wins — which is why your two personal repos still commit as gmail even though global is now the company address.

## Where a value came from

```bash

git config --show-origin --get user.name
```

Prints the file path alongside the value. This is the one that settles "why is it this and not that".

### CLAUDE [2026-09-18 21:43 IST]

Because blublas has no submodule. BluTrain has one, and git does not pass the token from the parent URL into the submodule clone — it uses the plain URL from `.gitmodules`, which fails.

That's the only difference. Run these from the right folder:

```bash
cd ~/Downloads/sft_research
rm -rf BluTrain
git clone https://<REDACTED:github-token>@github.com/BlubridgeAI/BluTrain.git
cd ~/Downloads/sft_research/BluTrain
git submodule set-url Tensor-Implementations https://<REDACTED:github-token>@github.com/BlubridgeAI/Tensor-Implementations.git
git submodule update --init --recursive
```

## If you genuinely want one repo

There is a way, but it's destructive: **remove the submodule and fold the files in**.

```bash
cd ~/Downloads/sft_research/BluTrain
git rm --cached Tensor-Implementations
rm -rf .git/modules/Tensor-Implementations Tensor-Implementations/.git
rm .gitmodules

```

That's what you did once before with the old BluTrain — flattened it into your own repo.

**Don't do it here.** This is the production repo with 4 contributors. Flattening breaks it for everyone, and you could never merge back.

## The actual cost of two branches

```bash
git checkout -b sft_gautam                    # once, in BluTrain
cd Tensor-Implementations && git checkout -b sft_gautam    # once, in the submodule
```

Two commands at the start. Then you just edit files normally — no extra steps while working. Only at the end: commit in the submodule, push it, then commit in the parent.

It's one extra command now and one extra push later. That's the whole difference.

## The decision that gates everything

**`ignore_index` in-kernel vs `loss_mask` multiply.**

My recommendation, unchanged: **take both.** Megatron's semantics for correctness (mask + one global division), PyTorch's early-out for speed (masked rows skip the whole 50,304-wide softmax, so masking becomes a ~2× speedup instead of pure overhead). They're compatible — one decides correctness, the other performance.

## The 7 changes, once you decide

| # | file | change |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `LossKernels.cu:188` fwd | early-out on ignored rows; write `loss=0`, `saved_max=0`, **`saved_sum=1.0f`** (0 → `inf`, then `inf×0` = NaN) |
| 2 | `LossKernels.cu` reduce | accumulate `n_valid` in the same pass |
| 3 | `LossKernels.cu:635` bwd | zero the gradient row |
| 4 | `LossOps.cpp:349` | **stop dividing** — return `(sum_loss, n_valid)` |
| 5 | `LossBackward.cpp:213` | `host_scale = 1/N_global` |
| 6 | trainer + `dist` | accumulate S and N across 64 micro-batches, all-reduce, divide **once** |
| 7 | guard | `N == 0` |

Item 6 is the one that matters most — per-micro-batch division weights short completions ~10× heavier, and loss/curve/maxRelErr all look normal while it happens.

```
- url  = https://github.com/kathir-23s/BluBridge-BLAS      ← original (two spaces)
+ url = https://github.com/kathir-23s/BluBridge-BLAS.git   ← now (one space, added .git)
```

Two tiny differences: the original had `url  =` with two spaces, and no `.git` suffix.

## Nothing wrong was done

That came from the `git submodule set-url` command we ran to strip the token out. `set-url` rewrites `.gitmodules`, and when it rewrote the line it normalised the spacing and kept the `.git` suffix.

The URL points to the same repo either way. It's cosmetic.

## `git checkout .gitmodules` is not a branch

This is a genuinely confusing part of git — the same command means two different things:

| command | meaning |
|---|---|
| `git checkout sft_gautam` | argument is a **branch** → switch to it |
| `git checkout .gitmodules` | argument is a **file** → restore that file from the last commit |

The second one just discards local edits to that one file. It doesn't touch branches at all.

Modern git split these apart to stop the confusion:
```bash
git restore .gitmodules      # same thing, clearer name
```

## Do you even need to?

No. It's 2 characters of whitespace. Options:

**Leave it** — it changes nothing functionally. It'll just show as modified while you work.

**Or revert it** so your branch starts clean and the diff only shows your real SFT changes:
```bash
cd ~/Downloads/sft_research/BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations
git restore .gitmodules
```

I'd revert it — when you open the PR later, you want the diff to be only the loss-kernel changes, not an unrelated whitespace edit that makes a reviewer ask why.

Then the branch:
```bash
git checkout -b sft_gautam
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
```

## Why two kernels — and only in the *without-stats* path

The two-kernel split is **not** "reducing two ways". They do completely different jobs:

| kernel | job |
|---|---|
| `sparseCEReduce_kernel_optimized` | recompute per-row **max and sum** (online softmax), writing `d_partial_max` / `d_partial_sum` |
| `sparseCENormalize_kernel_optimized` | use those to compute the **actual gradient** |

It's split because it uses a **2D grid** — `grid_reduce{2, batch_size}` — so two blocks share one row. Two blocks can't sync with each other inside a kernel, so the partials have to be written out, the kernel has to end, and a second kernel reads them back. It also `cudaMalloc`s two scratch buffers and frees them after.

**And your with-stats version launches exactly ONE kernel:**

```cpp

    sparseCENormalize_from_stats<<<grid_norm, block, 0, stream>>>(...);
}
```

No Reduce pass. No scratch allocation. No second launch. That's precisely what saving `max`/`sum` in the forward bought you — the whole recompute stage disappears. I said "two kernels" earlier; that was wrong, my grep window had run past the end of the function into the next one.

Yes, exactly that. Option A.

## The signature

```cpp
__global__ void sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec_save_stats(
    const T* logits,
    const T_idx* targets,
    T* losses,
    float* saved_max,
    float* saved_sum,
    int64_t batch_size,
    int64_t vocab_size,
    bool    sft = false,          // NEW
    int64_t ignore_index = -1     // NEW
)
```

## The check inside

```cpp
if (row >= batch_size) return;

if (sft && static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index) {
    if (tid == 0) { losses[row] = T(0); saved_max[row] = 0.0f; saved_sum[row] = 1.0f; }
    return;
}
```

## Behaviour

| `sft` | what happens |
|---|---|
| **false** (default) | `sft && ...` short-circuits — the check costs one boolean test and never reads `targets[row]`. Pretraining runs exactly as today |
| **true** | prompt tokens (where `targets[row] == ignore_index`) get loss 0, zero gradient, and skip the whole 50,304-wide softmax |

## Why `bool` and not `#ifdef`

- One build serves both. No separate pretraining and SFT binaries.
- The flag comes from the trainer at runtime, so the same library handles a pretraining run and an SFT run.
- `= false` default means **every existing call site keeps compiling unchanged** — you only pass the new args where you want SFT. That keeps the diff small and makes it impossible to accidentally turn masking on.

## Why also `ignore_index` and not hardcode 65535

Hardcoding bakes an SFT decision into a shared kernel. As a parameter you can use `65535` for uint16 targets, `-100` to match PyTorch when targets are int32/int64, and it's visible at the call site instead of buried in the kernel.

That's the design. Shall I write the edit for kernel #1 (`sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec`, line 71) so you can apply it and check?

### CLAUDE [2026-09-19 12:01 IST]

Good catch — this is worth getting right. Let me check what type the targets actually are:
> tool `Bash`: Check target dtype and vocab size

Now the numbers make it clear.

## Why not `-100`

Your trainer uses **`UInt16`** targets (`UInt16ShardView` in the dataloader). `uint16` holds **0 to 65535** — it physically cannot store `-100`. Write `-100` into a uint16 and it becomes `65436`.

PyTorch's `-100` works because its targets are `int64`, which holds negatives. Ours aren't.

## What we use instead

```
vocab_size = 50304
uint16 range = 0 .. 65535
```

So **50304 → 65535 are values a real token can never be**. Pick `65535` — the top of the range, obviously not a token.

## What `-1` is doing as the default

It's a "never matches" guard, not the real value.

The comparison casts the target up to `int64_t`:

```cpp
static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index
```

A `uint16` target casts to `0 .. 65535` — **always non-negative**. So `-1` can never equal it. Even if someone passed `sft=true` and forgot to set `ignore_index`, nothing would ever be masked. It fails safe.

## The full picture

| target dtype | usable sentinel | why |
|---|---|---|
| **UInt16** (your trainer) | **65535** | outside vocab 50304, fits the type |
| Int32 / Int64 | `-100` | matches PyTorch, negatives fit |
| default `-1` | matches nothing | safe no-op if unset |

That's why it's a parameter and not hardcoded — the right value depends on the target dtype, and the call site knows which one it has.

```cpp
kernel<<<...>>>(logits, targets, losses, ..., false, -1);

// SFT with uint16 targets
kernel<<<...>>>(logits, targets, losses, ..., true, 65535);
```

### CLAUDE [2026-09-21 15:06 IST]

Plain explanation, no analogies.

## What `ignore_index` is

It's just a number. The kernel compares each target against it:

```cpp
if (sft && static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index) {
    // skip this row
}
```

That's the whole mechanism. "If the target for this row equals this number, skip the row."

## What the targets actually contain

Your targets are `uint16_t`. A `uint16_t` can hold **0 to 65535**. Nothing else. No negative numbers.

Your vocab is **50304**. So a real token id is somewhere in **0 to 50303**.

That leaves **50304 to 65535 unused** — no real token ever has those values. We pick **65535** from that unused range as the "this token is masked" marker.

## The cast

```cpp
static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row])
```

`targets[row]` is `uint16_t`, value 0–65535. Casting it to `int64_t` doesn't change the number — 65535 stays 65535, 42 stays 42. It's still **always 0 or greater**.

`ignore_index` is declared `int64_t` so the two sides are the same type and the comparison compiles cleanly for all three target types.

## Why the default is `-1`

`-1` is a number that **can never be produced** by that cast. The cast output is always 0 or higher, so `something >= 0 == -1` is always false.

So if the default is `-1`, the condition never fires. Nothing is ever masked.

That's the point. It's a "do nothing" default:

| situation | result |
|---|---|
| `sft = false` | condition short-circuits, never even reads `ignore_index` |
| `sft = true`, `ignore_index` forgotten (stays `-1`) | condition never matches → nothing masked → behaves like pretraining |
| `sft = true`, `ignore_index = 65535` | rows with target 65535 are masked |

The middle row is the reason. If the default were `0` instead, and someone enabled `sft` without setting `ignore_index`, every row whose target is token id 0 would get silently dropped from the loss. With `-1`, a mistake does nothing instead of doing something wrong.

## What gets passed in practice

```cpp
// pretraining
kernel<<<...>>>(logits, targets, losses, ..., /*sft=*/false, /*ignore_index=*/-1);

// SFT, uint16 targets
kernel<<<...>>>(logits, targets, losses, ..., /*sft=*/true,  /*ignore_index=*/65535);
```

`-1` is never the real working value. It exists only so the parameter has a harmless default.

## Why not just hardcode 65535 as the default

Because `65535` is only correct for `uint16` targets. With `int32`/`int64` targets you'd want `-100` to match PyTorch's convention. The parameter lets the caller pick; the `-1` default just means "nobody picked yet, so mask nothing."

### CLAUDE [2026-09-21 15:15 IST]

Because **-100 cannot be stored in your target array.** That's the whole reason.

## The physical problem

Your targets are `uint16_t`. That type holds **0 to 65535 only**. There is no way to put a negative number in it.

If the preprocessing script tries to write `-100` into a `uint16`, it wraps around:

```
-100  stored as uint16  →  65436
```

The byte pattern for -100 reinterpreted as unsigned is 65436. That's what would actually be sitting in the file.

## So what would happen

Kernel compares:

```cpp
static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index
//        65436                    ==   -100        → FALSE, always
```

The target reads back as **65436**, never as -100. The comparison never matches. **Nothing gets masked, silently.** Loss trains on prompt tokens and nothing errors.

## PyTorch can use -100 because its targets are int64

`int64` is **signed** — it holds negatives. So PyTorch writes a real `-100` into the tensor, and `-100 == -100` matches.

It's not that -100 is a magic universal value. It's that PyTorch's target dtype can physically store it, and ours can't.

## Your options

| approach | works? | cost |
|---|---|---|
| **`uint16` targets + sentinel `65535`** | ✅ | none — vocab is 50304, so 65535 is unused |
| `uint16` targets + `ignore_index = 65436` | ✅ technically | that IS -100 wrapped; confusing, no benefit |
| `uint16` targets + `ignore_index = -100` | ❌ **never matches** | silent no-op |
| change targets to `int32`, use `-100` | ✅ | dataloader rewrite, 2× target memory, conversion kernel |

## Why not make 65535 the default then

You could. The reason I'd keep the default as `-1`:

`65535` is only the right answer **when the targets are `uint16`**. The kernel also compiles for `int32` and `int64` targets, where `-100` would be the natural choice. A default of `65535` would be wrong for those — and worse, if someone used `int32` targets and a vocab above 65535, token id 65535 would be a **real token** that silently vanishes from the loss.

`-1` matches nothing in any of the three types. So the default never does damage, and the caller states the value that's correct for its dtype.

**What you'll actually use:** targets stay `uint16`, preprocessing writes `65535` for prompt tokens, trainer passes `ignore_index = 65535`. PyTorch's -100 convention doesn't apply here because the dtype is different.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-21 15:17 IST]

Sharp catch. They're in **two different places**.

| | type | can hold negatives? |
|---|---|---|
| `targets[row]` — **the data in the file** | `uint16_t` | ❌ no |
| `ignore_index` — **the function parameter** | `int64_t` | ✅ yes |

```cpp
if (sft && static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index)
//          └── from uint16 data: always 0..65535 ──┘    └── int64 param: -1 is fine ──┘
```

`-1` never goes into the target file. It only ever sits in the parameter, which is `int64_t` and holds negatives without any problem.

## And that's exactly why it works as the default

The left side is **always 0 or higher**. The right side is `-1`. They can never be equal. So the condition is always false → nothing is masked.

That's the behaviour I want from a default: harmless.

## So why does -100 fail, if -1 works?

The difference isn't the parameter — it's the **data**.

For `ignore_index = -100` to ever match, the target array would have to *contain* -100. But the array is `uint16`, so writing -100 stores 65436 instead. Then:

```
65436 == -100   →  false, forever
```

`-1` and `-100` behave identically as parameters: neither can ever match a uint16 target. The difference is that **-1 is meant to never match** — that's its job. **-100 is meant to match**, and it can't, so it's a silent bug.

## Summary

| value | where it lives | result |
|---|---|---|
| `-1` | parameter only | never matches → **nothing masked** → correct default |
| `-100` | parameter only, can't be in uint16 data | never matches → **nothing masked** → silent failure when you wanted masking |
| `65535` | parameter **and** written into the data | matches → **masking works** |

The rule: `ignore_index` must equal a value the target array can actually hold. `uint16` can hold 65535, cannot hold -100.

### CLAUDE [2026-09-21 15:21 IST]

From the beginning, with your actual numbers.

## 1. What the model produces

Your model reads text and predicts the next token. Text is split into **tokens** (word pieces). Your vocabulary has **50,304** of them, numbered `0` to `50303`.

For each position in the text, the model outputs **50,304 numbers** — one score per possible next token. These are called **logits**.

```
position 5, logits = [ 2.1, -0.4, 7.8, 0.3, ... ]   ← 50,304 numbers
                       tok0 tok1  tok2 tok3
```

Higher score = model thinks that token is more likely. Here token 2 scores highest (7.8).

Your batch is B=2, T=4096, so you have `2 × 4096 = 8192` positions. Logits are `[8192, 50304]` numbers — **412 million** per step.

## 2. What targets are

The **target** is the token that actually came next in the real text. One number per position.

```
targets = [ 2, 847, 15, 9021, ... ]   ← 8192 numbers, each 0..50303
```

Position 5's target is `2`, meaning "the real next token was token #2".

The model's job: make the logit at the target index the highest one.

## 3. What cross-entropy measures

It answers: **how wrong was the model here?**

Step one, turn logits into probabilities with **softmax**:

$$p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}$$

`z` is the logits. Exponentiate each, divide by the total, so they sum to 1.

```
logits  = [2.1, -0.4, 7.8, 0.3]
e^z     = [8.2,  0.7, 2441, 1.35]      sum = 2451
probs   = [0.003, 0.0003, 0.996, 0.0006]
```

Step two, the loss is the **negative log of the probability assigned to the correct token**:

$$L = -\log(p_{target})$$

If target is 2: `p = 0.996`, so `L = -log(0.996) = 0.004`. Tiny loss — model was right.

If target had been 1: `p = 0.0003`, so `L = -log(0.0003) = 8.1`. Big loss — model was badly wrong.

Training pushes this number down.

## 4. Why "sparse"

The general form of cross-entropy takes a full probability distribution as the label — 50,304 numbers per position, one-hot: all zeros except a single 1.

**Sparse** cross-entropy takes just the **index** instead. Rather than 50,304 numbers that are 50,303 zeros and one 1, you pass `2`.

That's the only difference. Same maths, and it saves storing 412 million mostly-zero numbers.

## 5. The formula the kernel actually uses

Writing out $-\log(p_{target})$:

$$L = -\log\frac{e^{z_{target}}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} = \log\left(\sum_j e^{z_j}\right) - z_{target}$$

There's a problem: `e^z` overflows. Your logits can reach 20 or 30, and `e^30` is huge; a few hundred of those in `float` overflows to infinity.

Fix — subtract the maximum first:

$$L = \log\left(\sum_j e^{z_j - m}\right) + m - z_{target}, \qquad m = \max_j z_j$$

Mathematically identical, but now the largest exponent is `e^0 = 1`, so nothing overflows.

That is **exactly** the last line of your forward kernel:

```cpp
float loss = logf(final_sum) + final_max - target_logit;
//           └─ log(Σ e^(z−m)) ─┘   └─ m ─┘   └─ z_target ─┘
```

## 6. What the kernel does, step by step

One **block** of 512 threads handles one row (one position). 8192 blocks total.

**Step 1 — find max and sum together.** Each thread walks part of the 50,304 values, keeping a running `local_max` and `local_sum`. When it meets a value bigger than the current max, it rescales the sum it has so far:

```cpp
if (val > local_max) {
    local_sum = local_sum * expf(local_max - val) + 1.0f;   // rescale to new max
    local_max = val;
} else {
    local_sum += expf(val - local_max);
}
```

This is **online softmax** — one pass instead of two (one to find max, one to sum).

**Step 2 — combine the threads.** Tree reduction in shared memory, halving each round: 512 → 256 → 128 → … → 1. Same rescaling rule when merging two partial (max, sum) pairs.

**Step 3 — thread 0 writes the answer:**

```cpp
saved_max[row] = final_max;
saved_sum[row] = final_sum;
float loss = logf(final_sum) + final_max - target_logit;
losses[row] = loss;
```

**Step 4 —** a second kernel sums all 8192 row-losses into one number, then it's divided by 8192 to give the mean.

## 7. Why `saved_max` and `saved_sum` exist

The **backward** pass needs the gradient — how much to nudge each of the 50,304 logits. For cross-entropy it's:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i} = p_i - [i = target]$$

"Predicted probability, minus 1 if this is the correct token."

But computing `p_i` needs `max` and `sum` again. Recomputing means another full 50,304-wide pass.

So your forward **saves** them. Backward reads them straight off:

```cpp
const float final_max = saved_max[row];
const float inv_sum   = 1.0f / saved_sum[row];
out_grad.x = (expf(vec.x - final_max) * inv_sum - (col == target ? 1.0f : 0.0f)) * f_scale;
//            └──────── p_i ────────────────┘    └──── minus 1 if target ────┘
```

That's why there are two versions of everything: the **with-stats** pair (forward saves, backward reuses) and the **without-stats** pair (backward recomputes with its own Reduce kernel).

## 8. Now — what SFT changes

In pretraining, every position is a real prediction, so every one contributes to the loss.

In SFT the text is a conversation:

```
User: What is 2+2?     ← the prompt
Assistant: It is 4.    ← the answer
```

You only want the model trained on producing **the answer**. It shouldn't be learning to generate the user's question. So the prompt positions must be **excluded from the loss**.

Excluded means: loss 0, gradient 0, and not counted in the average.

## 9. How you mark a position as excluded

The target array holds one number per position. You need a value meaning "skip this one".

Your targets are `uint16` — that type holds **0 to 65535 only, no negatives**.

```
0     .. 50303   real token ids
50304 .. 65535   unused
```

So pick **65535** from the unused range. Preprocessing writes 65535 at every prompt position.

```
targets = [65535, 65535, 65535, 847, 15, 9021]
           └── prompt, skip ──┘  └─ answer, train ─┘
```

The kernel then checks:

```cpp
if (sft && targets[row] == ignore_index) {   // ignore_index = 65535
    losses[row] = 0;
    return;                                   // skips the whole 50,304-wide pass
}
```

## 10. Why not -100

PyTorch uses `-100` for this. PyTorch's targets are `int64`, which **is signed** and stores -100 fine.

Yours are `uint16`. Writing -100 into a `uint16` stores **65436** instead — the bit pattern reinterpreted as unsigned. Then the check `65436 == -100` is false, always. Nothing gets masked, and nothing errors.

-100 isn't a universal constant. It works in PyTorch because the dtype can hold it.

## 11. Why the default is -1

`ignore_index` is a **function parameter** of type `int64_t` — it can hold negatives. The **target data** is `uint16` — it cannot. Two different things.

```cpp
static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index
//   always 0..65535                    -1 by default
```

Left side can never be negative. Right side is -1. They never match → nothing masked.

That's deliberate: if someone turns on `sft` but forgets to set `ignore_index`, the result is **pretraining behaviour**, not wrongly-masked data. A mistake does nothing instead of something wrong.

`-1` is never the working value. You pass `65535` when you mean it.

## Now — `ignore_index = -1`

**There are two separate places. That's the whole thing.**

**Place 1 — the data in the file.** Your targets are `uint16`. That type stores **0 to 65535**. It has no way to represent a negative number. Not "shouldn't" — *cannot*.

**Place 2 — the function parameter.** You just wrote it yourself:

```cpp
int64_t ignore_index = -1
```

`int64_t` is **signed**. It holds negatives perfectly fine. `-1` lives here, never in the file.

**The comparison joins them:**

```cpp
static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index
//         ↑                                ↑
//  from uint16 data:               the parameter:
//  always 0 to 65535               currently -1
```

Left side can never be negative. Right side is -1. **They can never be equal.** So with the default, nothing is ever masked.

**That is the purpose.** It's a "do nothing" default:

| | result |
|---|---|
| `sft=false` | check short-circuits, never runs |
| `sft=true`, forgot to set `ignore_index` | nothing matches → behaves like pretraining |
| `sft=true`, `ignore_index=65535` | masking works |

Row 2 is why it's `-1`. A mistake produces **normal training**, not silently-wrong training.

**Why `-100` doesn't work here:** for -100 to match, the *file* would need to contain -100. Writing -100 into `uint16` stores **65436** instead. Then `65436 == -100` is false forever — masking silently does nothing. PyTorch gets away with -100 because its targets are `int64`, which can hold it.

**Why not default to `65535`:** 65535 is only correct for `uint16` targets. This kernel also compiles for `int32` and `int64`, where a vocab above 65535 would make 65535 a **real token** that silently disappears from the loss. `-1` is safe in all three.

**What you actually pass:** `65535`. `-1` is never the working value.

**1. Index layout — matches.** Reduce writes `d_partial[xbid + row*2]` → slots `2r, 2r+1`. Normalize reads `d_partial[row*2 + i]` → same slots. ✓

**2. Both blocks must write.** With `grid_reduce{2, batch_size}`, each row has two blocks. Each computes its own `bid`, so each writes its own slot naturally — the early-out handles this correctly with no special casing. ✓

**3. Sentinel arithmetic — I traced the merge by hand.** Two partials of `(max=0, sum=1)` through the loop at 723–733:

```
i=0:  p_max=0 > g_max=-1e38  →  g_sum = 0*exp(...) + 1 = 1,  g_max = 0
i=1:  p_max=0 > g_max=0? NO   →  g_sum += 1*exp(0-0) = 2
final_sum = 2  →  inv_sum = 0.5    finite ✓
```

With `sum = 0.0f` instead: `g_sum` stays 0 → `inv_sum = 1/0 = inf` → gradient becomes inf/NaN. **So 1.0f is mandatory here too.**

**4. `grad` is never written by Reduce** — 0 occurrences. It's an unused parameter. Reduce only produces stats, so no gradient safety concern here.

**5. `targets` is currently never read by Reduce** — only in the signature. Our check adds the first real read of it. Fine, but it means the `sft &&` short-circuit genuinely costs zero on the pretraining path.

In kernels #1 and #2:

Your early-outs in #1 and #2 `return` before this line, so masked rows never reach it. **That makes the forward early-out a correctness requirement, not just an optimisation.** Worth knowing: if anyone ever removes it as "just a speedup", they reintroduce an OOB read.

Kernel #4 is safe by luck — it only *compares* `col == target_idx`, never indexes with it, and 65535 simply never matches.

## What this means for our edit

It changes how I'd write the zeroing. If I zero via the `float4` path and someone ever instantiates with bf16, we'd write `vocab*4` bytes into a `vocab*2`-byte row — an out-of-bounds **write**, far worse than the existing read issue.

So the zeroing loop uses **plain `T`**, not `float4`:

```cpp
for (int64_t c = tid; c < vocab_size; c += bdim)
    row_grad[c] = static_cast<T>(0);
```

Correct for every `T`, no aliasing assumption, still fully coalesced.

## Kernel #5 — the edit

**Signature, line 661:**
```cpp
    const T *grad_output, float host_scale,
    bool sft = false,          // SFT: enable label masking
    int64_t ignore_index = -1  // SFT: target value meaning "skip this row"

```

**After line 666:**
```cpp
  const int row = blockIdx.x;
  if (row >= batch_size)
    return;

  // SFT label masking: an ignored row must receive a ZERO gradient. This is a
  // CORRECTNESS requirement, not an optimisation — without it the model trains
  // on prompt tokens.
  // Zero with a plain T loop, NOT the float4 path below: that path assumes
  // sizeof(T)==4, and this kernel is also instantiated for float16/bfloat16
  // where a float4 write would run 2x past the end of the row.
  if (sft && static_cast<int64_t>(targets[row]) == ignore_index) {
    T *row_grad_z = grad + row * vocab_size;
    for (int64_t c = tid; c < vocab_size; c += bdim)
      row_grad_z[c] = static_cast<T>(0);
    return;
  }

  const T *row_logits = logits + row * vocab_size;
```

## Why this one differs from #1–#3

| | |
|---|---|
| **no `tid == 0` guard** | all 256 threads participate — each zeroes its own strided slice. #1–#3 wrote a single scalar, so only thread 0 acted |
| **`return` still outside** | every thread reaches it after its loop; no `__syncthreads()` is skipped |
| **declares its own pointer** | `row_grad` isn't defined until line 669, after our insert point |
| **writes, doesn't skip** | #1–#3 could just return; here the gradient buffer is uninitialised allocator memory, so leaving it untouched feeds garbage into the backward pass |

That last point is the one to be careful about: `grad` comes from `CachingCUDAAllocator`, which does **not** zero. Skipping the row without writing would leave whatever the previous allocation left there.

## The rule that governs this

In C++, a default argument may be written **exactly once** across a declaration and its definition. So:

- **header** → gets `= false` / `= -1`
- **`.cu` definition** → same params, **no defaults**
- **instantiation macro** → the type list must match the new signature, or it won't link

Get that wrong and you get either *"default argument given twice"* or an undefined-symbol at link time.

Threading two extra params through 4 wrappers × 3 places = 12 careful edits, and every one is a chance to mismatch a signature.

Then each wrapper takes one `SftMask mask = {}` instead of two params. Same behaviour, but the signature grows by one type rather than two, and adding anything later (say `label_smoothing`) costs zero further signature churn.
