first , a small background , so d1 , d2 , d3 and f4 make sense ,,, ,
--- fp32 stores a number in 4 bytes and keeps about 7 digits , bf16 stores it in 2 bytes and keeps only about 3 digits , near 1.0 bf16 can only hold 1.0 , 1.0078125 , 1.015625 and so on (a gap of 0.0078125) ,,, ,
--- whenever a result has to be stored in bf16 , the gpu stores the nearest bf16 number , that is a rounding , and anything smaller than half the gap simply disappears , for example 1.0 + 0.003 stored in bf16 stays 1.0 ,,, ,
--- one rounding at the end of a sum changes the result by at most 0.39% , but rounding after every single add keeps losing the small values , and that loss piles up ,,, ,

1) how the embedding tensor [50304,2304] is used in one micro-step :-

what i traced :
--- with weight tying the embedding tensor is used 2 times , first at the very start as a lookup (each of the 8 x 4096 = 32768 positions copies the row of its token , a pure copy , nothing is multiplied) , and at the very end as the lm_head matmul (hidden states [32768 x 2304] x embedding transposed [2304 x 50304] = the logits) ,,, ,
--- the same token gives the exact same numbers only until rope and attention , after that every position is different , so every repeat of a token later brings a different gradient vector ,,, ,
--- in backward the embedding gets 2 gradients , the lm_head part (every one of the 50304 rows gets a value) and the lookup part (only the tokens present in the batch , a token seen 300 times gets the sum of its 300 position vectors) , these 2 are added , the sum goes into an fp32 gradient buffer every micro-step , and the optimizer updates the table once per step ,,, ,
--- at every update every row of the table changes , not only the tokens in the batch , because of the lm_head part , weight decay and adam momentum , and muon never updates the embedding , it is always updated by adamw ,,, ,

2) fp32 vs bf16 initialization of the embedding ---> d1 , d2 , d3 :-

what i found :
--- the forward is almost the same in both cases , the lookup only copies rows , the lm_head always uses a bf16 copy of the table , and with a bf16 residual the rows become bf16 right after the lookup anyway ,,, ,
--- the whole difference is in the backward of the embedding gradient , in 3 places , d1 = summing the repeated tokens (lookup backward) , d2 = adding the lookup part and the lm_head part , d3 = the path from the micro-steps to the optimizer and to other gpus ,,, ,
--- on our sft branch (dist_side_merge) the bf16 sum at d1 uses atomic adds , so every repeat of a token rounds the running total again , in a random order , for example 1.0 + 0.003 + 0.003 + 0.003 should be 1.009 but in bf16 it comes out 1.0 or 1.0078125 depending on the order , so frequent tokens (like "the" , the chat template tokens and eot in sft data) lose the most , and the result changes from run to run ,,, ,
--- on dist_side_merge_bluccl the colleagues' new fused embedding kernel (sort by token , add everything in fp32 , write once) removes that repetition problem , but it runs only with the fused trainer and bluccl_fused_emb=1 ,,, ,
--- the bf16_reduce flag brings back 2 roundings per step even with an fp32 embedding ,,, ,
--- a bf16 embedding saves half the table memory (231.8 mb instead of 463.6 mb) and one extra bf16 copy of the table for the lm_head every micro-step , the optimizer keeps an fp32 master copy in both cases ,,, ,

| place in the embedding gradient | fp32 embedding | bf16 embedding |
|---|---|---|
| d1 , sum of repeated tokens | fp32 , no rounding | 1 rounding per micro-step (bluccl fused kernel) , 1 rounding per repeat with atomic add (dist_side_merge) |
| d2 , lookup part + lm_head part | fp32 , no rounding | 1 rounding per micro-step |
| micro-step gradient buffer | fp32 | fp32 |
| d3 , send to other gpus | fp32 , no rounding | 1 rounding per step |
| d3 , switch result (8 gpus) | fp32 , no rounding | 1 rounding per step (the switch adds in fp32 but returns bf16) |
| total | 0 roundings to bf16 | 2 per micro-step + 2 per step |

--- the real size of these roundings on real data is the next measurement , it decides whether sft keeps a bf16 embedding ,,, ,

3) f4 bug ---> the 1-gpu bf16 round trip in all 3 zero-1 optimizers :-

the concept :
--- zero-1 keeps a send buffer to exchange the gradients between gpus , for a bf16 model that buffer is bf16 , to halve the bytes sent ,,, ,

the mistake :
--- at 1 gpu nothing is sent anywhere , but adamw v1 , adamw v2 and muon still turned the full fp32 gradient into bf16 and back into fp32 before the gradient norm and the update , so every step every bf16 weight's gradient was rounded for nothing (up to 0.39% per number) ,,, ,

the fix :
--- at 1 gpu the fp32 gradient now goes straight to the optimizer , the 2 conversions are removed (and 1 extra copy in adamw v1) , the multi-gpu path is not touched at all , it is built on top of the latest in-place change on that branch (which had already removed the plain copy for v2 and muon) , and the send-dtype flags have no effect at 1 gpu , a note is printed if they are set ,,, ,

Saved. Now your question. Checking in the code what "fused" refers to, both in the kernel file and in the trainer:
> tool `Bash`: Find what the fused trainer fuses

**"Fused" means several steps done together in ONE GPU program (one kernel launch), instead of one program per step.** Normally each step is its own kernel: it writes its result to GPU memory, and the next kernel reads it back. When they're fused, the data stays on the chip in between. That means fewer launches and less memory traffic. The math is the same.

## 1. Kruthik's "fused embedding kernel" (`embedding_fused.cu`)
- The file's header says it has 2 paths:
  - **UNFUSED:** the embedding backward alone, as 3 phases plus the sort.
  - **FUSED:** "embedding backward + reduce-scatter in one cooperative launch". That is, the embedding backward **and** the sending of its gradient to the other GPUs in the same launch (`embedding_bwd_rs_rowsliced` / `_featuresliced`).
- **But what actually runs in training is the unfused path.** The hook calls `run()` (`:1305-1318`), and `run()` launches `embedding_bwd_launch_unfused` (`:1211-1225`): the CUB sort, then `bounded_direct` / `chunks` / `fold`. The 2 fused kernels are never called by the hook.
- So the "fused" in the name comes from the file and the flag (`BLUCCL_FUSED_EMB`). What really runs is **Kruthik's new sort-based embedding backward**: sort by token, add in fp32, write once. For the EOD, "kruthik's new sort-based embedding kernel" is the more exact wording.

## 2. The "fused trainer" (`bluscript_zero_ckpt_bluccl_fused.cpp`)
- It's the BluCCL trainer plus the **"tail fusions"**: steps at the end of each optimizer step, combined into single kernels. It switches on:
  1. the embedding backward hook above (`install_fused_embedding_backward`, `:1154`, with `BLUCCL_FUSED_EMB=1`);
  2. `BLU_FUSED_ADAMW`: the AdamW update **and** sending the new weights to the other GPUs (all-gather) in one kernel. Its comment (`:1158`): "The OTHER half of the tail fusion, AdamW + AllGather";
  3. `BLU_FUSED_CLIP_ADAMW` (gradient clip + AdamW + all-gather) and `BLU_FUSED_MUON_PUBLISH` (Muon's update + cast + publish).
- The plain BluCCL trainer, `bluscript_zero_ckpt_bluccl.cpp`, has **none** of these flags (checked with grep).
- 2 limits, from its own comments and code:
  - The fused AdamW kernel is **fp32-only**, so under `BLU_ALL_BF16=1` the big AdamW group declines it (`:1165-1170`).
  - The fusions that include sending need a BluCCL process group, so more than 1 GPU. Only the embedding hook works at 1 GPU too, because it sends nothing.
